t.yateras@20.4,-75.0:
Yateras is coffee country in the hills of Guantánamo province, at the far eastern end of Cuba, and getting here feels like leaving the island most visitors know. The municipality climbs from the dry lowlands around Guantánamo city into green, steep mountains, part of the great Nipe-Sagua-Baracoa range that runs along the north-east of the island. The main settlement, Palenque, sits in its folds, and the small town of Río Guayabal de Yateras lies a few kilometres from these coordinates.

The landscape is the story. Rivers have cut deep valleys into old rock, and the slopes are planted with coffee and cacao under shade trees, with royal palms standing above the canopy and bunches of plantain hanging by the houses. In the wet months clouds sit on the ridges for days, and in the mornings the valleys are full of mist that burns off as the sun climbs. Birdsong is everywhere, including the tocororo, Cuba's national bird, whose red, white and blue plumage echoes the flag.

There is a human story here that few people know. The communities of Yateras, around La Ranchería and Caridad de los Indios, include families who trace their descent to the indigenous peoples of Cuba, and they have kept elements of that heritage alive in their farming, their crafts and their memories, long after the history books declared the original islanders extinct. Approach with curiosity and respect, and local people may share some of it.

Be realistic about the riding. The roads up from Guantánamo are narrow, steep and frequently broken, with potholes, washouts after storms, loose gravel and long sections where the tarmac simply gives up. Horses, ox carts and trucks converted into buses share the road, and you will be stopping often anyway for the views. This is ground for a light, robust bike with good suspension, not for a heavy tourer.

Fuel is the great Cuban question. Supply is unreliable across the country, stations in small towns can be dry for days, and foreign riders should fill up in Guantánamo whenever there is the chance and carry a reserve. The same goes for water and some food: there are small shops and paladares in the larger settlements, but nothing to count on. The dry season, roughly November to April, is the time to come, when the roads are firmer and the mountain air is fresh enough to make you forget how hot it was down on the coast.
t.alejandro de humboldt national park@20.5:
Alejandro de Humboldt National Park is generally considered the richest patch of nature in the whole Caribbean, and on a bike you approach it the hard way, through mining country and over some of the worst roads in Cuba. The park covers a huge block of mountains and rainforest in the far east of the island, between the nickel town of Moa and Baracoa, and runs down to the coast at Bahía de Taco, where a small visitor station organises guided walks and boat trips into the mangroves.

The secret is in the soil. Much of the park sits on serpentine and other ultramafic rocks, laden with metals and poor in nutrients, which is exactly why the same hills are mined for nickel around Moa. Plants that manage to grow on such ground have had to adapt, and isolation over a very long time has produced an astonishing number of species found nowhere else. Botanists still turn up new ones. UNESCO listed the park in 2001 and named it after the German naturalist who travelled through Cuba in 1800 and 1801 and wrote extensively about the island.

Animals are mostly small and shy. The almiquí, a strange, long-snouted insectivore called the Cuban solenodon, lives here; so do tiny frogs, colourful land snails and the Cuban parrot. The ivory-billed woodpecker was last reliably reported in these mountains in the 1980s, and naturalists still dream of a sighting. The guided trails lead to waterfalls and river pools that are as good as any reward after the ride in.

The ride in deserves its own warning. The coastal road between Moa and Baracoa is notorious, with stretches of rubble, deep potholes and sections washed out by the heavy rain that falls here throughout the year. Expect to stand on the pegs, expect trucks, and allow far more time than the map suggests. The red earth turns to grease when wet. Further inland, the area around Río Guayabal de Yateras offers another approach through coffee hills, no easier but with fine views.

Fuel is scarce and supply uncertain across Cuba, so fill up in Moa or Baracoa when you can and carry spare. Baracoa, the oldest Spanish settlement on the island, is the better base: a small, friendly town with cocoa and coconut in its cooking and El Yunque, a flat-topped mountain, standing guard behind it. Bring rain gear in any season and something warm for evenings in the hills.
t.al asfar lake@25.5,49.8:
The Al-Ahsa oasis in eastern Saudi Arabia is a green island in a very large desert. Under the sand lie huge aquifers, and springs rise to the surface to feed an area of about eighty-five square kilometres of date palms, said to be the largest oasis in the world, with perhaps two and a half million trees. It lies not far from the Gulf coast, near the city of Hofuf, and it has been settled for thousands of years, from the Bronze Age through the ancient Dilmun culture and into Islamic times. UNESCO listed it in 2018 as an evolving cultural landscape.

Al-Asfar Lake, the Yellow Lake, lies on the edge of the oasis, a shallow stretch of water that in part collects the drainage from the irrigation system, surrounded by reeds, dunes and a ring of low hills. It looks quiet, almost lonely, with flamingos and herons among the reeds, and changes colour with the light. The label also includes Jawatha, a mosque said to be one of the first in the Gulf region, where tradition holds that Friday prayers were held soon after the Prophet's time, and Al-Oyun village, a settlement named after its springs.

Riding in Saudi Arabia is a matter of heat and distance. The roads are modern and well-surfaced, with long, straight highways through desert and wide dual carriageways around towns. Summer temperatures easily climb above forty-five degrees, which is dangerous to ride in, so the time to visit is from November to March. Mornings and evenings are the best times, when the sun is low and the oasis glows green against the sand. Foreign riders should check the rules on licences, permits and insurance, because they are strict and subject to change.

The oasis is full of small roads between walls of mud brick, with palm groves and irrigation channels, and the shade is welcome. Al Markaz, the nearest town, has a few shops, and Hofuf, the main city, has fuel, hotels and restaurants. The date is the heart of local life, and shops sell many varieties, along with Arabic coffee flavoured with cardamom. Bring water and sun protection, and accept the hospitality, which is generous.
t.ain qinas archaeological site@25.6,49.6:
Ain Qinas is a spring, one of many that bubble up through the oasis of Al-Ahsa, and it is one of the reasons for the place's long life. The water emerges warm from deep rock, at a steady temperature, and has been channelled for centuries into stone-lined pools and a network of canals that irrigate the groves. For people crossing an arid peninsula, this must have seemed like a miracle, and the springs and their surroundings are part of the oasis's World Heritage listing. The site is a pleasant, shaded corner where palm trees lean over the water and the sound of running water is constant.

The wider area has a layered history. The oasis was a trading centre in the ancient world, and it was home in the tenth century to the Qarmatians, a radical Islamic sect who set up their own state here, built a capital and, in 930, famously raided Mecca and carried off the Black Stone, which they held for twenty years before returning it. Later, the Ottomans and the Al Saud family each held it in turn. Nearby Qasr Sahood, a mud-brick fort of a type typical of the region, is part of the story, with thick walls, a watchtower and an old gate.

For a rider, the contrast between the green oasis and the empty desert is the whole point. The roads leading in from the highways are good, and in the oasis they twist among palm groves and farms. Dust storms, called shamal, blow from the north-west, sometimes in summer, and visibility can fall sharply. As with all of the Gulf, the summer heat makes midday riding inadvisable, and a winter trip is much more comfortable. Rules on foreign riders in Saudi Arabia are strict and vary, so check them before you plan.

Julayjilah and Al Qurayn are the nearest towns, with shops and basic fuel stations, and Hofuf has all the services. Sit with a small cup of cardamom coffee and a handful of dates, and take in the quiet. Drink plenty of water, wear a hat and respect local customs, including modest dress and avoiding photographs of people without their permission.
t.jawatha mosque@25.5,49.7:
Al-Ahsa is an oasis the size of a small country, and everything about it feels improbable. The eastern province of Saudi Arabia is mostly sand and flat gravel, yet here several million date palms stand in green groves watered by natural springs that rise from deep aquifers. The oasis is on the UNESCO list for exactly this reason: people have farmed here for thousands of years, and the system of canals and gardens is still working. Jawatha Mosque is part of that story, an old mud-brick building in a village among the groves, near the shore of Al-Asfar Lake.

Local tradition holds that this is one of the earliest mosques outside the Arabian west, tied to the early days of Islam, when the people of the area converted in the seventh century. Historians treat precise claims with caution, and the building you see has been rebuilt and restored over the centuries, so take the dates as tradition rather than as a record. What you can say with confidence is that the mosque is old, the architecture is simple and shaped for the heat, and that it makes a striking sight against the palms.

Riding here means flat roads, lots of date farms and steady traffic in the towns of Al Qarah, Al Battaliyah and Al Qurayn, all within a few kilometres. The best months are November to March, when the days are warm rather than punishing. In summer the temperature goes far above forty degrees, and a ride after sunrise or at dusk is the only comfortable option. Dust storms can reduce visibility sharply in spring, and sand can drift across the road at the edges of the groves, so slow down on the transitions between farmland and desert.

Fuel is not a concern, as there are stations on every main road, and the market town of Hofuf is the usual base for food and shops. Check local customs: dress modestly, do not enter a mosque unless invited or clearly open to visitors, and avoid photographing people without asking. Dates are the local specialty, from fresh khalas to the sticky dried varieties, and a cup of Arabic coffee with dates is the traditional welcome. Al-Asfar Lake itself is shallow, shaped by drainage from the farmland, and its edge is a place for birdwatchers in the cooler months.
t.northern oasis@25.5,49.6:
The northern edge of the Al-Ahsa oasis is where the groves thin out and you can see the join between farmland and desert. Al Qurayn, a town of about 12,000 people, lies right next to this point, with Julayjilah and Al Mutayrifi close behind, and the whole cluster is one continuous patchwork of date gardens, walls, irrigation channels and low flat-roofed houses. The label talks about a northern oasis, and from the ground the point is simply that the green does not stop abruptly: it frays into scrub, then dunes.

Two sights are tied into this stretch. Qasr Khuzam is a fortress-like palace in Hofuf, the oasis's main town, long associated with the rulers and governors of the province, and it is one of the more recognisable historic buildings in the region. Al-Oyun, the village whose name means the springs, belongs to the same landscape and recalls the abundance of water that made the oasis. Locals have used these springs for as long as anyone can say, and some of them are now lined and used for swimming and farming.

The riding is flat, hot and straightforward. Roads between the farms are narrow, with speed bumps near villages and the odd tractor or truck loaded with dates, and the main arteries are wide and fast. The best light is early in the morning, when the palms look dark green and the air still smells of damp soil. Summer afternoons are extreme, with temperatures that can top 45 degrees, so plan your stops around shade and carry water, not just for you but for the bike's cooling system if you are idling in traffic.

Fuel and food are easy to find, with stations on the main roads and plenty of shops and cafés in Al Qurayn and Hofuf. The old covered markets of Hofuf, with their rows of stalls selling spices, dates, brass and bisht cloaks, are the best place to browse if you have time to stop. Keep to conservative dress in town, ask permission before taking photographs of people, and remember that Friday midday is prayer time, when many shops close. The oasis is also known for its traditional pottery and weaving, and rice and lamb dishes are the usual fare at a sit-down meal.
t.te anau@-45.4,167.7:
Te Anau is the last proper town before Fiordland, and nearly everything about it is a preparation for the wild country beyond. It sits on the eastern shore of the lake of the same name, the biggest lake in the South Island, with the Kepler and Murchison mountains rising on the far side, and about two thousand people live here, serving the hikers, boaters and bus tours that pass through. Maori knew the area as a source of greenstone and a place to hunt weka and eel. In 1948 a doctor named Geoffrey Orbell found a small population of takahe, a large flightless bird thought extinct for fifty years, in a remote valley in the Murchison Mountains across the water, one of the great wildlife stories of New Zealand.

For riders the town is the hinge between two famous roads. The Southern Scenic Route runs in from the south through sheep country and tussock, while the Milford Road, State Highway 94, heads north-west for about a hundred and twenty kilometres to Milford Sound. That road is one of the world's great drives, running through beech forest, the open glacial valley of the Eglinton, the Mirror Lakes and finally up to the Homer Tunnel, a rough rock bore of more than a kilometre that drops steeply out of the mountains on the far side. In winter and spring, avalanches can close the road, and chains may be required.

The most important practical point is fuel. Te Anau has petrol stations, and there are none along the Milford Road, so fill up here before you go, and again on the way back. Food, supplies and accommodation are plentiful in town, but summer demand is heavy, so book ahead. The weather is the other consideration. Fiordland is among the wettest places on earth, and rain can arrive within minutes and last for days, though the waterfalls it creates are spectacular. Sandflies are fierce at the roadside stops, so carry repellent.

There are glowworm caves across the lake, reached by boat, and walking tracks start close to town, including the first section of the Kepler. The best riding months are December to March, with long evenings, but even then pack a proper waterproof and warm layers.
t.as seef@25.4,49.6:
Al-Ahsa is the biggest natural oasis on the planet, and it looks like a mistake in the middle of the Eastern Province: a dark green carpet of date palms, millions of them, spread across a flat plain of pale desert. The oasis exists because springs rise from deep underground and water the whole area. Hofuf, the main city, and Mubarraz, its neighbour, sit within the palms, and the two together hold close to six hundred thousand people. UNESCO listed the oasis in 2018.

People have lived here for thousands of years. The springs made it a stop on trade routes between the Gulf coast, central Arabia and Mesopotamia, and over the centuries different powers fought over it, among them the Ottomans, who left a fortress in Hofuf. The Qaisariyah market, with its covered lanes, sells spices, dates, brass and gold, and the old Jawatha mosque is said to be among the earliest mosques in the eastern part of the Arabian Peninsula. The oasis is also known for its sheep, its woven bisht cloaks and its dates, which come in dozens of varieties and are served with coffee in every house.

Al-Oyun means the springs, and the village that bears the name sits in the northern part of the oasis, close to Lake Al-Asfar, a shallow lake that fills in winter and draws flamingos and other water birds. In the palm groves, channels carry water in a pattern that is centuries old, and walking beside them in the shade is a cool contrast to the heat outside. The smell of wet earth and date fronds is surprisingly strong.

For the rider this is long, straight highway riding with very little elevation. The roads are good, the speed limits are enforced by cameras, and the traffic can be fast and unpredictable. Summer heat is severe, with temperatures well above forty degrees, so go in winter, from November to March, or at dawn and dusk. Fuel is cheap and easy in Hofuf and Mubarraz, and the cafes are plentiful, with strong coffee and dates. Be aware that riding rules and dress customs are different from Europe, and that riders should check the current local regulations before travelling.
t.qasr ibrahim@25.4,49.6:
Hofuf is the main town of Al-Ahsa, in eastern Saudi Arabia, and Al-Ahsa is not what you picture when you think of the Arabian desert. It is a vast oasis, one of the largest in the world, with some two and a half million date palms fed by natural springs that rise from deep aquifers and flow through channels and canals. The green of the palms against the sand around it is striking, and UNESCO listed the oasis in 2018 as a cultural landscape that has been inhabited since the Neolithic era.

Qasr Ibrahim is an old fortress and palace in the middle of Hofuf, a thick-walled complex of mud brick and stone from the Ottoman era, with a mosque, a tall tower and barracks. It served as a garrison, a governor's seat and later a centre of regional power, and its position beside the springs and caravan routes was strategic. Close by, the Suq al-Qaysariyah is a covered market of arched passages where traders have sold spices, textiles, copper goods and traditional robes for generations.

Al-Asfar Lake, on the edge of the oasis, is a body of water with a different story. It is fed by the drainage from irrigated farmland, and in winter it attracts flocks of migratory birds, including flamingos, which stop on their journey between Africa and Asia. To the south of town, Jebel Qarah is a sandstone hill pierced with cool caves that have been a popular escape from the summer heat for generations, and the rock is carved by wind into strange shapes.

Roads around Hofuf are wide and fast, with long straight dual carriageways and roundabouts, and traffic is heavy and sometimes aggressive in town. Summer heat is severe, often above forty-five degrees, so ride early or in the evening, and winter is pleasant. Hofuf and neighbouring Al Mubarraz are big cities with plenty of fuel stations, workshops, hotels and restaurants. Try local dates, which are famous across the kingdom, with Arabic coffee. Dress modestly and check entry rules and visa requirements for riding in Saudi Arabia before you travel.
t.segment q omer moqo nicasio@-15.1,-70.3:
Lampa, twenty-four kilometres away, is known in Peru as the Pink City, and it gives you a place to orient this high, windswept stretch of the altiplano north of Lake Titicaca. The Inca road passed through this country as part of the Qhapaq Ñan, tying Cusco to the Collao plateau, and the segment from Q'omer Moqo, a name that means something like green hillock in Quechua, to Nicasio crosses plains of tall grass, small farms and broad skies.

The land here is quieter than around the lake. Sheep, alpacas and cattle graze on thin soils, adobe houses sit behind low stone walls, and potatoes, quinoa and barley grow in small plots in the short wet season. Clouds build over the distant ranges in the afternoon, thunder rumbles and, on some days, a rainbow arches over the plain. The sky is huge. At this altitude, around 3,900 metres, a sunburn is easy to get and so is a cold.

Lampa itself is worth a pause. Its main square is surrounded by pale stone buildings and holds a large church whose interior is full of colonial paintings, with an unusual replica of Michelangelo's Pietà and, below, catacombs. The area also has deep roots in pre-Inca history. Not far to the north, the site of Pukara was the centre of a civilisation that flourished over two thousand years ago, and little ceramic bulls from the nearby village, the toritos de Pucará, still sit on rooftops across the Andes for luck.

Roads are paved on the main routes and gravel on side tracks, with potholes, livestock and dust. Speed bumps in villages can be sudden. Local drivers in shared taxis and trucks are quick, so keep right and stay alert. Fuel is available in Lampa, a town of nearly five thousand, but supplies are small, and Juliaca, the big regional hub, has plenty.

Weather in the dry season, May to September, is clear, cold and bright; between December and March, rain turns gravel roads to mud and fills the rivers.
t.gloucester@42.6,-70.7:
Gloucester claims to be America's oldest seaport, settled in 1623, and the town has been pulling fish out of the Atlantic ever since. It sits on Cape Ann, the granite thumb that sticks out of Massachusetts north of Boston, where the coast is a tangle of coves, boulders and working harbours instead of the long sandy beaches farther south. The bronze fisherman at the wheel on the waterfront, put up in 1925, looks toward the sea with the words about those who go down to it in ships, and the memorial lists thousands of local names lost over the centuries. Sebastian Junger's book The Perfect Storm, set among a Gloucester swordfish crew, made that grief known to the rest of the world.

The town has also been an artists' harbour. Winslow Homer painted here in the 1870s, Edward Hopper came for the light, and the Rocky Neck colony still runs on that tradition. Granite was the other great industry. Quarries on Cape Ann supplied stone for buildings and paving up and down the coast, and abandoned pits now fill with water that locals swim in. You see the stone in the sea walls, the gate posts and the rock that comes through the lawns.

Riding Cape Ann is a short, slow and rewarding loop. Route 127 follows the shore, past Magnolia, Rockport and Annisquam, in a series of tight, tree-lined bends with glimpses of the ocean and lobster buoys hung on shed walls. Roads are narrow and potholed after the winter, and in summer weekends traffic crawls, especially around the beaches and Rockport's Bearskin Neck, so aim for a weekday morning or an autumn day, when the maples go red and the crowds thin. The fog can roll in quickly, cooling the air by ten degrees.

Gloucester has fuel and everything else a traveller needs. Fried clams and lobster rolls are the staples, and the Italian bakeries and sandwich shops reflect the Sicilian and Portuguese fishing families who settled here. At the end of the day, find a spot on Eastern Point near the lighthouse and watch the boats come in as the light drops.
t.qasr sahood@25.4,49.6:
Al-Ahsa is the world's largest date-palm oasis, and Qasr Sahood stands in the middle of it, in the busy city of Al Mubarraz. The oasis owes its existence to natural springs that rise from deep aquifers, so abundant that for centuries they fed canals and pools across tens of thousands of hectares of gardens, with several million palms shading rice, vegetables and fruit trees underneath. In the middle of an enormous desert, the effect is startling: green, wet, shaded and noisy with birds. UNESCO recognised the oasis in 2018 as a cultural landscape, and the fortress and the old mosques are part of the picture.

Qasr Sahood is a palace and fortress of the Ottoman and early Saudi periods, a mudbrick building with thick walls and towers, designed to protect the town and to impress visitors. Such buildings were both homes and strongholds in a region that lay between competing powers, and the history of Al-Ahsa, with Ottoman governors, local dynasties and tribal confederations, is a long tangle of shifting alliances. Nearby lies the Jawatha mosque, one of the oldest in the Gulf, said to date from the seventh century, and the Qaisariya market in Hofuf, where traders sell spices, carpets and the famous local textiles.

Riding in Al-Ahsa is easy in the sense that roads are wide, new and well kept, with a grid of motorways and plenty of roundabouts. It is not exciting. The best trips are those into the oasis itself, where narrow roads run between palms and canals, and to Jabal Qarah, a low mountain of sandstone and limestone with natural caves that stay cool even in the heat. From the summit, the view across the palms to the desert beyond shows how thin the line is between green and sand.

Fuel is plentiful and cheap throughout the area, with stations on every main road, and Al Mubarraz and neighbouring Hofuf have everything else, including cafés and restaurants serving Arabian dishes such as kabsa, a spiced rice with lamb or chicken. The best time is from November to March, when daytime temperatures are pleasant and evenings are cool. Summer heat is extreme, and between June and September it is best to ride only in the early morning. Dates, fresh or dried, are on sale everywhere, and the local varieties are worth buying for the road.
t.glenorchy lake road photo pull off@-45.4:
The Mavora Lakes lie in a high valley of tussock and beech forest east of Fiordland, about thirty-five kilometres from Te Anau, and they are one of the quietest places on the South Island. Two long, clear lakes sit between glacial hills, with the Mavora river winding through the tussock, and the peaks of the Thomson mountains rising in the distance. Film-makers have used the valley for the landscapes of Middle-earth, and the long beech forests and open tussock do look suitably epic. There are free campsites by the lake, where the sandflies are fierce and the stars are brilliant.

The Glenorchy label refers to a village at the head of Lake Wakatipu, to the east, but the pin lies in a different part of the country. Access to the Mavora valley is by a gravel road from the Te Anau to Mossburn highway, which is rough in places, with corrugations and stream crossings, and is best taken slowly, particularly on a heavily loaded bike. Mossburn, a small farming town, calls itself the deer capital of New Zealand. The gravel demands a gentle hand, and after rain the surface can become soft and slippery. It is not a road for a sports bike.

The area is the start of the Greenstone and Caples tracks, two popular walking routes that link the valley to the Wakatipu basin, and anglers come for the brown trout in the rivers and lakes. The stop is marked for swimming, and the lakes are clear and very cold, fed by mountain snow, so a quick dip is refreshing rather than comfortable. Watch for sudden weather changes, which are common in the mountains.

Te Anau, the nearest town, has stations, supermarkets and cafés, and a drive in from Queenstown takes about two hours on the main road. Fill the tank, buy supplies and carry water and warm layers.

Early morning is the time to see the lakes. Mist rises from the water, birds call in the beech forest, and the mountains emerge slowly from the cloud. For a place that is a little off the main route, it offers a sense of space and silence that is increasingly rare.
t.the catlins@-46.5,169.7:
The Catlins is a region of southeast New Zealand, a patchwork of rainforest, rocky coast and rolling farmland that most people drive straight past on the way to Invercargill or Dunedin. It sits on the southeastern corner of the South Island, between Balclutha and Fortrose, and it is wilder and quieter than the more famous parts of the south. There are very few towns, a lot of sheep and long unsealed stretches that make the area feel properly remote.

The coast is the attraction. Nugget Point has a lighthouse, built in the 1870s, on a cliff above a scatter of rocky islets that look like nuggets, with fur seals and sea lions lounging below. Curio Bay has a fossilised forest, some one hundred and eighty million years old, exposed on the shore at low tide, and yellow-eyed penguins, among the rarest in the world, come ashore at various places along the coast in the evening. Purakaunui Falls, a tiered waterfall in the forest, is one of the most photographed in the country. The rainforest here is cool, wet and mossy, with ferns and podocarps, and birdsong everywhere.

On a bike, the Southern Scenic Route winds through the area, with farm roads, forest sections and open views to the sea. The tarmac is generally good on the main route, though it narrows and can be patchy in places, and some side roads to the beaches and falls are gravel. Weather is changeable, with cool air from the Southern Ocean and sudden rain, and wind can be strong on exposed headlands. Summer is the best time, but even then warm layers are wise. Sheep and cattle sometimes wander onto the road.

Services are scarce. Papatowai is a tiny settlement with a shop and cafe, and Owaka and Balclutha, further north, have shops and fuel, but you should not rely on anything in between, and it pays to fill up before entering the area. Mobile coverage is patchy.

Take a picnic and enough time. The Catlins rewards slow travel, and you will want to stop at several beaches, walk a forest track and watch the light fade over the rocks before you move on.
t.qasr khuzam@25.4,49.6:
Hofuf is the capital of the Al-Ahsa oasis, in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia, and Al-Ahsa is a surprise: a green island in a desert of sand and salt flats. It is the largest date-palm oasis in the world, with some two and a half million palms growing on land watered by natural springs that rise from deep aquifers beneath the Arabian Peninsula. Springs and channels have fed farms here for thousands of years, and in 2018 the oasis was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list. Hofuf, with nearly three hundred thousand people, and neighbouring Mubarraz stand at its heart.

Qasr Khuzam is one of the old fortified residences of the town, a walled residence of thick, plain masonry built in the long period when the oasis was contested between Ottoman governors, local tribes and Gulf powers. It belongs to the same urban world as the old market and the other forts, and a visit shows how a town grew up behind walls on the edge of the palms. Opening hours and entry arrangements here change, so check before going rather than relying on anything written ahead of time.

The riding is on straight, fast highways. The landscape is flat, open and often hazy with dust, and the road from Dammam and the Gulf coast crosses scrub and sand before the palm groves suddenly appear. Sand blowing across the tarmac is a real hazard, particularly in spring, and so is the heat: from May to September, temperatures climb above forty-five degrees, and riding midday is just dangerous. Winter, from November to March, is the season to be here, with mild days and cool nights. Drive carefully, since road manners are fast and unforgiving, and you will see many pickup trucks and plenty of tailgating.

Fuel is available everywhere in the Hofuf and Mubarraz area, with big stations on the main roads, and you will find cafes serving Arabic coffee, flavoured with cardamom and served in small cups, and bakeries selling dates stuffed with almond. Al-Ahsa dates, especially the variety called khalas, are among the best in the Gulf, and buying a box from a market stall is the right souvenir. In the evening, when the heat drops, the oasis smells of wet earth and woodsmoke, and there is a gentle breeze under the palms.
t.suq al qaysariyah@25.4,49.6:
The Qaysariyah is Hofuf's old covered market, and it has the layout of a bazaar that grew in the days when caravans crossed the desert to reach the oasis. Long, shaded passages run between rows of small shops, with arched ceilings, thick walls and shuttered entrances, and the air inside is noticeably cooler than the street. The oasis of Al-Ahsa has been a trading crossroads for centuries, the place where the desert people of Arabia met merchants from the Gulf coast, Iraq and India, and the market was built to serve them.

What is sold is traditional and sensible: dates, spices, coffee, incense, brass and copper, bisht cloaks of fine wool edged in gold thread, woven mats, perfume oils and the long gowns the region is known for. Al-Ahsa is famous for its dates, especially the khalas variety, and the shops sell them in pressed blocks, in paper bags or in loose heaps in baskets, with a generous taste for any customer. Shopkeepers will offer coffee, usually flavoured with cardamom, and a negotiation is part of the pleasure. Ask before taking photographs of people.

The nearby Ibrahim Palace and the other historic forts of the old town give the area its character, and the oasis lies just beyond, a tangle of palm groves and irrigation channels that appear green and cool from the road. Springs here run warm even in winter. The best time to walk through is early in the evening, after the afternoon prayer, when the market comes alive and the light is soft.

For the rider, Hofuf is a city of almost three hundred thousand people, with wide roads, heavy traffic and fast driving. Streets near the market are narrow and congested, and parking can be awkward, so allow time to find a place and walk the last stretch. Fuel is everywhere. Summer temperatures often exceed forty-five degrees, so the cooler months from November to March are the right time, and midday should be spent in the shade. Dust is common, and strong winds in spring can bring sandstorms with little notice. Close the visor against grit, and take water, because the market is dry and the air is arid.

The coast of northern Chile is a place where almost nothing happens, and that is its character. The Camarones river rises in the high Andes and runs west through one of the driest landscapes on Earth, cutting a narrow green valley through the Atacama before it reaches the Pacific at a small mouth south of Arica. In dry years the water gives out before it reaches the sea, and the final stretch is a mixture of reeds, sand and salt pans, a patch of green on a coast of brown and grey. Birds congregate here: gulls, pelicans, terns and, in the right season, waders that come all the way from the northern hemisphere.

The land around is hard, dry desert. The coastal range falls straight to the sea in cliffs and slopes of crumbling rock, with fog, the camanchaca, rolling in from the Pacific on many mornings and condensing into a fine mist that supports the thin plants on the hills. Rain is almost unknown, and the sky is often grey and low in the morning and brilliant by midday. The Humboldt current keeps the sea cold and rich with fish, and fishermen from small coves work the coast in open boats.

The road along this coast is Ruta 5, the Pan-American Highway, which runs inland of the shore across the desert pampa, and the side roads that reach the coast are dirt or poorly kept asphalt. Distances are long, nothing is signed in English, and services are almost non-existent. The ride is a lesson in emptiness: straight roads, enormous skies, and occasional trucks heading for the mines or the border. Winds can be strong in the afternoon, and the light at the end of the day, low and golden on the cliffs, is a good reason to be out.

Treat the area seriously. Arica, the nearest city, is the place for fuel, and the next reliable station may be a long way off, so fill up and carry water and a spare bottle of fuel if you plan to head off the main road. There is no phone signal in many places. Spring and autumn are the mildest seasons, and midsummer can be hot inland. Take food with you, because nothing is waiting at the river mouth, and respect the nesting birds and the fragile vegetation.
t.settlement and artificial mummification:
The Chinchorro were fishers who lived on this coast, and they were doing something extraordinary with their dead at a time when nothing like it existed anywhere else. Around seven thousand years ago, they began to preserve their dead by taking the body apart, drying the skin and bones, reassembling them on sticks, packing the body with clay, plant fibre and ash, and covering the face with a mask of clay. These are the oldest known artificially mummified bodies in the world, older than the better-known Egyptian mummies by some two thousand years. The tradition included children and infants, and no one is quite sure why.

UNESCO added the Chinchorro settlement and mummification sites in Arica and Parinacota to the World Heritage list in 2021. The land they lived on is a thin shelf between the Pacific and the desert, with plenty of fish, shellfish and sea mammals in the cold water, and almost nothing else. They lived by the sea, fished with hooks of shell and bone, and left behind village sites, burials and middens along the shore. The dry air preserved things that would have rotted elsewhere.

The nearest city is Arica, a port of nearly two hundred thousand people about three kilometres away, and this is where the story is told best. The museum at San Miguel de Azapa in the valley outside the city holds a large collection of mummies and the objects found with them, and an explanation of the technique. It is a sober, unusual visit. The city itself sits at the foot of El Morro, a great rocky headland with a fortress on top, where a decisive battle of the War of the Pacific was fought in 1880.

For the rider, Arica is a pleasant place. The coast road is flat and straight, the climate is mild, with little rain, and the sea is cold and often misty in the morning. Fuel is easy in the city, and cafes and seafood restaurants along the waterfront serve fresh fish and ceviche. Take a layer for the morning fog and sunscreen for the afternoon, because the sun is strong and the shadows are short. Opening times at the museum are best checked locally, since they change.

In 2004 a construction crew working in the middle of Arica, on a street called Colón, struck something that stopped the job and made the news: human remains, carefully preserved, lying in the sand. The site, known by the number of the street, turned out to be a Chinchorro cemetery in the middle of a modern city, and the excavation that followed uncovered dozens of mummies, some of them over five thousand years old. Colón 10 became one of the key sites of the Chinchorro culture, and is part of the UNESCO listing that was granted in 2021.

The find changed the way people see the city. For decades, Arica had been a border town and a port, known for its beaches and its role in the War of the Pacific, and for its position near the Peruvian frontier. Suddenly it was also an archaeological capital, a place where the earliest embalming in human history had been practised. The Chinchorro mummies were not made for kings, as in Egypt, but for fishing families, which makes the practice even more remarkable.

What you see in Arica depends on what you ask for. Many of the finds are held at the museum at San Miguel de Azapa, a short drive inland, and some are displayed at the university or at local exhibits. In the city itself, there are signs and plaques where excavations took place, and the museum staff can say what is open to visitors. It is an easy place to combine with a walk up El Morro, the headland that overlooks the harbour, where a fortress and a small museum stand.

Practical details are simple. Arica is a city with fuel stations, cafes and hotels, a mild, dry climate, and a seafront with surf beaches and good seafood. Traffic is manageable, and the centre is small enough to walk. A ride out of town heads into the desert and, further on, up the long road to the altiplano. Check the weather before you climb, and take warm layers if you go high. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons, with temperatures in the low to mid twenties and rarely any rain.

Garden City is the tidy, tree-lined heart of Nassau County, a planned suburb laid out in the 1870s by the department-store magnate Alexander Turner Stewart on the flat grassland known as the Hempstead Plains. Stewart's grand vision, which included a cathedral that still dominates the skyline, was meant to be a model community, and the wide avenues, handsome houses and quiet greens still feel more European than most of Long Island. It is also not far from where aviation history was made: Roosevelt Field, just next door, was the starting point for Charles Lindbergh's solo flight across the Atlantic in 1927.

The flat plain here once held the largest natural prairie east of the Alleghenies, and a small remnant survives. Today it is a landscape of malls, parkways and suburban lawns, and the riding is flat, congested and slow. Long Island is not known for motorcycle roads, and this part, close to the city, is a sea of traffic lights. But it does offer everything you need before a long haul: fuel at every corner, diners, bakeries and the sort of delis where a bacon-egg-and-cheese is served wrapped in foil.

Starting here, the way to the Hudson Valley is by bridge or tunnel, through the congestion of the Queens and Bronx approaches. Time your departure to avoid rush hours, since the Long Island Expressway and the Cross Island Parkway can be a parking lot, and weekend traffic to the beaches adds to the mess. A dawn start pays off handsomely, and Sunday mornings are often quiet.

Notice the parkways: they were built in the early twentieth century for pleasure driving, with landscaped edges and stone-faced bridges that are low, so trucks and buses cannot use them. Riders enjoy the gentle curves, though police enforce the limits closely. In autumn, the maples and oaks turn colour, and the avenues of Garden City glow with it. Use the town as a launch pad, load up on coffee and a bagel, and then head north and west toward the Hudson, where the roads start to climb and wrinkle.

The woods north of Stamford, Connecticut, feel a long way from the coast a few miles south. The pin falls in the leafy, rolling country of North Stamford, where stone walls thread through hardwood forest and old farmhouses sit back from the lane. The Merritt Parkway runs close by, one of the most beautiful roads in the Northeast, and a good reason for a rider to be here. It is lined with trees, shaped to the landscape and crossed by more than sixty bridges, each with its own design in stone, concrete or steel, built in the 1930s.

The parkway is a delight and a trap. It carries only passenger vehicles, so no trucks, and its curves are gentle, but the lanes are narrow, the shoulders are minimal, and there are tight on-ramps with short merges. The speed limit is about fifty-five, and state police are watchful. It is also notorious for deer, especially at dusk, and for the occasional tree branch dropped after a storm. In autumn, the maples glow orange and red on either side, and the tunnel of foliage is spectacular.

Stamford itself has about a hundred and twenty thousand people and is a corporate hub, with offices and expensive houses along the water. For the rider, that means fuel and food are never far away, though prices are high. The nearby Bartlett Arboretum and the Mianus River Gorge give a taste of the woods, and New Canaan, to the north, has a handsome village centre and some modernist houses from the mid-twentieth century.

The back roads are the better ride. Long Ridge Road and Route 104 climb and fall over the glacial hills, with blind corners, stone walls close to the tarmac and patches of leaf litter in the shade. Speeds should be sensible: the roads are narrow and often shared with cyclists. Weekday mornings are busy with commuters, so go on a weekend, early, with mist still in the hollows. It is Connecticut at its leafy best, a world of white steeples and colonial houses.

Washington Irving made this corner of the Hudson Valley famous, and the place has never quite shaken the habit. Sleepy Hollow, a village of about ten thousand people on the east bank of the river, took the name of his 1820 story only in 1996, when it dropped the older title of North Tarrytown, and the town has leaned into the legend ever since. The Old Dutch Church, which appears in the tale, stands beside a graveyard where Irving himself is buried, and every October the place fills with people hoping for a headless horseman.

Above the village, the land rises into the wooded hills of Pocantico, where the Rockefeller family built their estate. Rockefeller State Park Preserve protects a big piece of it, with carriage roads and quiet ponds, and the stone mansion called Kykuit sits on a hilltop with views down the river. The roads here are narrow, tree-lined and stone-walled, and the glimpses of the Hudson from the ridges are very good. Route 117 and Route 448 wind through the hills, and Route 9 runs along the river toward Tarrytown and Ossining.

The Croton Aqueduct, which carried water to New York City from the 1840s, runs beneath the area, and its old trail is now a linear park for walkers. To the east, reservoirs fill the hollows, and the roads crossing the dams give good views over still water. It is a gentle, civilised ride, rather than a thrilling one, with corners that are mostly tidy and speed limits that are low and enforced. Cyclists and horses use the same lanes, so keep it measured.

The Mario Cuomo Bridge, which replaced the old Tappan Zee, rises across the river to the south, a long, sleek span that dominates the skyline. Fuel and food are easy in Tarrytown and Sleepy Hollow, which has bakeries, taverns and some quite good restaurants. Visit in October for the foliage, or on a weekday in spring, when the dogwoods bloom and crowds are thin. Evenings are best, with long light on the river and a mist rising in the hollows.

Parsippany sits in Morris County, New Jersey, where the Highlands start to roll out beyond the suburbs of Newark, and it is the kind of place that is mostly offices, shopping centres and highway junctions. About fifty thousand people live in the township, and it is crossed by Interstates 80 and 287 and Route 46, so traffic is a permanent condition. Still, a rider can use it. Fuel is at every junction, though New Jersey is almost alone in the country in requiring a station attendant to pump the petrol for you, so keep the helmet on and expect to wait.

The land here has more history than it shows. The Rockaway and Passaic rivers wander through the area, and in the nearby Troy Meadows the wetlands still hold herons and turtles. Further south and east, the Great Swamp, a national wildlife refuge, preserves a huge stretch of marsh and woodland that was saved from becoming an airport in the 1960s. West of Parsippany, the hills rise into the New Jersey Highlands, with winding roads, stone walls and reservoirs, and these are where a rider wants to go.

The ride out is best done early. Route 202 and Route 23 head north and west into quieter country, and from there, smaller county roads wind through woods and old farm country. The surface is variable, with potholes and frost heaves after winter, and deer are plentiful. Autumn brings spectacular colour, and the lanes can be busy with leaf-peepers. Summer weekends are humid, with hazy air and thunderstorms in the late afternoon.

Lake Hiawatha and the little lakes around Boonton, west of town, give some places to stop and look. Boonton also has a handsome old downtown, with a waterfall and the ruins of an ironworks. Food here is varied, with Indian, Italian and diner breakfasts all excellent, and the supermarkets make it easy to stock up. Treat Parsippany as a transit point, and spend your time in the hills.

Manasquan lies on the Jersey Shore where the Manasquan River meets the Atlantic, in a tidy beach town of about six thousand people at the northern end of Ocean County. The inlet is a busy place for fishing boats and charter skippers, and it also marks the start of the sheltered Intracoastal Waterway that runs south behind the barrier islands. The beaches are wide and clean, with a handful of old summer cottages and a small downtown with bakeries, delis and pizza counters.

The surrounding area is a flat, sandy and gently wooded plain, part of the Atlantic Coastal Plain, and the roads reflect it. Route 35 runs along the shore with traffic lights and strip malls, while quieter streets in Brielle and Point Pleasant wind past marinas and bridges. It is not a place for corners, but a pleasant, slow ride on a calm morning. The Manasquan Reservoir, a few miles inland, has a long loop trail and some small hills, and offers a glimpse of the pine barrens' edge.

Summer is the busy season. The shore towns fill with day trippers and holidaymakers, parking is hard and the roads crawl, especially on Friday evenings and Sunday afternoons. In May, June and September the crowds are thinner and the weather is mild, with long, soft light over the ocean. Winter is quiet and bleak, with a hard wind off the sea, but the beaches are empty and the light can be glorious. Hurricane Sandy damaged much of this coast in 2012, and rebuilding is visible in raised houses and new boardwalks.

Fuel is easy in town and along the highway, though remember that in New Jersey an attendant fills the tank. Local diners do excellent breakfasts, and seafood is fresh from the inlet. For a rest, the bench by the inlet watching boats pass is hard to beat, and the sound of halyards clinking is a pleasant accompaniment. Beyond the town, a couple of fine lighthouse and park stops lie within easy reach, along the coast road.

Dayton, New Jersey, is a flat, unassuming township in Middlesex County, in the broad belt of farmland, warehouses and new housing that runs between New Brunswick and Trenton. The pin falls near Route 130, one of the old highways of the state, with a long history as the main road between the two cities. Cranbury, a handsome little village with a long main street of colonial and Victorian houses, lies a short distance to the south, and Princeton, with its university and stately lawns, is within a quarter-hour's ride.

The land is the Piedmont plain, once rich with wheat and orchards, and a good deal of it is still farmed, with sod farms, corn fields and nurseries between the distribution centres. The Delaware and Raritan Canal, dug in the 1830s to link the two rivers, runs through the area, and its towpath is now a long, shady trail beside quiet water. The Millstone River nearby carried the early mills. Princeton Battlefield, just beyond, is where Washington won a small but crucial victory in January 1777.

For the rider, this is a place for a stop, not a destination. Roads are flat and straight, speed limits are low, and the major highways carry heavy truck traffic, so there is little to do but keep alert. But the back roads of Cranbury and Plainsboro are quieter, and, in the early morning, with mist lying in the fields and the corn rustling, they have a gentle charm.

Fuel is available all around, and as in the rest of New Jersey an attendant will fill the tank. Diners are plentiful, and the town of Jamesburg, a few miles east, has a small old-fashioned centre. Spring and autumn are the pleasant seasons. Summer can be hot, humid and hazy, and the winters bring slush and salt. Plan to be out of here early, heading either toward the hills of the Hunterdon countryside to the west or the shore to the east, depending on the ride ahead.

West of Danbury, Connecticut, the land has a lumpy, glacial character, with rocky ridges, small lakes and thick woodland, all of it close to the New York line. Danbury itself, a city of about eighty-five thousand people, was once the hat-making capital of America, producing millions of hats a year in the nineteenth century until fashion changed and the factories closed. The old Hatters' tradition is still remembered in the city's museum and in a few brick factory buildings. Today the city has fuel stations, supermarkets and diners at every turn, so it is a sensible place to refuel.

The pin sits in the hills just beyond, near Peach Lake, a little lake that straddles the state border and is ringed by small summer cottages, many now year-round homes. The country roads around here are narrow, hilly and winding, with stone walls, old farmhouses and a lot of trees. Route 35 and Route 121 wander through, and the pavement can be rough after winter. Candlewood Lake, the largest lake in Connecticut, lies to the northeast, an artificial reservoir created in the 1920s, with long shores and hills.

The riding is gentle but demanding in its own way. Corners are often blind, with trees closing in and walls close to the edge, and leaf litter, gravel and wet patches in shaded places make grip unpredictable. Deer, cyclists and local drivers who know the roads too well add to the interest. Take it slowly, enjoy the foliage, and the lanes reward you. Autumn is the time, when the maples and oaks turn bright and the air has a snap.

For a rest, the little village centres, such as Ridgefield to the south, offer coffee, bakeries and a pleasant green. Ridgefield has a handsome main street, a revolutionary battle site and an excellent small art museum. Summer weekends bring traffic to the lakes, so go early. Winter is quiet, with snow and ice, and some roads can be treacherous after storms. In a good late September morning, this is New England at its best.
New City is a suburban town in Rockland County, New York, where the Hudson's west bank rises into the Palisades and the long, wooded ridge of Hook Mountain. It has about thirty-three thousand people, a modest centre with courthouse and shops, and a lot of leafy streets and cul-de-sacs. For a rider, the usefulness is practical: fuel is at the corner, and diners, bagel shops and delis are plentiful. It makes a good stop before heading out onto the better roads in the hills.

The best of the neighbourhood is Rockland Lake State Park, a short ride east, where a pair of small lakes sit below the steep Hook Mountain cliffs. In the nineteenth century, the lake was a major source of ice, cut in winter and shipped to the city by barge, and the old ice houses stood along the shore. Today the park has walking trails, a swimming pool, a golf course and wide views. A road climbs toward Hook Mountain, and in autumn, thousands of hawks migrate along the ridge, drawing birdwatchers with binoculars.

Route 9W runs along the river's edge, passing Nyack, a lively old river town with antiques shops, restaurants and a long history of artists, among them Edward Hopper, who was born there. Further south, the road leads to Piermont and its long pier, and to the Palisades Interstate Parkway, where the speed limits are low but the curves and woods are lovely. It is gentle riding, with polite traffic.

Hawk's Nest, the famous cliff road along the Delaware, is a long way northwest, but the Hudson's side of Rockland County offers its own enjoyments. Take the mornings, when the light is soft, the roads are empty and mist clings to the river. Autumn is the season, with the foliage at its best. In winter, snow and ice can make the hills treacherous. Plan for a coffee in Nyack, then see where the river road takes you.

Montvale lies on the New Jersey side of the border with New York, in the Pascack Valley of northern Bergen County, a prosperous suburb of leafy streets, corporate parks and a small commuter railway station. It has about eight thousand people, and its position, a mile or so below the state line, makes it a convenient place to start or finish a ride up the Hudson. The Garden State Parkway runs nearby, and the Palisades Interstate Parkway is a short distance to the east, so it is easy to reach the better roads.

The Pascack Brook runs through the valley, and the land is gently rolling, with remnants of woods and old stone walls between the houses. West of town, the Ramapo Mountains rise in a dark, wooded ridge, a rugged barrier with a few winding roads. The Hackensack River lies to the east, and the Palisades, the long cliffs that face New York across the Hudson, rise beyond. Much of the countryside is protected as park land, and the roads through it are some of the most beautiful in the New York region.

The ride from Montvale north into Rockland County is a gentle introduction. Route 303 and Route 304 cross the state line into New York, with good views of the hills and a flow of commuters. The Palisades Parkway, a short distance east, is the gem: wide, well-surfaced curves through dense forest, with stone-faced bridges and viewpoints over the river. Trucks are banned, and the speed limit is fifty, which police enforce. In the early morning light, it is a joy.

Fuel is easy to find in Montvale, and as in all of New Jersey, an attendant fills your tank. Diners and delis open early for the commuters, and there are good bakeries in the neighbouring towns. Weekday mornings bring heavy traffic, so aim for the weekend, and set out before eight. Autumn is the best season, with the hardwoods in full colour, and winter can be bitter, with ice on the shady bends. Use the town as a gate to the Hudson Highlands.

Palisades is where the river's western cliffs begin: a long wall of dark basalt rising some hundred metres above the Hudson, running north from the George Washington Bridge into Rockland County. The pin falls on the New Jersey side, near Alpine, a quiet, wealthy village high on the cliff top, with the river glittering below and the towers of Manhattan visible to the south on a clear day. The nearest fuel is in Yonkers across the river or in the towns of Bergen County, so fill the tank before you go.

The cliffs have a history of protection. In the late nineteenth century, quarrymen were blasting the rock for building stone and paving, and the damage so alarmed local women and conservationists that the Palisades Interstate Park was created in 1900 to stop it. Today the park includes more than thirty miles of shoreline, with hiking trails and old carriage roads. The Palisades Interstate Parkway, which runs along the top, was built in the mid-twentieth century and remains one of the most beautiful roads near the city, curving through hardwood forest with stone-faced walls and bridges.

For a rider, the parkway is a treat, with long, gentle curves, smooth tarmac and no trucks, though police enforce the fifty-mile-an-hour limit rigorously. In the early morning, with mist in the trees and few cars, it feels private. Alpine Lookout, a short stop on the way, offers a wide view over the river toward the Hudson Highlands. Birds of prey migrate along the cliff in autumn, and the hardwoods turn bright in October.

Weekends bring crowds of cyclists and families, so choose a weekday if possible. In winter, the road may be icy in shaded places, and salt and sand make it slippery. The day's route, north to the Hudson Highlands and the Catskills, follows the river through some of the loveliest country in the Northeast. Starting here, you leave the city's edge and follow the Hudson upriver, past Piermont and Nyack, and the countryside widens with every mile.
t.bear mountain bridge@41.3,-74.0:
The Bear Mountain Bridge, opened in 1924, was the longest suspension bridge in the world at the time of its construction and the first to span the Hudson south of Albany. It leaps across the river at its narrowest and deepest, between the steep granite flanks of Bear Mountain on the west and Anthony's Nose on the east, and the setting is dramatic: dark cliffs, a wide gleaming river, forested hills layered one behind the other. A toll is collected, and motorcycles pay like everyone else.

The bridge has some quirks. The Appalachian Trail, which runs all the way from Georgia to Maine, crosses the Hudson here on the walkway, and at about a hundred and twenty feet above sea level, this is the lowest point on the whole trail. Hikers cross beside the traffic, and the Bear Mountain Inn, a stone-and-timber lodge nearby, is a favourite stop. Fort Montgomery, just across the river, has the ruins of a Revolutionary War fortress that tried to stop the British from sailing up the river in 1777, and failed.

For a rider, the pleasure is in the approach. From the west, Route 9W curves along the river with a steep rocky slope on one side and sudden views of the water on the other. From the east, Route 9D or Route 6 climbs through the Hudson Highlands, with stone walls and woodlands. The bridge deck itself is a metal grid that hums under the tyres and can be slippery when wet. Take it slowly, and keep to the middle of the lane, as the grating can feel odd under a bike.

Perkins Memorial Drive, on Bear Mountain, climbs to a stone tower on the summit with a view over the river, the Highlands and, on clear days, the Manhattan skyline. The road is narrow, twisty, and closed in winter. Plan a stop on the western side for coffee, then walk to the lookout on the bridge approach for a photo. Autumn is the season, when the whole valley turns russet and gold, though weekends are busy.
t.cold spring@41.4,-74.0:
Cold Spring is the kind of Hudson river village that looks like a stage set, a single steep Main Street of antiques shops, cafés and brick storefronts running down to the river and a small bandstand on the waterfront. It has fewer than two thousand residents, and it fills each weekend with day-trippers from the city who arrive on the Metro-North train. Across the water rise the walls of West Point, and the Hudson narrows here between steep, wooded hills, a fjord-like stretch called the Highlands.

The village owes its origin to iron. In the early nineteenth century, the West Point Foundry on the edge of town cast cannon, including the Parrott rifle, which helped win the Civil War, and its brick ruins still stand beside a stream, now a pleasant heritage trail. Nearby, Boscobel, a restored mansion from the early 1800s, has gardens with views over the river. Behind the village, Breakneck Ridge and Storm King Mountain climb steeply, popular with hikers and a source of the most famous views in the valley.

Route 9D runs through, a lovely road of curves and rises between the river and the hills, with stone walls and old trees leaning over the pavement. It is narrow, popular with cyclists, and has a low speed limit, so ride it at a gentle pace and enjoy the views. Route 301 climbs eastward into the hills, quiet and winding. In autumn, the maples and oaks flare red and orange, and the traffic thickens on weekends. A weekday morning is calmer.

Food is the main point of the stop: bakeries, a deli, a couple of pizzerias, and several places for a proper breakfast. Fuel is less convenient, as the village has little, so fill up in Fishkill or Peekskill. The train station lies at the foot of the street, and on busy days the sidewalks overflow. Park the bike by the river, find a bench, and watch the barges. In winter the village is quiet, frost whitens the roofs, and the river steams on cold mornings.

Pepacton Reservoir fills a long, bent valley in the western Catskills, a deep blue lake many miles long, built in the early 1950s to supply drinking water to New York City, a hundred and thirty miles away. The East Branch of the Delaware was dammed at Downsville, and the rising water drowned four villages, including Pepacton itself, along with farms, roads and a good many orchards. The old foundations, it is said, still lie beneath the surface, and in dry years the water drops enough to show a few of them.

Route 30 follows the lake's shore for much of its length, a quiet, winding road with views over the water and the forested hills beyond. It is not a high-speed road, but it is a fine, easy one, with long gentle curves and little traffic, especially on weekdays. The Catskills here are older and rounder than the Alps, worn by glaciers into rolling ridges, with hemlock and hardwood forests and rushing creeks. Autumn colours are famous, and the weather can turn cool and misty in any season.

The reservoir is strictly a water supply, so swimming, boating and wading are banned, and the shore is patrolled by watchful rangers. Fishing is allowed with a permit, and the trout in these cold waters are famous; the Delaware's branches are some of the most storied fly-fishing streams in the country. Downsville, at the dam, has an old covered bridge from the 1850s, a lovely wooden span over the river, and a small fishing museum nearby.

Services are thin. Livingston Manor, Roscoe and Margaretville are the nearest places for fuel and a meal, and Margaretville has a pleasant main street and a few diners. Fill the tank before you come, since the stretch along the lake has none. Cell service is patchy. Winters bring snow and ice, and some small roads close, while spring brings mud and fog. Late September to mid-October is the best window, with the hills ablaze and the air crisp. Bring a camera and an extra layer.

Carteret is an industrial borough on the Arthur Kill, the narrow tidal channel that separates New Jersey from Staten Island, and the pin falls at its heart. Princeton sits high in central Massachusetts, in the hills below Mount Wachusett, and it feels farther from Boston than the forty-odd miles of the map. The town is a scattering of old farms, stone walls, white churches and woods, and at around three hundred metres it is cooler than the lowlands, with an early autumn and snow that comes sooner and stays longer. A well-known ski area and a state reservation share the mountain, and in autumn the hillsides are among the brightest in the region.

Mount Wachusett, at about 611 metres, rises alone from the rolling country, and on a clear day gives views to Boston's towers in the east and the peaks of Monadnock in New Hampshire to the north. The Wachusett Reservoir, a huge lake to the east, supplies water to much of eastern Massachusetts, and its shores are protected, so the area around it is quiet woodland. A summit road, open in season, winds up the mountain, and the hiking trails are well kept. The Midstate Trail runs through the town.

The riding is pleasant rather than dramatic. Roads such as Route 62 and Route 140 run through the hills in smooth, rolling bends, with tree-lined stretches, small villages and farm stands that sell cider doughnuts and apples in fall. Surfaces are mostly decent but frost heaves can be rough in spring, and traffic can be heavy on weekends in October, when leaf-peepers fill the roads. Sunrise from a hilltop pull-off is a good start to a day, and the smell of woodsmoke carries on cool evenings.

Princeton itself is small, with a general store and a few places to eat, so fuel is better found in Sterling, about ten kilometres away, or in Holden and Fitchburg. Rain can come quickly, and mist often hangs on the mountain in the morning. The best months are May and September, when the roads are quieter and the air is clear.
t.bethel@44.4,-70.8:
Bethel is a quiet village on the Androscoggin River, in the western mountains of Maine, close to the New Hampshire border. White clapboard houses and a green stand beside the church, and the Mahoosuc Range, rugged and wooded, rises just to the north. The town has about 2,500 people and an old academy, Gould, founded in 1836, whose brick buildings give the place a New England college look. In winter, the Sunday River ski resort a few kilometres north turns the area busy, but in summer and autumn Bethel is peaceful.

The big ride from here is north on Route 26 through Grafton Notch. The road follows the Bear River into a narrow pass between steep, forested walls, with places to stop for short walks to cascades, a gorge and a cave. Screw Auger Falls sends water spiralling down a polished chute of granite, and Moose Cave, a short loop trail, runs through boulders. The Appalachian Trail crosses the road in the notch, and hikers in muddy boots turn up at the roadside. Moose are common here, especially at dawn and dusk, so keep your speed down and watch the edges.

Surfaces are good, the bends moderate, and the views of the hills are superb in late September and early October, when the maples turn scarlet. Spring is mud season, with soft shoulders and frost heaves, and black flies are ferocious in May and June. Weather in the mountains can be cold and wet even in summer, so pack warm layers and rain gear.

Bethel has fuel, a few cafes, shops and inns, and it is a good place to stop for a meal. For larger services, Paris, about twenty-eight kilometres to the south-east, is the nearest town of any size. Little lies north of the notch for a long way, so fill the tank before heading to Rangeley, and expect long gaps between settlements.
t.lindis pass and tekapo@-45.5,168.8:
South of the Wakatipu basin the country opens up. This point lies near Kingston and Garston on the road that runs south from the lake toward Southland, in a landscape of tussock hills, schist outcrops and long sheep paddocks, with the Mataura River slipping through on its way to the southern plains. Behind you, the Remarkables show their sharp snow-capped line, and ahead the horizon flattens out as the high country gives way to farmland.

Kingston is a small place at the southern tip of Lake Wakatipu, and it is known for a vintage steam train, the Kingston Flyer, that has run excursions on the old railway for decades with a few pauses. The lake itself is a long, deep glacial trough shaped like a lightning bolt, and the Māori story says that a giant's heart beats beneath it, which explains the way the water rises and falls a few centimetres every few minutes. In reality it is a seiche, a standing wave, but the legend is better.

The road, State Highway 6, follows the lake shore along a shelf cut into the mountainside, the Devil's Staircase, which is a fast and winding stretch with views across the water to the Remarkables. The surface is good, the bends are open and the traffic is a mix of tourists in hire cars, trucks and the occasional motorcyclist enjoying himself. Beware of hire-car drivers who are not used to driving on the left and stop suddenly for photos.

For fuel, rely on Queenstown or Frankton at the north end of the lake, since the small settlements here have limited services. The weather is changeable, and the high country can be cold even in summer, with snow on the tops from April to November. Wind is common, strong and gusty on the open stretches, and the best light is early morning and late afternoon, when the tussock turns gold. Stop for coffee in a small town and spend a moment looking at the hills.

The map pins this spot on the Southland plains near Mossburn, a tiny farming township south of Te Anau that likes to call itself the deer capital of New Zealand. The country here is flat to gently rolling, laid out in square paddocks, with the Oreti River winding through on its way south, and the mountains of Fiordland and the Eyre range standing back on the horizon. It is a long way from the snowy peaks that the ride's name promises, and the high point of the day is a modest road rise rather than a mountain pass.

Deer farming took off in New Zealand from the 1970s, when wild deer, descendants of animals released in the nineteenth century by settlers who wanted something to hunt, were captured by helicopter and brought into paddocks. Venison now goes to Europe, and the sight of tall fences enclosing red deer on the hillsides is part of the landscape. You may also see sheep, cattle and the odd paddock of crops, and the rivers are known for brown trout.

The roads are straight and fast, with long views, wide shoulders and little traffic outside the tourist season. State Highway 94, which links Lumsden and Te Anau and carries on to Milford Sound, is the main route, and heavy tourist traffic uses it in summer. The wind can be strong on the plains, and winter brings frost and occasional ice, so watch the surface in the shade. Speed limits are strictly enforced, and the police do check tourists.

Services are limited. Mossburn has a small shop and a cafe, and for fuel and a larger choice of food you should look to Lumsden to the east or Te Anau to the north. The best time to ride is summer, from December to February, with long, warm days, but be prepared for rain, since Fiordland is one of the wettest places in the country.
t.mount cook high country@-45.2,168.4:
West of Lake Wakatipu, across the water from the road to Glenorchy, lies a stretch of high-country sheep station land with no sealed road to its name. The coordinates fall near Mount Nicholas, where a farm stands on the lakeshore at the foot of the Thomson Mountains, and the only practical way to reach it is by boat or by long gravel tracks from the south. The steamship TSS Earnslaw, a coal-fired vessel built in 1912, crosses from Queenstown to the nearby Walter Peak station, and the sight of its black smoke on a clear day is one of the lake's emblems.

Wakatipu is a deep, glacier-carved lake, and its water is cold, blue and clear. The lake got its present shape from the great ice sheets that once flowed down from the Southern Alps, and the Remarkables on the eastern shore are a good example of what that ice left behind. Maori believed the lake was the burned imprint of a giant, and a legend explains the rise and fall of the water in the same way. Fishermen come for trout and salmon.

If you want to ride in this area, the usual route goes round the lake on State Highway 6 and then south, or along Highway 6 to Kingston, from where gravel roads lead west into the back country. The gravel is rough, steep in places and unsuitable for a heavy touring bike, so check with locals before you start. The more realistic ride is the paved road along the lake's eastern shore, with views across the water to the mountains.

Fuel is the main practical question. Queenstown, about twenty-five kilometres away as the crow flies, is the main source, and Kingston is smaller still. Fill up before you leave and carry some water. The best season is summer, with long days and the lake warm enough to paddle, though the nights remain cool, and autumn, when the beech forests on the slopes turn orange and red, is memorable. Rain can arrive quickly and the temperature can fall by ten degrees in an hour.
t.mount cook high country high point@-45.2:
Greenstone is the old name that everyone in this region knows. The valley of that name runs north from the Mavora Lakes toward Lake Wakatipu, between the Livingstone and Thomson mountains, and it was one of the great trade routes of the South Island. Ngāi Tahu carried pounamu, the green nephrite that they prized for tools and ornaments, from the upper valleys over the passes to the coast, and the route now forms part of the Greenstone and Caples tracks that walkers use in summer.

The coordinates here fall on the western side of the Wakatipu basin, in country that is largely roadless. A gravel road leads from Mossburn on State Highway 94 to the Mavora Lakes, a chain of beech-fringed lakes in a tussock valley, popular for camping and fishing, and from there the track toward the Greenstone becomes a four-wheel-drive and walking route. It is not a place for a heavily laden road bike, and the river crossings can be dangerous after rain.

Even so, the surrounding country is wonderful. Beech forest climbs the slopes in dark green, tussock covers the valley floors in pale gold and snow lies on the tops from late autumn to spring. You may hear the call of the bellbird, a clear, bubbling song, and see the small fantails flitting after you on the track. Rain falls often, and in the mountains the weather can change with little warning, so carry waterproofs and an emergency layer.

For fuel and supplies, look to Te Anau, Mossburn or Queenstown, since none is available here. The Mavora Lakes road is gravel, usually maintained, but washboard sections and loose stones need care, and a sensible rider treats it as an adventure that deserves slow speeds and caution. The reward is a quiet campsite beside the lake, with the sound of water and the smell of wet beech leaves. The stars at night, far from any town, are bright and thick.
t.queenstown south island@-45.2,169.3:
Clyde is a small, handsome town on the Clutha River in Central Otago, and it lies in one of the driest and sunniest parts of New Zealand, where schist hills run in smooth brown folds under a huge sky. The old gold-rush town of the 1860s survives in its main street, with stone buildings, cafes and a historic hotel, and the Clyde Dam, completed in the early 1990s, now holds back the waters of Lake Dunstan to the north. It was a major engineering project and a controversial one, and the old Cromwell town was partly drowned in the process.

The Otago Central Rail Trail, one of the country's most popular cycling routes, ends here, and the town is full of cyclists in the summer months. The dry climate makes the district a centre for apricots, cherries and stone fruit, and fruit stalls beside the road sell them in the warm months. In autumn, the poplars and willows along the river turn bright gold, and the contrast with the brown hills is memorable.

Riding here is easy, relaxed and enjoyable. State Highway 8 follows the river with long, flowing bends, passing orchards and vineyards, and the surface is generally good, though the traffic can be busy in summer. The wind can be strong and dry, and the temperature swings from over thirty degrees in January to well below freezing in July. The Roxburgh Gorge and Alexandra, a larger town with more services, lie a short distance to the south.

Clyde has a few cafes and a bakery, and fuel is available in Alexandra or Cromwell. Take a swim in the river or the lake if the day is hot, though the water is cold, and bear in mind that currents below the dam can be strong. The old town is a good place to walk around, and the stone buildings, the gold-miners' history and the quiet pace of the place give it a character that is hard to find in busier parts of the country.
t.mount cook high country@-45.4,169.1:
The pin here lies in the schist uplands between the Garston district and the Kawarau, where the Nevis Valley runs through a high, treeless plateau of tussock, rock outcrops and old gold-mining ruins. It is a remote part of Central Otago, empty and quiet, and there are no towns close by. The nearest settlement is Garston, a small farming community to the south, and Kingston and Cromwell are both more than thirty kilometres away.

The Nevis Road, which runs through the valley between Garston and Bannockburn, is among the highest public roads in New Zealand, a gravel track that climbs through tussock country and crosses the Nevis River many times. It is a four-wheel-drive and adventure-bike route, rough, rocky and subject to closure in winter and after rain. The road is described as one of the best back-country drives in the country, with extraordinary views of the Garvie Mountains and the Remarkables, and it has a great deal of history, with old gold-rush huts and stone cottages scattered along the way. Check the conditions locally before you go, because river crossings are real and help is far away.

This is not a place for a casual food stop. The nearest options are in Garston, which has very limited services, and in Cromwell or Queenstown for anything serious.
