The sky here is huge, and the silence is complete, broken only by the wind, the odd sheep and the call of a skylark. Hawks hang over the slopes in the afternoon, and at night the stars are bright.

The best time to visit is the summer and early autumn, from December to April, when the road is dry and the days are long. In winter the plateau is covered in snow and the road is closed, and the cold can be severe. In any season the weather can change quickly, so carry warm clothing, and let someone know where you are going.
t.haast pass west coast@-45.3,169.0:
South-east of Kingston, the land climbs out of the Wakatipu basin and becomes the Old Man Range country, a high plateau of schist tors and tussock that forms the backbone of Central Otago. The pin falls on the western side of those uplands, a few kilometres east of the Garston area, where the Mataura River's headwaters collect and the valley opens toward the south. The nearest towns are Kingston and Cromwell, both a long way off, and the sparse sheep stations here are among the highest in the country.

The Old Man Range rises to about 1,680 metres at the Obelisk, a summit reached only by long tracks in summer, and the plateau around it is a landscape of alpine herbfields, cushion plants and bare rock. It is cold, windy and treeless, and in winter the whole area is under snow. The schist outcrops here, flat slabs of folded metamorphic rock, give the landscape a faintly Scottish feel, and the gold rush of the 1860s left old water races cut across the hillsides that you can still see.

Riding in the area means gravel, as there is no public road over the range itself, and the surrounding sealed roads offer a good experience of the country. State Highway 6 between Kingston and Garston is quiet and scenic, running through farmland with views to the mountains. The surface is good, bends are mild and the main hazard is the odd stock truck or sheep crossing the road. Wind can be strong, and a loaded bike should be handled with care.

Do not expect services. Fuel comes from Queenstown, Frankton or Cromwell, and the nearest food is likely to be a cafe in Kingston, so plan accordingly. A fuel gate on a ride like this is a reminder to fill the tank while you can. The weather is changeable, and the sky is often large and grey with snow showers possible in any month at higher elevations. Take warm clothing, and if you see a hawk hanging over the tussock, stop and watch for a while.
t.haast pass west coast high point@-45.6,1:
The Mataura River gathers in the hills near Garston and then runs south across the Southland plains, and the stretch of State Highway 6 along its upper valley is one of the quiet pleasures of the South Island. The coordinates here lie south-east of Kingston, near Nokomai and Athol, in a country of tussock slopes, willow-lined paddocks and old sheep stations, with the Eyre Mountains and the Garvie range standing back on either side. It is farmland, but of the big, open, hard sort.

The Mataura is famous among fishermen. Its brown trout are large and wary, and anglers come from around the world to fish its pools and riffles with dry flies, so you may see a figure in waders standing motionless in the current at dawn. The town of Athol, a tiny place with a pub and a small shop, is the sort of settlement that survives on passing trade and loyal regulars, while Garston, to the north, is the last small settlement before the lake country.

For a rider, the road is relaxed and satisfying, with long straights, gentle bends and fine views. It runs between Kingston and Lumsden, a small railway junction town, and the surface is generally excellent. Traffic is light outside summer, and the biggest hazards are wind and stock trucks. Lumsden is the useful town at the end of it, a sensible place to refuel and eat before pushing on toward Gore or Invercargill.

The weather in Southland can be wet and cold even in summer, and a bike with good luggage and waterproofs is a sensible choice. Frost makes the road slippery in winter, and fog sometimes settles in the river valleys in the early morning. Take your time, stop at a bridge to look into the water, and watch the birds. Paradise shelducks, in noisy pairs, are everywhere on the paddocks, and the pūkeko, with its blue plumage and red beak, wanders along the verge.
t.haast pass west coast scenic road@-45.4,:
The Mavora Lakes lie in a high valley between the Eyre Mountains and the Livingstone range, a short way off the Mossburn to Te Anau highway, and they are among the loveliest places in Southland. Two lakes, North and South Mavora, are linked by a short river and fringed by beech forest, with tussock flats and snow-dusted peaks beyond. A gravel road from State Highway 94 near Mossburn leads here, and the valley is a favourite with trampers, anglers and anyone who likes an empty horizon.

Film-makers have noticed it too, and the area was used as a location in Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings films, standing in for parts of Middle-earth. You do not need to be a fan to see why, since the combination of mountain beech forest and open tussock land has a primeval look that suits fantasy. In reality it is a conservation park, and the birdlife includes the bellbird, the tomtit and the fantail.

The riding is gravel, usually graded, and the road is long enough to feel remote. The surface changes from smooth to corrugated and from firm to loose, and there are fords and cattle stops on the way. It is a good adventure ride on a lighter bike, but a heavily loaded tourer will find it hard going, so check the conditions locally. After rain the road becomes soft and the creeks rise, and in winter it can be icy or blocked by snow.

The nearest services are in Mossburn and Te Anau, so fill your tank and carry lunch. The Department of Conservation runs simple campsites beside the lakes with basic toilets, and no bookings are required for most of them, which makes it a pleasant place for a night under canvas. Sandflies are an issue around the lake margins, and a good repellent makes a difference. At dusk, the light on the mountains turns pink, and the stillness on the water is remarkable. In the morning, frost whitens the grass, and the first coffee tastes unusually good.
t.arequipa@-16.4,-71.5:
Arequipa announces itself from a distance with a volcano. El Misti, a near-perfect cone of about 5,800 metres, stands behind the city, flanked by the broader mass of Chachani and the older, eroded Pichu Pichu, and on a clear morning the three seem to hang above the rooftops. Arequipa is Peru's second city, home to well over eight hundred thousand people, sitting in a dry valley at roughly 2,300 metres, so you arrive here after a long climb from the coast with your lungs and your engine both a little short of breath.

The city is called the White City because so much of the old centre is built from sillar, a pale volcanic tuff quarried nearby. Carved into arches and domes, it gives the Plaza de Armas its glow, especially at sunset when the stone turns peach. The city was founded by the Spanish in 1540, and the old colonial architecture survived many earthquakes, though not all of it. Santa Catalina Monastery, a walled town within the town, with narrow alleys painted blue and orange, is the sight everyone mentions, and for good reason. Plan a half day.

Riding in is simple enough, but the traffic is busy and chaotic, with minibuses cutting across lanes, so keep alert on the approach roads. The city has fuel at every turn, plenty of mechanics, and a thriving food scene built around local dishes like rocoto relleno, a stuffed hot pepper, and adobo, a pork stew traditionally eaten for breakfast. Sit down for a plate of either and you will understand the pride.

From Arequipa the road toward Colca Canyon leads up and over a high pass, close to 5,000 metres on the way, across a barren altiplano where vicuñas graze and the air is thin and cold. Prepare for altitude properly: spend a day acclimatising in the city before climbing, carry layers, and watch the weather, as snow is possible at the top even in what feels like summer.

The south coastal Panamericana, by contrast, lies far below in desert and fog. Arequipa is the natural pause between the two, a bed, a hot shower and a good meal before the next stage.
t.chivay@-15.6,-71.6:
You will feel Chivay before you see it, in the lungs. The town stands at about 3,600 metres in the Colca Valley, and anyone who rode up from Arequipa at near sea level on the same day tends to arrive a little dizzy, thick-headed and surprisingly hungry. The road does it to you in stages: out of the desert suburbs, up past the cones of Misti and Chachani, across a bleak plateau of alpaca pasture and vicuña at something close to 4,900 metres, and then down again into a green valley that looks like another country entirely.

Chivay is the valley's working capital rather than a showpiece, a market town of four and a half thousand people with a plaza, a handful of simple hotels and the sort of stalls where women in embroidered hats sell potatoes in a dozen colours. The Collagua people terraced these slopes long before the Incas arrived, and the Spanish later gathered the scattered villages into the neat grid towns you still see, each with a whitewashed church of stone and a Spanish name. The terraces are still farmed. Just outside town are hot springs where you can lower yourself into steaming water with the mountains going pink above you, and that is the right way to spend an evening after the altitude.

The ride is the real subject. The tarmac is generally good, but the pass is long and exposed, with fierce cold, sudden hail and thin air that starves a carburetted engine, so give the bike a moment and yourself more. Further along the valley the road follows the canyon rim toward Cabanaconde, passing the Cruz del Cóndor lookout, where Andean condors ride the morning thermals. Be there early, since the big birds tend to show between about eight and ten.

For practical matters, treat the fuel tank in Arequipa as your main supply and top up whatever you can in Chivay, where small stations serve the valley. Drink plenty of water, go easy on the first night, and try the coca tea, which locals swear by and which at least gives you something warm to hold. Evenings drop close to freezing even in the dry season.
The pin falls in the Pine Barrens, near Lakewood and the villages of Vista Center and Cedar Glen West, and the landscape is the great surprise of New Jersey. The Pinelands cover about a million acres of sandy soil, scrub pine, oak and cedar swamp, and they form the first national reserve in the United States, protected since 1978. Beneath them lies an enormous aquifer of pure water, and the streams that run through the forest are stained a deep tea colour by cedar tannins, so that you cross a small bridge over a dark river as clear as brandy.

The Barrens have long been a source of legend. The Jersey Devil, a winged creature with hooves and a horse's head, is said to have been born here in 1735 to a woman named Mother Leeds, and sightings are still reported. Whether you believe it or not, a quiet evening in the deep pines, with an owl calling and mist on the road, makes it easy to see where the stories began. Not far away, at Lakehurst, the airship Hindenburg burst into flames while landing in May 1937, an event that ended the age of passenger airships.

For riders, the roads here are flat and straight, running between walls of pine, with long views and little traffic away from the main routes. It is gentle riding, ideal for a quiet morning, although sand can drift onto the road in places, and deer are common at dusk. Route 70 and the smaller county roads cross the forest, and speed limits are strictly applied. The high point on the label is a matter of a few tens of metres, since this is a coastal plain.

Fuel is available in Lakewood, a large town to the north, and along the main routes, but the forest roads have few services, so keep the tank topped up. Summer is hot and buggy, and ticks are common in the woods, so check yourself after a walk. Autumn gives the best conditions, with crisp air and gold-brown leaves, and in spring the pinelands bloom with wildflowers and blueberry flowers, since this is also the heart of New Jersey's blueberry farms.
t.taconic parkway backroads scenic road@40:
Gladstone and Peapack sit in the hills of Somerset County, New Jersey, in a country of horse farms, stone walls and large estates that has been the preserve of wealthy New Yorkers since the late nineteenth century. It is called the Somerset Hills, though the hills are modest, a rolling ridge country of oak woods and meadows dropping to the North Branch of the Raritan River. The area has the unhurried look of old money, with long driveways, white fences and stables, and it is surprisingly rural, only an hour's drive from Manhattan.

Far Hills, next door, hosts a famous steeplechase every October, when thousands of people picnic on the hillside and watch horses jump the fences, and the Golf House of the United States Golf Association is nearby, with a museum of the game. A few kilometres to the east, Morristown holds a place in American history. George Washington's army spent the harsh winter of 1779 to 1780 in the hills there, in log huts, suffering through the coldest weather of the century, and Jockey Hollow, part of the National Historical Park, preserves the camp and the countryside.

The riding is pleasing. The roads wind through woods, past farms and over small streams, with bends that are tighter than you expect, and many are lined with old trees and stone walls that come close to the road. The surface is mixed, with some rough patches from frost, and the traffic can be heavy at commuter hours. It is a place for a relaxed ride, particularly on weekday mornings and in autumn, when the maples and oaks turn red and gold. Watch for deer, which are abundant, and for cyclists, who use the roads in numbers on weekends.

Fuel is available at a few stations in the nearby towns of Bedminster and Chester, and attendants will pump it for you, as New Jersey law requires. A coffee shop in Peapack or Gladstone offers a simple stop, and the larger town of Morristown has many restaurants. The early morning light over the fields, with a thin mist rising from the meadows, is one of the quieter pleasures of the state.
t.haast@-45.3,169.0:
East of Kingston the lake country loosens its grip and the land turns to schist hills, tussock and wide, dry valleys with merino sheep spread across them like a scattering of rice. This point lies in that stretch, between the southern end of Lake Wakatipu and the Cromwell Basin, in a region where stone walls, shearing sheds and old gold workings tell the history of the Otago high country.

Gold is the thread that runs through it. After 1861, when Gabriel Read found gold at Tuapeka, prospectors flooded into the area, sluicing the creeks and tearing apart the riverbanks, and the remains of their water races and stone huts survive in the hills. Later came sheep runs of enormous size, many of which are still working stations today. The land is harsh, hot and dusty in summer and bitterly cold in winter, and the vegetation, mostly tussock and scrub, has an austere beauty that grows on you.

Kingston, a small settlement with a couple of thousand people, sits at the lake's southern tip and was once the terminus of the Kingston Flyer, a steam train that ran to Fairlight. Cromwell, about thirty-five kilometres away, is the main town of the region, known for stone fruit, with a giant fibreglass piece of fruit by the roadside as a monument to its orchards. Between them the roads run through open, rolling country with long visibility and often a strong wind, and the traffic is light.

The Haast Pass route begins from this country and heads north, but here you are still far from the mountain walls. Riding is easy, with good surfaces and gentle gradients, and the main hazards are crosswinds, stock on unfenced roads and the glare of low sun. In winter, black ice may form on shaded corners at dawn. Expect cold nights even in summer, and dry air that parches your throat.

For fuel, use Cromwell or Queenstown, as small settlements have limited hours. Cromwell also has bakeries and fruit stalls in season, so a stop for apricots or cherries in summer is almost obligatory. Water is worth carrying, as shops are few and far between.

The light is best early or late, when the tussock glows gold and the hills cast long shadows. This is a landscape of space, and it rewards a slow pace.
t.te anau overnight@-45.4,167.7:
Te Anau is a small town with a large job. It sits on the shore of the lake of the same name, the biggest in the South Island, and serves as the gateway to Fiordland National Park, one of the wildest places in New Zealand. About two thousand people live here year-round, many of them working in the tourism that comes through, and in summer the main street is full of campervans and people with boots and cameras.

What lies beyond is extraordinary. Fiordland is a mountainous rainforest country of glacier-carved valleys and sea inlets, shaped by some of the heaviest rainfall in the country. Milford Sound, at the end of the 119-kilometre road from Te Anau, receives so much rain that waterfalls appear by the dozen after a downpour. The Milford Road itself passes through the Eglinton Valley, with its wide flat floor and beech forest, then the Mirror Lakes, where the peaks reflect on calm water, and finally the Homer Tunnel, a rough-hewn tunnel about 1.2 kilometres long that was completed in 1953 after decades of work, with a steep descent to the sound on the other side.

The riding is superb but needs care. The road is mostly well surfaced, with gentle bends in the valley and tighter ones near the tunnel, and in wet weather it can be slippery. Avalanches close the road in winter and spring, and snow chains may be required. Rain can arrive suddenly, and you should expect to be wet at some point. Sandflies swarm at every stop, so carry repellent.

In town you can find a bed, a meal and a bakery. Fuel is essential here, since services beyond Te Anau are almost non-existent, so fill up before you set out for Milford and back. The Te Anau Wildlife Centre keeps takahē, a large flightless bird once thought extinct and found again in the Fiordland mountains in 1948, and it is a good rainy-day stop. Boat trips to the glowworm caves on the far side of the lake are popular.

Spend the evening on the lakeshore with the light fading on the Murchison Mountains. Rise early the next day for Milford, before the coaches arrive.
t.crown range and wanaka high point@-45.1,:
Between Cromwell and the Carrick Range the land is bare, brown and enormous, an old schist plateau broken into long ridges and dry valleys, and the high point here belongs to that world rather than to the famous passes. It is Central Otago, the driest, coldest-in-winter and hottest-in-summer region in the country, a place of tussock and thyme, rabbits and rock outcrops that look like crumbling castles. Cromwell, eighteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, and Arrowtown lies to the west.

Riding in this district is a matter of picking your road. State Highway 6 and the roads along the Kawarau Gorge are fast, rolling and exposed, running by blue-green water through country that was dredged and sluiced a hundred and sixty years ago. Beyond the pavement there are gravel roads that lead high into the ranges, and some of them, like the Nevis Road, are famous for their remote beauty, and only for riders with proper tyres, a sound plan and a taste for loneliness. Summer is the season for those, and the weather up there can turn from sunny to bitter in half an hour.

The landscape is a lesson in geology. The schist you see here was pushed up and tilted in a long, slow collision between two tectonic plates, and glaciers then planed the surface and left behind great, smooth basins and gravel terraces. Wind and water have done the rest, leaving the strange, stacked tors the locals call Otago castles. It is an odd, spare, lovely place, and the light at either end of the day turns the tussock gold and the shadows blue.

Cromwell is the town for fuel, groceries and a decent meal. The old Cromwell township was drowned when the Clyde Dam closed in the early 1990s and the waters rose to form Lake Dunstan, and the new Heritage Precinct beside the lake preserves what could be saved. It is worth a look. Fruit stalls along the highway sell cherries, apricots and peaches in season, and a bag of those on the pillion seat is one of the minor joys of Central Otago in January.
t.crown range and wanaka photo pull off@-4:
Kingston is a tiny, calm settlement at the southern tip of Lake Wakatipu, and getting there from Queenstown is half the point. The road, State Highway 6, runs along the lake shore under the long, bare ridge of the Remarkables, rising and falling through a sequence of bends known locally as the Devil's Staircase. It is wonderfully good riding, with the water on your left in a shade of blue so deep it looks like ink, the mountains looming on your right and a surface smooth enough that you can concentrate on the line. In the early morning, with mist on the lake and the sun catching the peaks, it is as good as this country gets.

The lake itself has a legend, and a strange fact to match it. The Māori story tells of a giant, Matau, burned in his sleep, whose heart still beats under the water. The real explanation, a seiche, makes the lake rise and fall by a few centimetres every twenty-five minutes or so, which does look rather like a heartbeat. The Lake sits in a trough carved by ice, and the water is deep and very cold, though people swim in it on hot days.

In Kingston you will find a pub, a cafe or two and a railway of some fame. The Kingston Flyer, a historic steam train, used to carry passengers between here and Fairlight, and while its operation has been intermittent in recent years, the old station is a pleasant place to idle. The village itself has just a couple of thousand people, and offers basic services, but for serious fuel and supplies you are better off in Queenstown, about thirty kilometres back.

From here the road splits: south to Lumsden and Fiordland, or east toward Cromwell and the old goldfields. The wind picks up in the afternoons, especially in summer, and a westerly can find the open corners with some venom, so keep a firm grip on the bars. Bring a warm layer, since the shadow of the mountains falls early and the temperature drops quickly once the sun goes behind the ridge.
t.crown range and wanaka@-45.2,168.3:
There is no road to speak of at this spot, and that is the interesting thing about it. The coordinates lie on the far, western side of Lake Wakatipu, in the empty hill country that falls toward the lake from the Mavora and Mount Nicholas side. Queenstown is nearly forty kilometres away across the water and Kingston about as far by the long road around the south end. What you find here is a landscape of tussock slopes, beech gullies and grey rock that has barely changed since the first sheep were driven in during the 1860s.

This is high-country station country, and one of the best-known stations lies a short boat ride from town. Walter Peak is reached by a steamship, the TSS Earnslaw, a coal-fired vessel launched in 1912 and still carrying passengers across the lake. Watching it plough its way across the water, belching smoke and with the Remarkables as a backdrop, is one of the best sights in Queenstown. Station life up here still follows an older rhythm, with muster, shearing and the long winter feeding of stock, and travellers are welcome at some of the farms for a meal.

For a motorcyclist, the interest is mostly in what you can reach and what you cannot. The unsealed roads on this side of the lake lead into very remote terrain, and you should treat them accordingly. Take a spare, tell someone where you are going, and do not expect a mobile signal. The sealed road from Kingston toward Lumsden is the sane choice, a pleasant, fast, empty ride across farmland with long views toward the Eyre Mountains.

If you want a meal, the places to look are Queenstown and Kingston, and do not expect much in between. Fill your tank before you start. The weather on the lake side of the ranges can be wild, with squalls running down the water, and the temperature falls fast when cloud lowers. A warm hat and a flask of something hot are a good idea even in summer, and the stars at night, in a place with no light pollution to speak of, are astonishing.
t.catlins@-46.5,169.7:
The Catlins is the part of New Zealand that people tend to skip, and then regret skipping. It is a ragged southeastern coast, running from Waipapa Point on the Southland side to the Clutha River mouth, a country of dense rimu and rata forest that comes down to the sea, of black cliffs, remote beaches and heavy Southern Ocean surf. Papatowai is a tiny settlement near the middle of it, with Balclutha a long way north and Owaka a smaller place to the east, and you feel the isolation immediately. The road, part of the Southern Scenic Route between Dunedin and Invercargill, is mostly sealed but narrow and twisting, rarely straight for more than a few hundred metres.

What makes the Catlins special is its wildlife and its geology. At Curio Bay, at low tide, you can walk across a rock platform that holds the stumps of a Jurassic forest, around a hundred and eighty million years old, with the stone logs still lying where the trees fell. Yellow-eyed penguins, or hoiho, one of the rarest penguins in the world, come ashore at dusk on some of the beaches, and sea lions and fur seals haul out on the sand. At Nugget Point a lighthouse sits on a narrow ridge above a scatter of rocky islets, and the Cathedral Caves can only be reached at low tide.

The forests are damp and green, with ferns and moss thick on every trunk, and waterfalls such as Purakaunui, tiered and beautiful, are a short walk from the road. Expect rain at any time of year, and cold wind off the ocean even in summer. The roads can be slippery under the trees, with wet leaves and patches of gravel, so keep a generous margin. Sheep and cattle are often on the road, and slow vehicles are common.

Fuel is thin here, and you should plan for it. Fill the tank in Balclutha or Invercargill before you enter the area, and treat any station you pass in the Catlins as a bonus. Food is limited, though small cafes in Owaka and a roadside stall or two offer simple fare, and fresh fish and chips from a coastal shop taste better here than anywhere else.
t.lindis@-45.5,168.8:
Here the lake country gives way to northern Southland, a region of broad river flats, low mountains and farms that stretch to the horizon. The coordinates sit south of Kingston, in the valley of the Mataura River, where the water runs clear and cold over stones and anglers stand in the shallows with fly rods.

The Mataura has a reputation among fishermen that reaches well beyond New Zealand. Its brown trout are large, wary and rewarding, and the season draws fly fishers from around the world, who stay in small lodges and farmhouses. Beyond the river, the hills are covered in tussock and merino sheep, and in places the land is crossed by old stone walls built by early settlers. The air is dry and clean, and in autumn the poplars along the river turn the colour of butter.

Kingston, a small township at the southern tip of Lake Wakatipu, is the nearest settlement. It was an important gateway in the gold rush and later became the terminus of a railway that took visitors to the lake steamers. The Kingston Flyer, a heritage steam train, ran on that line for many years. Today the town is quiet, with a few shops and a view over the water to the Remarkables.

The ride's name refers to the Lindis Pass, a very different landscape to the north-east, but the riding here has its own charm. The roads through Southland are generally straight and fast, with long views and occasional bends where they cross rivers and ridges. Traffic is light, with farm vehicles, trucks and the occasional campervan. Wind can be strong, and frost can lie on the road in the early morning. Look out for sheep and cattle crossing, since stock are moved along the road in places.

Fuel can be hard to find. Kingston has limited services, and the sensible plan is to fill up in Queenstown or Te Anau, where stations are reliable. Cafes in the small towns often close early, so pack a lunch. The nearest large town to the south is Invercargill, a long ride away.

Go in the afternoon, when the light is warm and the hills glow. Stop by the river for a few minutes and watch the water.
t.mount cook@-45.2,168.4:
Aoraki is the Māori name for New Zealand's highest mountain, and it matters. In Ngāi Tahu tradition, Aoraki and his brothers were sons of the sky who came down in a canoe, which ran aground and turned to stone; the canoe became the South Island, and the brothers became the peaks of the Southern Alps, with Aoraki the tallest. Mount Cook, the English name, honours the navigator James Cook, who never actually saw it up close. The summit stands at about 3,724 metres.

The mountain lies far to the north-east of this point, which sits in the mountains west of Queenstown, and the ride called Mount Cook High Country goes there by way of Twizel and Lake Pukaki. The lake is the great surprise on the way, with water of an almost unnatural turquoise colour, caused by rock flour from the glaciers, and the white mountain reflected in it. A road runs along its western shore towards the village at the foot of the mountain, with views that justify frequent stops.

The first ascent of Aoraki was made on Christmas Day 1894, by Tom Fyfe, George Graham and Jack Clarke, who climbed from the Hooker Valley without much equipment. Edmund Hillary learned his craft on its slopes, and the Hermitage hotel at the village has long been a base for climbers and walkers. The Hooker Valley track, an easy walk of a couple of hours, leads to a glacial lake with icebergs floating in front of the mountain, and it is hard to beat.

For riding, the road to the village is very good, with long, open bends beside the lake, exposed to wind from the mountains and sometimes crossed by sheep. The weather can change rapidly, with snow possible on the approach at any time of year, and cloud often hides the summit. The traffic is mostly coaches and campervans in summer. Make sure you have enough fuel, because services in the village are limited, and fill up in Twizel, which has stations and a supermarket.

The Mackenzie Basin is high, cold and dry, and the nights are brilliant with stars. If you can, camp or stay overnight and watch the mountain turn pink at dawn.
t.catlins coastal weekend@-45.2,168.6:
Everything in this corner of Otago is arranged around one odd, long, crooked lake. Wakatipu is shaped like a lightning bolt, about eighty kilometres from the Rees and Dart at the north to the flats beyond Kingston in the south, and so deep that its floor lies below sea level even though its surface sits well above it. The ice that gouged it was part of a huge glacier system that spilled out of the Southern Alps, and the moraine ridges you see around Frankton and the airport are what it left behind when it retreated. The name on the stop talks of the Catlins, which are a long drive south-east, but here you are firmly on the lake, with Queenstown nineteen kilometres off and Kingston just as far in the other direction.

For a rider this is the supply point. Frankton, at the eastern edge of the town, has fuel stations, supermarkets and a good cluster of places to eat, and it is the last easy place to fill up before you head toward Kingston, Cromwell or Wanaka. If you are going anywhere beyond, it makes sense to top the tank here and check the weather over the ranges before you leave. Mornings are clear and cold, afternoons can be warm and gusty, and snow on the Remarkables is possible nearly all year above the ski field.

The mountain wall behind the town gave the range its name, which is one of the better pieces of understatement in the country. The name is said to come from early settlers who looked at the long serrated ridge and the sheer drop to the lake and found it remarkable, and nobody has had a better word since. In the evening, when the sun drops behind Cecil Peak and the ridgeline turns pink, it is easy to see what they meant.

Queenstown itself grew from the gold rush and has since become a place of bungy jumps and jet boats, but the older heart is still visible in the small stone cottages near the lakefront and the wooden pub signs. Traffic can be heavy and parking tight, so a motorbike has the advantage, and in high summer the lakeshore road can be a slow procession. Go early, eat well, and leave while the light is soft.
t.catlins coastal weekend high point@-45.2:
From the water's edge on the Wakatipu shore the mountains on the far side rise in tiers, and the one you notice first is Cecil Peak, a steep, pointed block of rock that looks like a child's drawing of a mountain. Next to it stands Walter Peak, and beyond, further south and west, the long grey backbone of ranges leading toward Fiordland. The coordinates sit on the quiet western flank of the lake, a part of the country that most visitors only see from the water. Kingston is twenty-seven kilometres away by road, and Queenstown is further on.

The story of this landscape is a story of ice. During the last glaciation a giant tongue of ice flowed down the Wakatipu trough, scouring the sides into steep walls and leaving the lake bed far below the present waterline. When it retreated it left terraces, rounded spurs and long ridges of rubble that now carry the sheep tracks and the roads. The rock itself is schist, a layered metamorphic stone that glints in the sun and flakes into plates, and you can pick a piece off any outcrop and see the sparkle of mica.

Riding on this side of the lake is more demanding than the sealed road along the east shore. Roads are unsealed, often narrow, and in places badly corrugated, and the weather changes without notice. What you get in exchange is solitude, with long clear views of mountains, a very low volume of traffic, and wide tracts of tussock country where hawks ride the thermals and the wind brings the smell of warm grass and thyme. If you go, go in good weather, carry a repair kit, and be prepared to turn back.

Anyone wanting the easy version should stay on State Highway 6 along the eastern shore, which is sealed, well marked and entirely beautiful. Fuel and food are in Queenstown and Kingston, and the Kingston end has a sleepy pub where a pie and a pint taste excellent after a day in the wind. The days in winter are short, so make sure you are off the gravel by early afternoon. In spring you may see lambs in the paddocks beside the road, and in autumn the poplars at the farm gates turn gold.
t.catlins coastal weekend@-45.1,169.1:
Between Cromwell and Bannockburn the road runs through a country of vines. Rows of grapes now cover slopes that were once piled with the gravel left by gold sluicing, and some of the most admired pinot noir in the southern hemisphere comes from this hot, dry, unlikely patch of ground. Cromwell lies nine kilometres to the north-east, and the whole district is quiet and sun-baked, with rock outcrops, thyme and old stone cottages between the rows. It is the kind of place where you plan lunch around a cellar door, and a rider who stops has an easy and enjoyable afternoon.

The reason vines do so well here is the climate, with its long dry summers, cold nights and a warm autumn that lets the fruit ripen slowly. The reason the land looks the way it does is the gold rush. In the 1860s miners tore up Bannockburn with water cannon, sluicing whole hillsides into the creek to extract the metal, and the strange pinnacles and gullies of those sluicings are still visible, now a walking trail through a lunar landscape of pale silt. Old stone huts still stand among them, built by men who took their gold, or their disappointment, and moved on.

The roads here are quiet and pleasant, running through small farms, vineyards and open fields with the dry hills behind. The bends are mild, the surface generally good and the views wide, and you will meet far more cyclists than cars. Do keep alert on gravel entrances to vineyards, where loose stones can catch you out, and watch for bird-scaring cannons in autumn, which go off with a bang that can make a nervous rider jump.

Food is the point of this stop. Several wineries and restaurants around Bannockburn serve long, slow lunches in gardens, and many are used to riders and cyclists, but remember that tasting and riding do not mix, and the answer is to share one glass or buy a bottle to take home. Fuel and supermarkets are in Cromwell. If you have time, the old Bannockburn sluicings walk is short, quiet and unexpectedly moving, a reminder of how fast this country was changed by money and ambition.
t.catlins coastal@-45.2,168.6:
South of Queenstown the main road to Kingston hugs the eastern shore of Lake Wakatipu in a stretch known as the Devil's Staircase, and the coordinates here fall close to it. It is the best piece of lakeside riding in the district, a ribbon of tarmac cut into steep hillside above the water, with bends that tighten and release, and views down to the lake that make you want to stop at every turnout.

The name comes from the days before the road, when the track was so rough that it was said to be passable only by the devil himself. Today the surface is good and the road is well engineered, but it still has sheer drops on the lake side and the occasional rockfall after heavy rain. The lake is cold, deep and a rich blue, with the high peaks of the Mid Wakatipu on the far side, and in the evening the light on the mountains is superb. Traffic can be heavy in summer, with tourists in campervans, so patience is useful.

At the end of the road sits Kingston, a quiet township at the southern tip of the lake, where the Kingston Flyer once ran. Beyond it the road continues south through farmland towards Lumsden and then to Southland. The Catlins, which the ride is named for, lie on the far south-eastern coast, a long day away. The landscape in between is flat, open and green, in contrast to the mountains behind.

Riding here is a pleasure, with the lake on one side and cliffs on the other. Watch for gravel on the corners and for slow vehicles that stop suddenly for photographs. Weather can change quickly, with wind rising from the south and rain moving up the lake, so keep your waterproofs handy. Snow is possible in winter, and ice can form on shaded bends in the morning.

Fuel is available in Queenstown, about nineteen kilometres away, and in a limited form in Kingston, so fill up before you leave town. Cafes in Queenstown are plentiful, and the road itself offers many places to stop and picnic. If you are heading for the Catlins, pack food, since services are sparse.

Start early, when the lake is still and the traffic is light. The Staircase is at its best before the day-trippers arrive.
t.camana@-16.6,-72.7:
Camaná is a fishing and farming town at the mouth of a river that actually reaches the sea, which in this part of Peru is a minor miracle. South of Lima, the Pacific coast is one of the driest deserts in the world, a belt of sand and bare rock that goes on for a thousand kilometres, and only a handful of rivers carry enough water down from the Andes to make a green valley. The Camaná is one of them, and the ribbon of rice fields, orchards and reeds around the town is startling after hours of grey and yellow. The town has about sixteen thousand people, with beaches nearby, and it is a favourite summer holiday spot for families from Arequipa, who drive down the long road from the mountains.

The ride here along the Panamericana Sur is a long, hypnotic one. The road runs between sea and cliff, with the Pacific on one side, immense dunes and rocky headlands on the other and, now and then, a small fishing village hanging on the edge. The surface is mostly good, but trucks are heavy and frequent, and drivers overtake on blind bends, so stay alert and keep well to the right. Fog, locally called garúa, rolls in off the cold Humboldt Current and can hide the coast in the early morning, so wait for it to lift. Wind is common in the afternoons, and sand blows across the road.

Camaná is known for its shrimp, camarones, which are caught in the river and cooked in a rich, spicy stew called chupe, usually with potatoes and a poached egg. It is the dish to order here, and it tastes best at a simple family restaurant near the main square. Seafood generally is excellent, and there is fruit in plenty, especially in summer.

All services are available: fuel stations along the highway, banks, cafes and a range of hotels. After a day of riding along the coast, the beach is a good place to rest, though currents can be dangerous, so swim only where locals do. The sunsets over the Pacific are slow and red, and the town takes on a pleasantly sleepy air as the heat fades.
t.cabanaconde@-15.6,-72.0:
Cabanaconde sits right on the lip of the Colca Canyon, at a height of about 3,300 metres, and at the end of the road you simply look down into one of the deepest valleys on the planet. The canyon plunges more than three thousand metres in places, though people argue about the measurement, and the Colca River is a thin silver thread at the bottom. Terraces carved by pre-Inca peoples climb the walls in neat steps, and are still farmed with maize and potatoes, as they have been for centuries.

The village itself is small and unfussy, a collection of stone and adobe houses, a plaza with a church and a few simple guesthouses used by trekkers. Women wear embroidered hats and layered skirts, in the traditions of the Cabana and Collagua peoples, and the streets smell of woodsmoke and llama dung. A trail drops from the edge of the village to Sangalle, a green oasis of palms and pools at the canyon bottom, which takes a couple of hours down and a good deal longer coming back up.

The best-known sight is the Cruz del Cóndor, a viewpoint a short distance away, where Andean condors ride the morning thermals rising from the canyon. With a wingspan of up to three metres, they pass so close that you can hear the air in their feathers. Go early, because the birds fly best in the first hours after sunrise, and the crowds build quickly.

For a rider the road from Chivay is a journey in itself. It follows the canyon's rim, with sections of good tarmac and sections of rough surface, rockfall and the occasional landslide, and the views of the terraces and the volcano peaks are superb. The altitude is serious, and a motorbike loses power in thin air. Nights are cold, mornings can be frosty, and in the rainy season, from December to March, storms make the road greasy. Altitude sickness is a real risk, so ascend gradually and drink water.

Fuel is a point to plan for. Cabanaconde is tiny, and the dependable stop is Chivay, so fill up there before riding on, and carry a spare if you can. Warm clothes matter more than you expect, even at midday.

Spend the evening with a coca tea and watch the canyon turn purple in the dusk.
t.jeffersonville@44.6,-72.8:
Smugglers' Notch gets its name honestly. When President Jefferson's Embargo Act of 1807 closed trade with Canada, Vermonters hauled goods north through this narrow gap in the Green Mountains rather than go without, and a century later the same pass served bootleggers during Prohibition. Jeffersonville sits on the Lamoille River at the northern foot of that pass, a small village of white clapboard houses, a general store feel, and a covered bridge or two within easy riding distance. Mount Mansfield, Vermont's highest peak at 4,393 feet, looms behind it, and the village has long attracted painters and potters who came for the light and stayed for the quiet.

The ride up Route 108 is the reason to be here. Within a few miles of town the road narrows to little more than a lane and a half, hemmed in by cliffs that rise about a thousand feet and by car-sized boulders that have tumbled onto the slopes. Hairpins come close together, there are blind corners where the rock overhangs the tarmac, and the surface can be damp even in July. Take it slowly, stay well within your own side, and expect other riders, cyclists and walkers on the narrow sections. Large trucks and trailers are banned, which keeps the notch intimate. The road closes for winter, usually from about November until late spring, so check before you go.

At the top there is a small parking area with a short trail among the boulders, a few of which have been given names by generations of visitors, and the air is distinctly cooler than in the valley. Down the far side you reach Stowe, a resort town with plenty of cafes, bakeries and shops, and from there Route 100 returns through the Green Mountain valleys.

For practical purposes, Jeffersonville is small, and the best fuel and supplies are at Morrisville, about twelve miles away, so top up before you head into the hills. Local sugar houses sell maple syrup, cheese and cider donuts in season. September and early October bring the famous foliage, along with the traffic, and late spring, once the road has opened, is a good time for empty roads.
t.conway@44.0,-71.1:
Conway is the front door to the Kancamagus, and the road starts quietly, with a few motels and a gas station, and then plunges into the White Mountain National Forest. The Kancamagus Highway, New Hampshire Route 112, runs about thirty-four miles west to Lincoln, following the Swift River up a narrow valley and then climbing over a pass at nearly 2,900 feet, with forest on both sides and almost no buildings. The name comes from Kancamagus, a sachem of the Pennacook people in the late seventeenth century, who tried to keep the peace with English settlers before leaving the region.

The riding is relaxed and rhythmic, with long, flowing bends rather than anything tight, and views of mountain ridges, river pools and birch trees. Albany Covered Bridge crosses the Swift River near the start, and Sabbaday Falls, Lower Falls and Rocky Gorge are all short walks from roadside parking areas. Recreation passes are required for parking at many trailheads along the route.

Foliage is the big draw. From late September to mid October the maples, birches and beeches turn red, orange and yellow, and the Kanc, as locals call it, fills with cars and motorcycles. Weekends can be slow and crowded, so a weekday morning is a better time. In June the air smells of pine and wet leaves, and the road is quiet, with mountain laurel in bloom.

Conway is a small village with about eighteen hundred people, with North Conway, a short ride north, a larger resort town full of outlet shops, restaurants and a historic railroad station. If you want a good meal, there are plenty of choices, from diners to craft breweries. The larger town of Moultonborough, with fuel and more options, is further south. Winter closes nothing officially, but snow and ice make it a risky ride, so the sensible season runs from May to October.
t.port jervis@41.4,-74.7:
Port Jervis is a river town at the point where three states meet, and the meeting is the first thing the place wants to tell you about. At a spot where the Neversink River runs into the Delaware, New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania come together, and a stone monument, set up in the 1880s, marks the point. The town itself lies on the New York side, with the pale hills of the Kittatinny Ridge in New Jersey rising to the south and the Pennsylvania bank across the water at Matamoras. About nine thousand people live here, and there is all the fuel, coffee and breakfast any rider could ask for.

The town grew up with canals and railways. The Delaware and Hudson Canal, which carried anthracite coal from the Pennsylvania mines to the Hudson River, passed through here, and later the Erie Railroad built a major yard and a repair shop, which employed generations of local people. The Erie still gives the place its character, with old brick buildings, a handsome railroad station and a busy main street. Today it is a commuter link and a popular gateway to the Upper Delaware, and the diners and bakeries do a good trade with weekend visitors on bikes, canoes and motorcycles.

For a rider the town is the start of one of the loveliest river roads in the north-east. Route 97, which heads north-east along the Delaware, is a narrow, curving, scenic road with the river on one side and the rock on the other, and it begins just outside the town. The surface is generally good, though frost heaves can be rough in spring, and the road is popular, so on a sunny summer weekend you will share it with plenty of other bikes. The best times to ride are early on a weekday morning, or in the first week of October, when the leaves turn.

For food, the local diners serve generous breakfasts, and there are pizza places, bakeries and cafes along the main street. Fuel stations are on the main roads on the edge of town. The climate is typical of the upper Mid-Atlantic, with warm, humid summers, cold winters and sudden thunderstorms. Be careful on the bridge decks, which can be slippery when wet, and watch for deer at dusk, since they are common.
t.hawk s nest cliff road@41.4,-74.7:
Route 97 between Port Jervis and Barryville is one of those roads that every rider in the north-east seems to know, and the section called Hawk's Nest is the reason. The road was cut into the face of the cliff high above the Delaware River in the 1930s, and for a few kilometres it clings to the rock, with the rock wall on one side and a stone parapet on the other, and the river a long way below. The curves are tight and sinuous, the views through the trees are wonderful, and the whole stretch has the air of a miniature Alpine road. There is a small pull-off at the overlook, where you can park and look down at the river and the forested hills beyond.

The Delaware here is a broad, green, free-flowing river, and there is a good chance you will see canoes or rafts drifting below. In winter the river valley is a haven for bald eagles, which come south from the frozen north to feed on fish, and the stretch near Barryville is a popular place for eagle watchers. Further along the road is Lackawaxen, where the Roebling Delaware Aqueduct, built in the 1840s as part of a canal, is now a road bridge and one of the oldest wire suspension bridges in America. It was designed by John Roebling, who later built the Brooklyn Bridge.

The road is much loved, but it demands respect. Sight lines are short, there is gravel on the corners in spring, and the shoulders are narrow. Police patrol the road, and speed limits are enforced firmly, so take it at a measured pace. Weekends in summer are crowded, and the corners are full of cyclists, cars and other bikes, so a weekday morning is the best time to enjoy it. In autumn the foliage is spectacular, with the maples turning red and gold, and the river catching the light below.

Fuel is available in Port Jervis, about seven kilometres from here, and in the small towns along the river, but do not count on the stations being open late. A roadside stand or cafe at Barryville or Lackawaxen is a good place to stop for coffee or a sandwich. Be alert for deer on the road, especially at dusk, and for wet leaves in autumn, which can be as slippery as ice.
t.delaware river view@41.5,-74.8:
The Delaware is one of the quiet success stories of American rivers. From its sources in the Catskills it runs for hundreds of miles to the sea at Delaware Bay, and for most of that length it is free-flowing, without a major dam on its main stem, which makes it the longest undammed river east of the Mississippi. The stretch here, part of the Upper Delaware Scenic and Recreational River, a unit of the national park system, runs through a forested valley of low ridges and small farms, with the river broad and green in summer and grey and icy in winter. The pull-off here gives a view down onto the water, with a bridge or two and the hills beyond.

The river's water is clean enough to drink after treatment, and it supplies millions of people in New York City and Philadelphia. Fishermen come for trout and shad, canoeists for the easy rapids, and eagle watchers for the wintering birds, which perch in the big sycamores along the banks. On warm summer weekends the water is full of rafts and inner tubes, and the road is busy with trailers and trucks. In autumn the foliage along the valley is worth a detour in itself.

The riding here is relaxed and pleasant. The road follows the river with gentle curves, passing little villages, old inns and small farms, and the surface is mostly good, though patches of broken tarmac appear after winter. The traffic is moderate, and tends to build in the afternoon, so it makes sense to ride in the morning and find a place for lunch by two. Keep an eye out for turning trucks and for cyclists, who share the road, and take care on bridges, where the decks can be slick after rain.

Fuel is at Port Jervis, about ten kilometres south, and there is not much in between, so check your tank before you set out. There are small stores and diners in the villages, with the usual north-eastern fare of burgers, pie and strong coffee. The river is cold, even in summer, but there are public access points where you can wade or swim. Come at dawn if you can, when mist lies on the river and the only sound is the water.
t.high point new jersey@41.3,-74.7:
High Point is the highest place in New Jersey, a fact that surprises people who think of the state as a flat belt of turnpikes and refineries. It sits on the Kittatinny Ridge, a long, straight line of old rock that runs from the Delaware Water Gap in the south-west up toward the New York border, and at 1,803 feet above sea level, it is a modest summit by Western standards but a real one. A stone obelisk, 220 feet tall and built in 1930, crowns the top, and from its platform on a clear day you can see three states: New Jersey, Pennsylvania and New York. The Delaware River winds silver below, and the green farmland of the valley stretches out on every side.

The park around the monument is a protected stretch of forest, lakes and cedar swamp, with trails, picnic areas and the Appalachian Trail, which passes within a short distance. The ridge is a major migration route for hawks and eagles in autumn, and birdwatchers gather here in September and October to count them as they ride the updrafts. In summer the woods are full of warblers, in spring the dogwoods bloom, and in winter the ridge is a quiet white hush.

The road up to the monument is a climbing curve through hardwood forest, with a good surface and little traffic outside the weekends. It is not a challenging road, but it is a pretty one, and the ride along the ridge on Route 23 offers long views of the valley. The weather at the top can be cooler and windier than below, and in winter the road can be icy. The monument and the park roads are closed at times, so check the opening hours before you go.

Port Jervis, about seven kilometres away, has fuel, food and everything else you need. Matamoras, on the Pennsylvania side of the river, is closer and has a few shops and cafes. A bag of sandwiches and a thermos at the base of the monument, with the whole valley spread out beneath you, makes a fine lunch. Be careful of black bears, which live in these woods, and keep food out of sight when you leave the bike.
t.milford river@41.3,-74.8:
Milford, Pennsylvania, is a village of fewer than a thousand people, and it has a very large story attached to it. On the hill just above the main street stands Grey Towers, a French-style chateau of grey stone built in the 1880s as the family home of Gifford Pinchot, who became the first chief of the United States Forest Service and later governor of Pennsylvania. Pinchot was one of the founders of the American conservation movement, and it was here, at his family home, that he and other leaders of the movement planned their campaigns. The house is now a national historic site, open to visitors, and the grounds are lovely.

The village itself is a gem of old brick and white clapboard, with a courthouse, a handful of historic inns, shops, galleries and a tiny green. It sits on a bluff above the Delaware River, in a gentle and pretty landscape of hills, woods and farmland. A short drive away, Raymondskill Falls, the tallest waterfall in Pennsylvania, drops in three stages through a rocky glen, and a boardwalk and a short path lead to viewing platforms. The sound of water is a pleasure, especially after rain or in spring.

For a rider, Milford is a good lunch or coffee stop on the road along the river. The roads in the area are winding and scenic, with hills and woodland, and the surfaces are generally good, though frost heaves can be an issue in spring. Traffic can be thick on weekends in summer and autumn, when visitors from New York and New Jersey flood in. Come early on a weekday if you can. Along the river, the Delaware is broad and calm, with canoes and fishermen, and the sunsets can be fine.

The village has a few small restaurants, bakeries and cafes along Broad Street, and the nearest larger town for supplies and fuel is Port Jervis, about eleven kilometres away across the river in New York. Be careful of deer on the roads at dawn and dusk, and of the occasional bear. In autumn the foliage here is among the best in the region, and the village is at its most charming, with pumpkins on the porches and woodsmoke in the air.
t.warwick return roads@41.3,-74.4:
Warwick is a town built on onions, apples and a good deal of local pride. It lies in the Hudson Valley's Warwick Valley, a broad, green bowl of farmland between ridges of old rock, and the flat, black land to the south and east is known as the Black Dirt Region, a former swamp drained in the nineteenth century to reveal soil so rich and dark that it is called muck. Onions, lettuce and other vegetables grow there in vast quantities, and in the autumn you can see the crops being harvested by teams of workers under a sky full of gulls. About seven thousand people live in the town, so there is plenty of fuel and food.

The town centre is a handsome collection of brick and clapboard buildings around a small green, with a decent run of cafes, bakeries and shops, and the area is known for its farm stands, orchards and vineyards. Apple picking in September and October draws crowds, and the cider and the doughnuts are worth the queue. A winery and a distillery are close by, serving tastings on weekends, but remember that riding and drinking do not mix, and take your purchases home.

For riders, Warwick is a gateway to a network of small roads that wind through the hills toward Greenwood Lake and the New Jersey border. The roads are curvy, well surfaced and quiet outside the weekends, with long views over farmland, and the scenery is a gentle one of stone walls, red barns and maple woods. In early October the colours are superb, and it is hard to beat a ride through the valley in the low sun. The Appalachian Trail crosses the Pochuck valley nearby on a long boardwalk, which is a short walk from the road and worth a look.

Greenwood Lake, about seven kilometres from the town, is a long, narrow lake that straddles the state line, with small shops and restaurants on its shore. The mood in Warwick is relaxed, the weather in autumn is crisp, and the town is a welcoming place to stop for the night. Watch for farm vehicles on the roads in harvest season, and for deer, which are everywhere at dawn and dusk. A cold glass of cider by the green, with the maples turning, is a fitting way to end the day.
t.high@41.3,-74.7:
Port Jervis sits at a corner of three states, and if you stand at the right spot you can be in New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania within a few paces. The Delaware River swings around, the smaller Neversink River joins it, and a stone monument called Tri-States Rock, set at the edge of the water, marks the place where the borders meet. It is a quirk of geography that has long amused visitors, and the town has the look of a place built when railroads and canals mattered: a grid of old brick buildings, a Victorian railroad station and hillsides with white church spires.

From the town, the road north is the star. Route 97, known here as the Hawk's Nest, was blasted into the cliffs above the Delaware in the 1930s, and for a few miles it hugs the rock with the river hundreds of feet below, with tight curves, short straights and stomach-lifting drops on the outside edge. A pull-off gives a view up and down the valley, with the river a green ribbon and the ridges of the Pocono hills beyond. Motorcyclists love it, and so do state troopers, so keep your speed sensible and your lines tidy, especially on weekends when the road fills up.

High Point State Park, to the south in New Jersey, takes its name from the highest ground in the state, at 1,803 feet, topped by a stone monument visible for miles. The Delaware and Hudson Canal once carried coal from Pennsylvania to the Hudson River through this region, and traces of the canal can be seen at several points along the road.

Port Jervis has about nine thousand people, with fuel, diners and some good bakeries, and across the river Matamoras in Pennsylvania has more. Weekday mornings are the easiest time for the Hawk's Nest, and autumn weekends can be crowded with riders and leaf-peepers alike. Late spring, when the leaves are bright green and the river runs high, is another fine moment. Watch for loose gravel and for rock debris after storms, which can close the road briefly.
t.waterford new york@42.8,-73.7:
Waterford calls itself the oldest continuously incorporated village in the United States, and it is the sort of place where that claim feels credible. It sits where the Mohawk River flows into the Hudson, a few miles north of Albany, with old brick buildings, a small harbour, and the great stone works of the Erie Canal system around it. The Waterford Flight, five locks in a row, lifts boats about 169 feet in less than two miles, one of the steepest lock staircases in the world, and when the canal opens for the season in spring, you can watch the pleasure boats rise through the chambers.

The village is also the starting point for the Lakes to Locks Passage, a scenic route that follows the old Champlain Canal north toward Lake Champlain and Ticonderoga. The route passes through towns whose history was shaped by water and war: Saratoga, where in 1777 the American victory turned the course of the Revolution, then Fort Edward, Whitehall and the long, deep lake with its forts. In this part of New York, almost every crossroads has a historical marker.

Riding here is gentle rather than dramatic. The roads run along river bottoms and farmland, over small bridges, past canal locks and between low hills, with a rhythm of straight sections and soft curves. Surfaces are generally good, though frost heaves can appear in spring. Summer weekends bring boaters and cyclists, and in October the maples along the Hudson turn flame-red. Fog sometimes pools in the river valleys on cool mornings.

Cohoes, two miles away, has about sixteen thousand people and a large range of services, with fuel, groceries and diners, and the town is also home to the Cohoes Falls, a wide, ninety-foot cascade on the Mohawk. Waterford itself has a few cafes and a canal visitor centre on Peebles Island, where the rivers meet. May to October is the best time, with the canal open and the days long. Pick up a bag of apples at a farm stand in autumn.
t.saratoga springs@43.1,-73.8:
Saratoga Springs became a resort because of what comes out of the ground. Natural mineral springs, naturally carbonated and tasting of salt and iron, bubble up in several places in town, and since the early nineteenth century people have come to drink, bathe and gamble. The Victorian hotels have mostly gone, but the wide, tree-shaded Broadway still has a grand, leisurely air, with galleries, cafes and old brick buildings. The horse racing, which has been held here since 1863 at the Saratoga Race Course, is one of the great fixtures of the American summer, and during the August meeting the town fills with racegoers, trainers and hopefuls.

The countryside around Saratoga has played a part in history. In the autumn of 1777, a few miles to the east, American forces defeated the British army of General Burgoyne in a series of battles that are often seen as the turning point of the Revolutionary War, because the victory brought France into the conflict on the American side. The battlefield is now a national historical park, with a tour road, markers and a visitor centre, and it is a fine place for a quiet ride.

The roads around the town are rolling, pleasant and well surfaced, running past farms, woodlots and small lakes, and a few miles north the foothills of the Adirondacks begin. Summer weekends are busy, especially in August, and traffic around Broadway and the racecourse is heavy. Early morning is the best time to ride out of town. In autumn, the maples glow red and orange, and the roads are lined with pumpkins and apple stands.

Fuel, food and rooms are plentiful. The town has dozens of restaurants, bakeries and cafes, and the springs in Congress Park and the Spa State Park offer free drinks of the famously fizzy water, which you can taste if you are brave. A morning workout at the track is a quiet pleasure: thoroughbreds gallop in the mist while the sun comes up, and visitors can watch from the rail. Be sure to book a room well ahead in August, when the town is at its busiest and its prices at their highest.
t.lake george@43.4,-73.7:
Lake George is long, narrow, deep and astonishingly clear, and it lies in a trough between mountains, running about thirty-two miles from the village at the south end to Ticonderoga in the north. Thomas Jefferson, who visited in 1791, called it the most beautiful water he had ever seen, and the description has stuck. The lake is ringed by wooded hills and dotted with hundreds of small islands, and in the morning, when the surface is still, the whole scene is doubled in the water. Lake George Village, at the south end, is a cheerful, busy resort of souvenir shops, ice cream stands and arcades, with a long beach and a harbour where excursion boats leave on summer days.

The history here is heavier than the atmosphere suggests. The lake lay on the main route between Canada and the Hudson valley, and in the French and Indian War it was the scene of fierce fighting. Fort William Henry, at the southern end, was besieged by a French and Indian force in 1757, and the surrender was followed by a massacre that inspired James Fenimore Cooper's novel The Last of the Mohicans. The fort has been reconstructed and is open to visitors, with cannon firing and costumed guides.

For riders, the road along the western shore, Route 9N, is a pleasure. It runs close to the water, with views through the trees, and the curves are easy and well surfaced. Traffic is heavy in July and August, particularly around the village, where visitors crowd the sidewalks, so a weekday in June or September is far better. In October the foliage is fantastic, and the lake takes on a deep blue under bright skies. The air is clean and cool, and in the morning there is often mist on the water.

Queensbury, about ten kilometres south, and Warrensburg have fuel stations, supermarkets and diners, and there is no shortage of places to eat in the village itself. Pack a layer, since the evenings can be cold even in summer, and watch for deer on the roads at dusk. If you want to swim, the water is cold but clean, and the public beach in the village is the easiest place to get in.
t.ticonderoga@43.8,-73.4:
Ticonderoga is a small town with an outsized place in American history. The fort stands on a rocky point where Lake Champlain narrows, controlling the water route between Canada and the Hudson, and whoever held it held the door to the north. The French built it in the 1750s and called it Carillon, the British took it a few years later, and in May 1775, at the start of the Revolutionary War, Ethan Allen and his Green Mountain Boys, with Benedict Arnold, surprised the sleeping British garrison and captured it without a shot. The cannon taken from the fort were dragged by sled across the snow to Boston the following winter, and they helped force the British out of the city. The fort has been restored and holds regular demonstrations.

The town itself is a calm place, of about three thousand people, with a pleasant main street and the old Ticonderoga pencil factory a part of local lore. A small ferry crosses Lake Champlain to Vermont, running in the warmer months, and it is a fine way to see the lake from the water. Mount Defiance, a short drive away, gives a view over the fort and the surrounding lake, and the British used it to force the Americans to abandon the fort in 1777.

The road here, Route 9N and the lakeside roads, runs through gentle country of farms and woods, with the lake appearing now and then through the trees. It is an easy ride, with good surfaces and moderate traffic, and it makes a pleasing end to a journey from Waterford. Autumn is the best time, when the maples are gold and the lake is steely blue, though summer evenings are lovely too. The wind can be sharp off the water in spring and autumn.

Fuel and supermarkets are in town, along with a few diners and cafes, and across the lake, Vermont's villages offer more choices. Take your time at the fort, which deserves an hour or two, and have lunch at one of the town's cafes. If you have the energy, watch the sun go down over the lake, and think of the soldiers who fought and died here.
t.perkins memorial drive@41.3,-74.0:
Perkins Memorial Drive is a short, steep, winding road that climbs to the top of Bear Mountain, in the Hudson Highlands, about fifty miles north of New York City, and it is one of the best-known viewpoints in the region. At the summit, a stone tower built in the 1930s in memory of a conservationist and philanthropist, George Perkins, stands at about thirteen hundred feet, and from its top you can see the Hudson valley, the Catskills in the north and, on a very clear day, the skyline of Manhattan, forty miles to the south. The road is closed in winter, usually from late autumn to spring, and in icy conditions, so check before you go.

Below the mountain lies the Hudson, which here cuts through the Highlands in a deep fjord-like gorge. The Bear Mountain Bridge, opened in 1924, was the first bridge across the river south of Albany, and for a time it was the longest suspension bridge in the world. The Appalachian Trail passes close by, and, at a little zoo at the foot of the mountain, reaches its lowest point, only a few score feet above sea level. The park is run by the Palisades Interstate Park Commission, and it was one of the first protected areas in the New York region, set aside in the early twentieth century to save the mountains from quarrying.

Fort Montgomery, a short distance to the south, has a hard place in history. In October 1777, the British stormed the American forts here, Fort Montgomery and Fort Clinton, to open the river to their ships, and although the defenders fought hard, the forts fell, and the British burned towns upriver. The site of Fort Montgomery is now a state historic site, with a small museum and good views.

The drive up is a joy, with tight curves, a smooth surface and trees overhanging the road, and it is short enough to ride twice. Weekends are busy, and the summit car park fills with cars, so aim for a weekday. Fuel is in Highland Falls and Peekskill, and there are diners and delis in both. The best season is October, when the foliage glows below you, though a clear spring morning is almost as good. Dress warmly, since the summit is windy and cooler than the valley.
t.appalachian trail@40.3,-74.0:
The Jersey Shore has nothing to do with the Appalachian Trail, which is a long way off in the hills, and the coordinates here are firmly in Monmouth County, close to the Atlantic, near West Long Branch and Oceanport. It is flat, leafy, comfortable suburban country a few minutes from the beach, with big oaks, old estates, horse farms and the sort of golf courses that surround an affluent coast. The sense of the sea is never far, in the gulls and the light.

History has left a few marks. At Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, the great mansion known as Shadow Lawn stands on the campus, a grand building that was rebuilt after a fire in the 1920s. Its predecessor served as the summer White House of President Woodrow Wilson in 1916, when he accepted his party's nomination there. Not far away, Monmouth Park, in Oceanport, has hosted thoroughbred racing since the nineteenth century, and the Long Branch beachfront, once a resort for presidents, still has a long boardwalk and old Victorian houses.

The riding nearby is gentle coast and country. Ocean Avenue and the roads along the barrier beaches offer sea views and cooling breezes, though weekend traffic in summer is thick. In the inland lanes, you pass horse paddocks, farm stands with sweet corn and tomatoes, and tree-lined stretches with stone walls. Surfaces are generally good, though potholes appear after winter, and in July and August the shore can be slow and crowded. Sunrise rides along the oceanfront are a pleasure in May or September, when the roads are open and the beaches nearly empty.

Fuel, diners and delis are everywhere. West Long Branch has about eight thousand people, and the larger towns of Long Branch and Red Bank are close, with plenty of cafes and music venues. Asbury Park, famous for Bruce Springsteen and its restored boardwalk, is a short ride south. Pork roll breakfast sandwiches are the local speciality, and a boardwalk slice of pizza is a good lunch. May to October is the main season, and the quietest roads come on a weekday in September.
t.jersey highlands and greenwood lake@40.7:
New Jersey is a shorter, tighter state than people imagine from the turnpike, and the ride starts in the middle of it, at a fuel stop in Mountainside, close to Scotch Plains and New Providence. This is commuter country, a long way from the lake you are heading toward, so treat the start as a chance to get organised. One thing to remember if you are from elsewhere: in New Jersey you do not pump your own fuel. An attendant does it, which is a quirk the state has held to for decades, and it saves you getting your gloves smelly.

The ground under you is more interesting than the shopping streets suggest. The Watchung Mountains run in a pair of curving ridges right behind this stretch, formed from lava that poured out in the Jurassic, long before anyone thought of New Jersey. The Watchung Reservation, a large county park, protects a good piece of the forest, and from Washington Rock, further along the first ridge, George Washington is said to have watched British troop movements across the plain during the Revolution. So you are riding through ground where the American army hid, in a landscape of low ridges rather than big mountains.

The route is aiming at the Jersey Highlands and Greenwood Lake on the New York border, and getting there from here is mostly an exercise in stitching together quiet county roads. Expect stop signs, traffic lights, small towns and a pace set by local drivers. The reward comes later, when the roads narrow and climb through hardwood forest that turns hot orange in October. This is the time of year to do it, with May a close second.

Rest and food are no problem at this end, with plenty of delis, diners and coffee shops. Bagel shops are a local religion, and a bacon, egg and cheese on a roll is the standard breakfast. Fill the tank, eat well, and then head west and north toward the real riding. Roads can be crowded at weekends, so an early start is worth the alarm.
t.jersey highlands and greenwood lake high:
The high point here is a modest one, and it helps to say so. These coordinates fall between Warren Township and Bernardsville, in the rolling country of the Somerset Hills, a band of wooded ridges and old estates west of the Watchung Mountains. The elevation is a few hundred feet at most, but the shape of the land, with folds and dips and hidden valleys, gives it more character than you would guess from a map of central New Jersey.

Nearby is the Great Swamp, a large wilderness of marsh and woodland that was saved from becoming a jetport in the 1960s and is now a national wildlife refuge. Birdwatchers love it, and so do the deer, who treat the local roads as their own. A little further north lies Jockey Hollow, where the Continental Army spent the winter of 1779 to 1780, one of the coldest of the century, in huts built from felled oaks. The park is part of Morristown National Historical Park and gives a sober sense of how bleak that winter was. Bernardsville itself has the grand houses of the Gilded Age, built by New York financiers who wanted a country seat among the hills.

The riding is a pleasant, pastoral business of twisting two-lane roads with stone walls, horse farms and the occasional sudden hill. The corners are tight and the sightlines short, with deer, cyclists and drivers in no hurry, so it is a road for taking easy. Surfaces are mixed, with frost heaves and patches after winter. Autumn is the star season, and spring, with dogwoods and redbuds, is nearly as good.

The swim label is more of a hope than a promise. There are lakes and reservoirs in the area, but access is often restricted to residents or protected, so don't plan on a dip. Instead, plan on food in Bernardsville or Warren, where there are diners, bakeries and steady coffee, and fuel at the stations along Route 202. Ride this in the morning, when the mist hangs between the trees.
t.litchfield hills coffee loop@40.6,-74.1:
The start of this ride is on Staten Island, at the end of the New Dorp Beach shoreline, which is an unusual place to begin a trip named for the hills of Connecticut. The island is the quietest of New York's boroughs and the one that most feels like a seaside suburb, with low brick houses, a boardwalk that runs along the Lower Bay for a couple of miles, and a view across the water to the Jersey Shore and the distant ships waiting for the harbour. Miller Field, a former army airfield from the early days of flight, sits right behind the beach and is now part of Gateway National Recreation Area.

Staten Island has hills, though you would not know it from the coast. Todt Hill, in the middle of the island, is the highest natural point on the Atlantic seaboard south of Maine, and the Greenbelt, a spread of woodlands and trails, runs along the spine. The Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, which opened in 1964 and was the longest suspension span in the world for years, swings across from the northeast end and gives the area its wide, ocean-liner skyline. Fort Wadsworth underneath it is worth a short detour if you have time to spare.

For a rider, this fuel stop is an easy one. Staten Island has stations everywhere, and the commercial strips along Hylan Boulevard are lined with delis, diners and bakeries. Get gas, take some water, and be ready to deal with the traffic.
