Getting off the island toward Connecticut means crossing the bridges, so check tolls and the time of day, since Sunday mornings are far kinder than a weekday rush hour. Wind comes straight off the water here, and on a cold morning the beach air can nip at gloves.

From here the plan is to head north, away from the sea and toward the quieter ground of the Litchfield Hills, a part of Connecticut full of stone walls, covered bridges and small lakes. It is a long way to go for coffee, but after a good morning on the road, that is the point.
t.litchfield hills coffee loop high point@:
Rossville is the sleepy bottom corner of Staten Island, where the borough runs out of road and meets the Arthur Kill, the tidal strait that separates New York from New Jersey. Along it sit refineries, oil tanks, marshes and, close by, the enormous green mound that was once the Fresh Kills landfill and is slowly being turned into a public park. It is an odd high point for a ride, and the label says more about a feeling than a summit, because the land here is flat and close to sea level.

What makes the place worth knowing is Sandy Ground, the small historic neighbourhood in Rossville. In the 1830s free Black families, many of them oystermen from Maryland, settled here and built a community around the island's thriving oyster beds. It is counted among the oldest free Black settlements in the country that is still lived in, and its church and old houses survive on a few quiet streets. Oysters from Raritan Bay were once a major business, until pollution and disease wiped out the harvest in the early twentieth century.

As for riding, this is the south shore at its plainest, a run of long straight roads, strip malls, mixed traffic and low bridges. It does not offer thrills. What it does offer is a break in the grind, with local delis, pizza places and bakeries that open early for the workmen heading to the refineries. A coffee and a roll here costs less than anywhere in Manhattan, and the pace is slow enough that nobody minds a rider stopping to stare at a map.

Rossville has just over eighteen thousand people on the census map, and fuel is easy to find on Arthur Kill Road and Veterans Road West. Weather comes with the water. Fog sits on the kill in the early morning, and in winter a raw wind makes everything feel colder than the thermometer claims. Spring is the time to be here, when the marsh grass turns green and the egrets return.
t.litchfield hills coffee loop scenic road:
Little Falls is a small town on the Passaic River in northern New Jersey, and the name is almost an understatement. The river drops here in a series of rapids, and a few kilometres to the north it plunges over the Great Falls of Paterson, a seventy-seven-foot cascade that Alexander Hamilton picked as the power source for America's first planned industrial city in 1791. The mills that grew up around it made silk, locomotives and firearms, and the old brick factories still line the river like a row of abandoned cathedrals.

The coordinates put you among the Passaic County hills, on a route that threads between the river and the long ridge of the Watchung range. The roads here are mostly Route 23 and the lanes around it, which are busy, built-up and not particularly pretty, but they have a certain shabby charm and good local food. Little Falls has a classic main street, with diners and Italian bakeries that fill up with locals at breakfast, and the whole region leans toward good sandwiches and pizza. This is a food stop on a coffee loop, and the label is honest about what it offers.

For the bike, think of it as a threshold. To the west the land rises toward the Ramapo hills and the quieter roads that lead up toward the Litchfield Hills. To the east it falls away into the dense suburbs of Bergen County. Hills are short and sharp, curves are tight and the surface suffers through winter, so expect patches, potholes and the odd metal plate. Early on a Sunday the traffic thins out and you can enjoy the rhythm of the old river valley.

Fuel is easy to find on Route 23 and in the surrounding towns, with Little Falls at around ten thousand people and Wayne and Paterson close by. Rain turns the old brick and stone roads slick, so be careful on any cobbles near the falls. If you have an hour, walk to the Great Falls overlook, a short ride up the river, to see what all the fuss was about.
t.litchfield hills coffee loop photo pull:
Ridgewood is one of those Bergen County villages where the trees are so large that the houses seem to have grown up beneath them. It sits on the western edge of the county, a New York commuter suburb in miniature, with a proper downtown, a train station on the line to Hoboken and a long reputation for good schools and well-kept lawns. The coordinates put you here for a pull-off, and what you photograph is the village itself, with its brick storefronts, old churches and leafy side streets.

It is a small place by American standards, at roughly twenty-five thousand people, and it makes an easy stop. Main Street has cafes, bakeries and delis for a breakfast or lunch, and the pace is gentle enough that nobody gives a bike a second look. Behind the village the land rises gradually toward the Ramapo hills, the first real folds of the Appalachians as they drop toward the Hudson, and a short ride northwest will put you on quiet lanes with stone walls, horse paddocks and sudden glimpses of reservoirs.

Riding here is about patience and short pleasures. The roads are narrow and bordered by parked cars, mailboxes and mature maples, and the speed limits are low and well policed. t.westerly@41.4,-71.8:

t.providence@41.8,-71.4:
Providence is the sort of city that rewards an early start and a loose plan. Roger Williams founded it in 1636 after being banished from the Massachusetts Bay Colony, and the idea he built it on, freedom of conscience, shaped the whole of Rhode Island. Lovecraft spent his whole life here, which explains some of the atmosphere on a foggy night.

t.new milford@41.6,-73.4:
New Milford is big in a way that surprises people: it is the largest town in Connecticut by area, spread across both banks of the Housatonic River with a long green at its center. t.norwich@41.5,-72.1:
Norwich calls itself the Rose of New England, a nickname dating from the days when its elms and gardens drew admiration, and it sits at a point where geography did the planning. Two rivers, the Yantic and the Shetucket, meet the Quinebaug at the head of tide here and form the Thames, which runs down to Long Island Sound. That meeting made Norwich a port and a mill town, and the hilly streets above the harbor are still lined with big Victorian houses that hint at its old industrial wealth.

t.woodstock@41.9,-72.0:
Woodstock, Connecticut, has a pink house, and the pink house tells you a lot. t.greenwich@41.0,-73.6:

t.new canaan@41.1,-73.5:

t.trumbull@41.2,-73.2:

t.chester@41.4,-72.5:

t.east haddam@41.5,-72.5:

t.torrington@41.8,-73.1:

t.winsted@41.9,-73.1:

t.mystic@41.4,-72.0:

Morgan, a whaler launched in 1841 that is the last wooden whaling ship in the world.

t.putnam@41.9,-71.9:

t.lincoln@44.1,-73.0:

t.colebrook@44.9,-71.5:

t.newbury@43.3,-72.0:

t.henniker@43.2,-71.8:

t.keene@42.9,-72.3:

t.jaffrey@42.8,-72.0:

t.peterborough@42.9,-72.0:

t.dublin@42.9,-72.1:

t.hampton@42.9,-70.8:

t.exeter@43.0,-70.9:

t.candia@43.1,-71.3:

t.meredith@43.7,-71.5:

t.killington@43.7,-72.8:

t.rochester@43.9,-72.8:

t.waitsfield@44.2,-72.8:

t.newport@44.9,-72.2:

t.burlington@44.5,-73.2:

t.south hero@44.6,-73.3:

t.farmington@44.7,-70.2:

t.worcester@42.3,-71.8:

t.uxbridge@42.1,-71.6:

t.invercargill@-46.4,168.4:

t.al oyun village@25.6,49.6:

The Palisades Interstate Parkway, built in the 1940s and closed to commercial vehicles, is a quiet, tree-lined road with gentle bends that suits a relaxed morning. Weekends bring cyclists in packs and families heading for the state parks, so go early.

Nyack has fuel nearby, and the villages around it have cafés, bakeries and delicatessens. Parking for photographs is easy on the quiet side streets. If you want the Mohawk Trail itself, with its famous hairpin and its view across the Berkshires, that lies about three hours north. Here, the pleasure is the river light at dawn, when mist hangs on the Hudson and the first sun touches the cliffs.
t.montauk long island end run photo pull o:
Between Princeton and the Sourland Mountain lies a stretch of central New Jersey that visitors rarely expect, a quiet piece of country in the Hopewell Valley where horse farms, old stone houses and wooded ridges sit just an hour from the suburbs. The coordinates here are a very long way from Montauk, at the far end of Long Island, but it makes a fine launch point for a ride that heads east, and the countryside is a good start to the day.

Hopewell itself is a small borough of about two thousand people with a pleasant old main street. It is best known to history as the place where the infant son of Charles Lindbergh was kidnapped from the family's nearby home in 1932, a crime that dominated the news and led to a federal kidnapping law. The Sourland Mountain, rising above the valley, is a ridge of ancient diabase rock, thickly forested and surprisingly wild, with hawks and owls in the woods and a mountain-top that is a favourite of walkers.

The roads that cross the ridge are narrow, twisty and often rough. Corners come tight and fast, the surface is patched, and the overhanging trees leave puddles and leaf litter long after the rain. They are also quiet, and the drive from Hopewell to Rocky Hill or across to the Delaware River is an enjoyable half-day. The Delaware and Raritan Canal, a nineteenth-century waterway that carried coal across the state, runs through the area, and its towpath is a popular route for cyclists and runners, so expect them on the roads that cross it.

Bloomingdale, with almost eight thousand people, is the nearest sizeable place, and it has stations, supermarkets and a handful of places to eat. Hopewell and Ten Mile Run are smaller and quieter. The autumn here is lovely, when the maples turn and the stone walls glow in the low sun, but deer are numerous and traffic on weekends can be heavy near Princeton. Aim for early starts, and keep an eye on speed limits, which local police are careful to enforce on the narrow country roads.
t.delaware water gap long day photo pull o:
Hackettstown sits on the Musconetcong River in Warren County, New Jersey, about a third of the way across the state from the Delaware, and these coordinates fall just outside it on the green ridges to the east. The ride is named for the Delaware Water Gap, which lies further northwest, but this region is a fine place to start a long day, with farms, lakes and quiet woods on the doorstep. A swim is possible in summer in some of the nearby lakes, though many are private or restricted to residents.

The town has about ten thousand people, a pleasant old main street and, on the edge of it, one of the largest chocolate factories in the world. The Mars company makes M&Ms here, and on a warm day the smell of cocoa drifts through the streets. Budd Lake, a little to the east, is the biggest natural lake in the county, and Lake Hopatcong, the largest in New Jersey, is not far away. Allamuchy Mountain State Park rises to the west, a stretch of woodland with trails. The old Morris Canal, opened in the early 1830s, carried coal across the hills to New York harbour by a series of inclined planes that hauled the boats up and down the slopes, a remarkable piece of engineering for its day.

The riding here is gentle and rolling rather than thrilling, with roads that follow the river and cross low ridges. Corners are short and tidy, the surface is patched and speed limits are low. Traffic can be heavy on Route 46 and Route 206, so back roads are the answer. Autumn is the best time, when the oaks and maples turn and the air is crisp, and early mornings are quiet. Deer are a hazard at dusk.

Fuel and food are straightforward. Hackettstown has several stations and plenty of diners, and Budd Lake and Beattystown have a few more. If you are starting here for a long day, the Delaware Water Gap is about an hour away, and the road along the river to Dingmans Ferry is one of the finest in the northeast. Fill up before you leave, because stations are scarce on the upper reaches of the river.
t.hawk s nest and upper delaware scenic ro:
This corner of Union County, New Jersey, is a very different place from the Upper Delaware, and it is a long way from Hawk's Nest and the Hudson Highlands the ride is named for. Fanwood, Westfield and Scotch Plains are leafy commuter suburbs, where tidy lawns, brick colonials and railway stations make up the landscape, and the traffic can be fierce on weekdays. If your ride starts or ends here, the sensible approach is to treat it as a staging post and to leave early.

The ridge that rises behind them has a better story. The Watchung Mountains are two long lines of basalt hills formed from lava flows that poured across the region about two hundred million years ago, when the Atlantic was beginning to open. They form a curved wall that runs across northern New Jersey, and it was from their crest that George Washington watched British movements in the plain below during the winter of 1777. A rock on the hillside above Green Brook, known as Washington Rock, marks the spot, and the view east across the plains to the skyline of New York is excellent on a clear day.

The riding on the Watchungs is modest. Roads climb through woods and wind past reservoirs, and the Watchung Reservation, a large county park, has a network of narrow lanes that reward a slow ride. The surface is patched, the corners are tidy and there are many cyclists. It is a pleasant half-hour rather than a day, and it makes a good warm-up for the long run to the north.

You are close to everything in practical terms. Westfield, with over thirty thousand people, has fuel, restaurants and cafés, and Fanwood and Scotch Plains have more. Route 22 and the Garden State Parkway are close, which makes escape from the suburbs quick, though both are often congested. Aim to be on the road before seven on weekends, and you will have the lanes and the light to yourself. In autumn, the maples on the ridge turn red and the woods smell of woodsmoke and wet leaves.
t.kingston@41.9,-74.0:
Kingston has a good claim to be the first capital of New York State. The legislature met here in 1777, when the state's first constitution was adopted, and in October of that year British troops sailed up the Hudson and burned most of the town. The Stockade District, a neighbourhood of old stone houses, has been rebuilt on the same streets, and a number of the buildings date from the Dutch period of the 1600s. It is the kind of place where history sits on every corner, and the cafés and restaurants have taken advantage.

Down by the river is Rondout, the old canal port, where the Delaware and Hudson Canal once delivered Pennsylvania coal to the Hudson and the great ships. Natural cement mining nearby also supplied builders in New York, and the waterfront is dotted with brick warehouses and cast-iron fronts. A lighthouse built in 1915 stands at the mouth of Rondout Creek, and the maritime museum has boats, photographs and stories of tugboats and ice harvests. A walk here is a good way to break up a long ride.

For motorcyclists, Kingston is the gateway to the Catskills. Route 28 runs west along the Esopus Creek valley, past the Ashokan Reservoir, a vast sheet of water built in the early 1900s to supply New York City, and on towards Pepacton and the high peaks. The road is wide and fast at first, with long bends and good surface, then narrows and climbs into forest as it nears Phoenicia. On a clear autumn day the hills are on fire with colour, and the Hudson is a silver line to the east.

With over twenty-three thousand people, Kingston has all the fuel and food you need, and the last big supermarket for a good way. The chain stations by Route 28 and the Thruway exit are the most convenient. Beyond town, stations become scarce in the mountains, so fill the tank before you commit to the loop. Weekends in autumn bring heavy traffic to Route 28, with leaf-peepers and cyclists slowing the pace, so mid-week or early starts are the best option. Deer are common, and the roads can be icy from October.
t.poconos river road@40.9,-73.9:
Fordham is the Bronx at its most characteristic, a dense, cheerful neighbourhood of apartment buildings, shops and street life around Fordham Road and the Grand Concourse. Fordham University was founded here in 1841, when the area was still countryside, and has been run by Jesuits since 1846, and the campus, with its Gothic stone halls and tree-lined lawns, is a surprising pocket of calm in a very busy borough. Edgar Allan Poe lived in a small cottage nearby in the late 1840s and wrote some of his last poems there, and the cottage still stands in a little park.

The Bronx Zoo and the New York Botanical Garden are a short distance away, and Arthur Avenue, the old Italian market, sells bread, cheese and cured meats that Bronx families have bought for generations. A proper sandwich here is as good a reason to stop as any. The ride that this point serves is a day on the Poconos River Road, about a hundred miles to the west and north, so the Bronx is the place where you come back at the end, tired and wanting to refuel before the final stretch to wherever you are staying.

Riding in the Bronx needs patience and sharp eyes. The streets are crowded, delivery vans double-park, buses pull out without warning and the potholes can be serious. The Major Deegan Expressway and the Cross Bronx are the routes to the north and west, and both are often jammed. The Bronx River Parkway, built in the 1920s, runs north through parkland and is a more pleasant exit, with gentle bends and low stone bridges, but commercial vehicles are banned and the police are watchful.

Fuel is available all around, though stations in dense neighbourhoods can be cramped and prices are high, so a sensible rider fills up on the outskirts and not in the middle. Food is the strength of the place, with Dominican, Italian, Puerto Rican and Albanian kitchens within a few minutes' walk. Park in a lit, busy street and secure the bike with a lock and chain, because theft is a real concern. A damp, cold evening in the Bronx may not be romantic, but a hot plate of food and a short walk will repay the effort.
t.hudson highlands and storm king photo pu:
A flat, sandy piece of central New Jersey lies behind these coordinates, in the borough of Dayton and Jamesburg, about as far from the Hudson Highlands and Storm King as you can be without leaving the state. This is the Coastal Plain, a wide belt of low ground between the Appalachian ridges and the Atlantic, and the landscape here is made of farm fields, small lakes and rows of suburban houses. It is not what people picture when they think of the high wooded hills of the Hudson, but it has its own charm.

Jamesburg is a small town of about six thousand people that grew up around a railway junction and, later, a juvenile training school that was one of the first of its kind in America. Helmetta, a smaller place, was a mill village built around a snuff factory, whose brick buildings once defined the town. The Manalapan Brook winds through the area, feeding a string of lakes and woodlots, and Thompson Park, a large county park nearby, has a lake, a petting zoo and trails that are quiet on weekday mornings.

The riding is relaxed rather than exciting. Roads are straight, the corners are gentle and the surface is generally good, although traffic lights and cross-traffic interrupt the rhythm. Big warehouses and the New Jersey Turnpike lie close, and trucks are everywhere. The reward is the early light on the fields, with mist on the low ground and a flock of Canada geese crossing the sky. In the autumn, farm stands sell apples, cider and pumpkins, and a quick stop makes a pleasant change of pace.

To reach Storm King and the Highlands, the ride heads north, a good two hours on the highways, and the real riding begins on the other side of the Hudson. Dayton, with about seven thousand people, is the nearest town with services, and there are fuel stations on Route 130 and on the main roads through Jamesburg. If you are leaving at dawn, expect most cafés to be shut and plan to eat on the road. Remember that New Jersey law bans self-service fuel, so an attendant will fill your tank, which is a little slow but a nice break.
t.adirondack foothills weekend scenic road:
There is nothing to ride on here, because the coordinates put you in the Atlantic, a couple of kilometres off the barrier island of Long Beach, in New York. That makes this one of the stranger entries on a ride named for the Adirondack foothills, but the island is a good place to begin or end a day, and the sea air is a fine antidote to any amount of driving.

Long Beach is a narrow strip of sand and houses, a city of about thirty-three thousand people, with a boardwalk that runs for more than two miles along the ocean. It was a seaside resort in the early twentieth century, and in recent decades it has become a surfing town, with the board shops and cafés to match. Hurricane Sandy flooded the island in 2012, and the boardwalk was rebuilt afterwards. Lido Beach and Point Lookout lie on either side, quieter and more residential, and Point Lookout is the end of the road, with a small town park and a view across the inlet.

The way off the island is a handful of causeways and bridges, and the old Ocean Parkway runs east to Jones Beach, a huge state park that Robert Moses built in the 1920s and 1930s. Its tall brick water tower, bathhouses and wide beaches are a monument to the era of public works, and a ride along the parkway, with the ocean on one side and the bay on the other, is as relaxed as any in the state. Be aware that this road is limited to cars and motorcycles, with strict speed limits, and gusting winds can make it hard work.

For practical matters, Long Beach has a number of fuel stops, supermarkets and restaurants, and the autumn is quiet and uncrowded. In summer, parking is hard and the beach attracts crowds. If you want to see the Adirondack foothills, you need to head north on the Thruway for several hours, so an early start is vital. The Bear Mountain and Harriman Dawn ride begins closer to home, and a pre-dawn departure from Long Beach, with the first light on the ocean, is a sweet way to begin.
t.manchester by the sea@42.6,-70.8:
Manchester-by-the-Sea is a small town on Massachusetts's North Shore, a place of about five thousand people on the southern flank of Cape Ann, and it has the look of a New England postcard. White clapboard houses, a harbour full of small boats and a stone-walled park on the waterfront give it a tidy, old-fashioned charm. The town was called Manchester until 1989, when residents added the words by-the-Sea to avoid confusion with the New Hampshire city, and the 2016 film that borrowed the name made it known around the world.

The beach is the main attraction. Singing Beach, a long crescent of fine sand at the end of a quiet road, gets its name from the squeaking sound that the sand makes underfoot when it is dry. It is a lovely place at any time, but access for non-residents is limited, with a small parking fee and few spaces, so arrive early or take the train. The town was once a centre of cabinet making, and its summer residents built grand houses and gardens along the shore, with views of the sea and the islands.

Riding here is a matter of pace. Route 127 runs along the coast from Beverly to Gloucester, past granite outcrops, stone walls, tidal creeks and glimpses of the open sea. The road is narrow and winding, with tight corners, blind crests and little room for error. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, and cyclists and pedestrians crowd the shoulder. The reward is a series of views that change with every bend, with the Atlantic in the distance and the light that painters have loved for two centuries. Autumn is lovely, with the maples turning and the air clear and cold.

Manchester has a small centre with shops, cafés and a general store, but fuel is limited, so it is wise to fill up in Beverly or Gloucester, which both have several stations. Beverly Cove has a larger population and more services, and Essex, a little to the north, is known for its fried clams and antique shops. Plan for slow going, take time to look around, and be ready for fog, which rolls in off the sea without warning and cools the air quickly.
t.sandwich@41.8,-70.5:
Sandwich is the oldest town on Cape Cod, founded in 1637 by settlers from the Plymouth Colony, and it has the air of a place that has been looking at the same view for a very long time. Houses with weathered grey shingles stand around a village green, a mill pond and a small, historic grist mill, and the old Dexter Grist Mill still grinds corn on certain days. The town was home to the Boston and Sandwich Glass Company, founded in the 1820s, whose colourful pressed glass was once sold across America, and a museum on the main street displays the best pieces.

The Cape Cod Canal, completed in 1914, cuts across the base of the peninsula just beyond the town, with the Sagamore and Bourne bridges arching over it. A path runs along both banks, and watching the ships go through is a good way to spend an hour. The canal turned the Cape into an island, in the technical sense, and saved ships the long and dangerous passage around the outer shore.

The road that gives the ride its name is Route 6A, the Old King's Highway, which runs along the north shore of the Cape from Sandwich to Orleans. It is one of the loveliest roads in New England, a narrow, tree-lined lane that passes ancient houses, salt marshes, antique shops and sea captains' mansions. The speed limit is low, the bends are gentle and the surface is generally good, though the road is crowded in summer, when traffic crawls and parking is scarce. Early spring and late autumn are the quiet seasons, with fog, wind and light that is soft and silver. The Sandy Neck, a long barrier beach to the east, is a haven for birds, including piping plovers, which nest in the dunes in spring.

Sandwich has about three thousand people, with Sagamore and East Sandwich close by, and there are fuel stations and shops on Route 6A and on the main roads. For a wider choice, the nearest bigger town is Mashpee, about twelve kilometres south. Traffic on the bridges over the canal can back up badly on summer weekends, so aim to cross before eight or after six. In the off season, many restaurants and shops shut, so check before you set out.
t.essex@41.4,-72.4:
Essex is the kind of Connecticut river town that makes visitors suspect it has been arranged for their benefit. It sits on the west bank of the Connecticut River, a few kilometres from Long Island Sound, and its main street runs down to a waterfront crowded with sailboats, cruisers and old brick warehouses. It was a shipbuilding village from the seventeen hundreds, and the Oliver Cromwell, a frigate of the Continental Navy, was launched here in 1776. The Griswold Inn, which opened the same year, still serves meals in a tavern full of ship paintings and old guns, and it is possibly the oldest continuously operating inn in the country.

The river is the reason for the ride. The Connecticut is the longest in New England, and in its lower reaches it is broad, slow and tidal, with wooded hills on both sides and marshes full of ospreys and herons. Down here it flows through a landscape that is almost unspoiled, protected by decades of conservation. A steam train and riverboat run from Essex, the train going up the valley to Chester and the boat carrying passengers to the old opera house at Haddam, and the whole combination looks like a nineteenth century print.

Upstream, at Hadlyme, the road climbs to Gillette Castle, a fantastic medieval fortress of fieldstone built between 1914 and 1919 by the actor William Gillette, who made his fortune playing Sherlock Holmes on stage. He designed it himself, down to the wooden door locks, and he left it to the state on his death. The views over the river are superb. To reach it you can ride the Chester to Hadlyme ferry, one of the oldest in America, which has crossed the river since the 1760s, a short ride on an open deck that holds just a handful of vehicles.

The roads here are narrow, wooded and winding, with tight bends, low stone walls and trees that overhang the lane. They are slow, but they reward patience, particularly in autumn. Essex has fuel nearby, but the larger town of Old Saybrook, about seven kilometres south, has the stations and supermarkets, and Deep River has more modest services. In summer the villages are crowded with visitors, and a weekday morning is the best time. Late October, with the maples red and the river steaming in the cold, is the moment to come.
t.central otago vineyard sweep@-45.1,169.1:
Central Otago is the southernmost wine region in the world, and the pin sits in the heart of it, in the dry, rocky country south-west of Cromwell, around Bannockburn. The land here is stark, with schist outcrops, thyme-covered hills and wide skies, and the vineyards stand in neat rows against the pale slopes. Pinot noir is the star, thriving in the hot days and cold nights, and the wines have won a global reputation. Cromwell, the nearest town, has just over five thousand people and a large fruit sculpture at its entrance, a nod to its orchards of cherries, apricots and peaches.

The area's history is gold. In the 1860s, miners flocked to the Otago goldfields, and at Bannockburn they washed away entire hillsides with water cannon, leaving a landscape of strange pinnacles and gullies that can still be walked. Stone cottages, abandoned workings and old water races are scattered through the hills. Lake Dunstan, created when the Clyde dam was built in 1992, drowned the old town of Cromwell, and a new historic precinct has been rebuilt on the shore with some of the old buildings.

The riding here is a delight. Roads wind through the vineyards and over low ridges, with moderate bends, wide views and a smooth surface, and there is little traffic. The weather is dry and sunny in summer, hot in January and February, with cold, frosty winters. Autumn is perhaps the best season, with poplars turning yellow along the river and the grape harvest in full swing. The wind can be strong on exposed ridges.

Fuel is easy in Cromwell, which has several stations, and cafes and restaurants serve excellent local produce, with fresh fruit in season from roadside stalls. Many wineries offer tastings, but remember that you are on a bike, and a spit bucket is your friend. Take a hat and sunscreen, since the sun is fierce, and carry water. In the evening, the light on the schist hills is a pale gold.
t.central otago vineyard sweep photo pull:
Fiordland National Park begins right here, and the road is called the Milford Road. The pin lies in the Eglinton valley, a wide, glacier-carved trough between Te Anau and the sound, in country of red beech forest, golden tussock flats and snow-streaked mountains. It is a short ride from Te Anau, a town of about two thousand people on the shore of the lake of the same name, and the last place for supplies.

The valley floor is flat and open, with the river running in braids through gravel beds, and the mountains rising sheer on both sides. In autumn the tussock turns golden, and the beech trees show touches of red. Further along, the Mirror Lakes reflect the peaks in still weather, and at the head of the valley, the road climbs toward the Homer Tunnel, a 1.2 kilometre passage through the rock, begun in the 1930s by men with picks and opened in 1954. Beyond it, the road drops steeply into the Cleddau valley.

The riding is superb but demanding. The road is narrow, with sharp bends, rough patches and no shoulder in places, and tour buses are frequent. Rain is common, as Fiordland is one of the wettest places in the country, and when it falls the waterfalls pour from the cliffs in hundreds. In winter, avalanche danger can close the road, and chains are compulsory in some conditions. Keep to the left and give oncoming traffic plenty of space.

For a photograph, the golden hour in the Eglinton valley is hard to beat, with low light on the tussock and the mountains behind. Sandflies are a nuisance, so keep your visor down and carry repellent. Cafes at Te Anau serve good coffee and pies, and the tourist information centre has current road conditions. A hot drink from a flask is welcome on a cold morning.
t.central otago vineyard sweep scenic road:
Between Lake Wakatipu and the Mataura river, the country opens into a high, dry basin of tussock and sheep, and this pin sits in the southern part of it, about fifteen kilometres south-west of Kingston. The landscape is big and spare, with long gravel flats, low brown hills and the jagged tops of the Eyre and Hector mountains on the horizon. Fences, a few farm buildings and a line of poplars are the only signs of people, and the wind is a constant companion.

Kingston, at the southern tip of the lake, has a story that railway lovers know. The Kingston Flyer, a steam train that ran between Kingston and Fairlight for many years, was one of the last steam services in New Zealand, and its green carriages and glossy locomotive still make an occasional appearance on the old line. The railway was built in the 1870s to link the lake steamers with the south, and for decades the town was a transfer point for travellers heading to Queenstown. The old station and the stretch of track make a pleasant stop.

The riding is fast and open. State Highway 6 runs south from Kingston across the flats, with long straights, gentle curves and wide views of the mountains, and the surface is good. The smaller roads that cut across the high country are gravel, with loose corners and washboard, and they reward patience and a steady hand. Wind can be fierce, and in winter, frost and snow close the high roads. Summer is hot and dry, and the light is bright.

Fuel is available at Kingston, a village of about two and a half thousand people at the head of the road, but supplies are sparse beyond it, so fill up before heading into the back country. There is a cafe at the station, and simple meals are available at the pub. Take sunscreen, water and a spare layer, since the weather on the plains can change in an hour. The sunsets here are long, with the mountains turning pink.
t.central otago vineyard sweep high point@:
Mataura is a name that fishermen say with respect. The river rises in the hills near here and runs south through Southland to the sea, and it holds some of the best brown trout fishing in the world, with clear water, gravel runs and big fish that rise to dry flies in summer. Anglers from Europe and America make the trip every year, and local guides keep their favourite pools secret. The pin sits in the dry upland country between the upper Mataura and the Nokomai valley, about twenty kilometres from Kingston.

The land is high-country sheep station, where merino and corriedale sheep graze on tussock hills, and the shearing sheds and woolsheds stand beside the roads. The farms are huge, many covering thousands of hectares, and mustering in autumn is done by horse, dog and, increasingly, helicopter. The gold rush reached here too, and the old workings in the Nokomai valley and at Waikaia still scar the hills. Old stone huts, built by miners and musterers, are scattered through the country and are often open to walkers.

The roads here are a mix of sealed highway and gravel back roads. The sealed routes cross the high country in long, easy curves, with tussock hills on either side, and the gravel roads climb into valleys with fords and stock gates. A steady hand and careful speed are needed on the gravel, and a bike with good tyres is an advantage. The high point is a modest saddle, but the views reach to the Remarkables and the Southern Alps.

Remote areas have no mobile signal, so tell someone your plan. Close farm gates behind you, and give livestock plenty of room. Summers are hot and dry, and winters are severe, with snow on the saddle. The silence of the high country, broken only by a distant sheep and the wind in the tussock, is rare and good.
t.milford road expedition high point@-45.2:
Gold built the roads in this part of Otago, and the pin lies in the middle of the gold. The Nevis valley, south of the Kawarau gorge, is a long, high trough between the Carrick and Garvie ranges, a landscape of tussock, schist and braided stream where miners dug for gold from the 1860s. The ruins of their cottages, stone huts and water races still stand, and a handful of farms keep sheep and cattle in the valley. It is one of the loneliest places in the region, and the nearest town of any size is Cromwell, over twenty kilometres away.

The gravel road through the valley, the Nevis Road, links Bannockburn with Garston, and it is among the highest public roads in the country. It is rough, steep and exposed, with fords, narrow shelves and long drops, and it is usually closed in winter by snow. Many rental companies ban their vehicles from it, so it is best suited to experienced riders on adventure bikes with good tyres and spare tubes. Check conditions before you go, since weather can change quickly, and tell someone your plans.

The scenery is stark and fine. Tussock slopes glow gold in the late afternoon, schist outcrops stand in the hills like ruined walls, and the sky is huge. Native falcons hover over the ridges, and the Nevis River runs clear over gravel. At night, the stars are brilliant. The abandoned settlement of Nevis Crossing, with its old school and cottages, is a ghost town that tells a story of boom and bust.

Mobile coverage is nonexistent, so carry water, food, a first-aid kit and a puncture repair kit. If you are not comfortable on gravel, the sealed highways nearby give good views of the same mountains. The reward of the Nevis is silence and a sense of space that few roads in the country can match.
The Kawarau gorge is a cleft in the rock where Central Otago's biggest river squeezes between steep schist walls, and the pin sits on its southern edge, near Bannockburn. The river is a vivid turquoise, fed by the snowmelt and glaciers of the Southern Alps, and it races through the gorge in rapids and pools. State Highway 6 follows the water, cut into the cliff in places, and the road feels like a ledge between the rock and the river. It is one of the finest short rides in the country.

The bridge at Kawarau, a few kilometres west, is the birthplace of commercial bungy jumping, where in 1988 a New Zealand company first opened a jump from the old suspension bridge, launching a worldwide industry. Watching the jumpers fall toward the river is a popular pastime. The gorge was also a gold-rush route, and the Chinese miners who worked the river in the 1860s left stone huts and tailings. At Arrowtown, nearby, a preserved Chinese settlement tells their story.

The riding is lively. The road twists through the gorge, with tight bends, short tunnels and a few places where it is cut into the cliff, with the Nevis Bluff section carved into a sheer face high above the water. The surface is good, but the road is narrow, and trucks and campervans share it, so patience is needed. Early morning is the best time for a clear road, and the light on the water is lovely. In winter, ice and rockfall can cause closures.

Fuel is easy at Cromwell, about twelve kilometres away, and at Queenstown. Cafes and wineries offer food and coffee, and the Gibbston valley, to the west, is known for its cool-climate pinot noir. Carry a layer for the gorge, which is shaded and cold in the morning, and take care on the narrow sections. If you stop at the bridge, park safely and watch the jumpers for a while.
t.glenorchy lake road high point@-45.4,169:
Between the Wakatipu basin and the Mataura valley, the high country rolls on in long ridges of tussock and rock, and the pin lies in the middle of it, in the foothills of the Garvie mountains. It is dry country, with a few hundred millimetres of rain a year, and the hills are brown for most of the summer and white for much of the winter. Kingston is about twenty kilometres to the west, and the nearest town of any size, but there are many hours of silence between here and the lake.

The land holds stories of gold and wool. Miners dug here in the 1860s, and their stone huts and water races survive, while the sheep stations that followed are among the largest in the country, with merino flocks grazing the high tussock. The coordinates here fall a long way from the lake the ride is named for, in the dry schist country east of Lake Wakatipu, somewhere between Kingston and Cromwell. Eighteen hundred and three feet above sea level does not sound like much, but it is the highest point in New Jersey, and the monument that crowns it can be seen for miles. The Taconic Parkway, which lends the ride its name, is some distance north-east, but this pull-off offers a fine introduction to the quieter corner of the Delaware valley.

Connecticut built a parkway in the 1930s that deserves the word beautiful. Mendham and Chester stand in the part of New Jersey that most outsiders never see: a region of rolling hills, horse farms, stone churches and old inns, a gentle upland of the Highlands that is more like the English countryside than the state's reputation allows. Fair Lawn is a New Jersey suburb in Bergen County, on the Passaic River, and it holds one of the more interesting ideas in American town planning. A neighbourhood called Radburn, laid out in 1929 by the architects Clarence Stein and Henry Wright, was designed as a town for the motor age, with houses grouped around shared green spaces, roads that never cross footpaths, and underpasses that let children walk to school without meeting a car. Crawford Notch is a deep gash in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, a glacier-carved, U-shaped valley that squeezes between steep granite walls, with the road, a railway line and the headwaters of the Saco River all running through the gap at about 580 metres. The valley has a tragic story. In August 1826, after a night of torrential rain, a landslide roared down the mountain above a lonely house belonging to the Willey family, and nine people, the parents, their children and hired men, were killed trying to flee. The house itself was spared, split by the slide, and the story shocked the country and made the notch famous. Writers such as Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote about it, and the site is now a small state historic site with a little museum. Albertson is a small village in Nassau County, in the middle of Long Island, on a flat plain that was once something very different. Rockport sits at the tip of Cape Ann, on the Massachusetts coast north of Boston, and it is a town that lives by granite and by its looks. A red fishing shack on a wharf in the harbour, known as Motif Number 1, has been painted and photographed by so many artists that it is often called the most painted building in America, and a visit to the quay at dawn, with fishing boats and lobster pots in the light, shows why. Cohasset is where Boston's South Shore turns rocky. Scituate is a harbour town on the South Shore with two stories that people there tell with relish. The first concerns the War of 1812. In September 1814, a British warship was cruising off the coast, and two young sisters, Rebecca and Abigail Bates, who were alone in the lighthouse keeper's house while their father was away, are said to have grabbed a drum and a fife and hidden behind the dunes, playing as loudly as they could. The British, believing a company of militia was approaching, turned back. The story has been told so often that the sisters are known as the Army of Two, and the little lighthouse, built in 1811 on Cedar Point, is one of the oldest on the coast.

For more than a century, Scituate was the centre of Irish moss harvesting, a red seaweed that was raked from the rocks at low tide, dried in the sun and sold for use as a thickener in food, and the trade made a modest living for many local families. A small museum on the harbour tells the story of the moss gatherers, along with the fishermen and the shipbuilders. t.lanesborough@42.5,-73.2:
Lanesborough sits at the foot of the Berkshire Hills in the far west of Massachusetts, at about 350 metres, in the broad valley of the Hoosic River, with the great bulk of Mount Greylock to the east. The Appalachian Trail passes over the summit, and hikers with huge packs are a common sight. A cup of tea in the lodge at the top, with the whole of the Berkshires below, is a quiet pleasure.

Freeport has a street built for people who like boats, fried fish and sunsets over the water. Hanover is a town that exists around a college, and you feel it the moment you roll in. The Palisades begin right here, and the fuel stop at Englewood Cliffs gives you a first look at them. Kings Point is at the tip of the Great Neck peninsula on the north shore of Long Island, where the land runs out into the sound. Scott Fitzgerald lived at nearby Great Neck in the early 1920s, and many readers see in these shores the model for the setting of The Great Gatsby.

The stretch of New Jersey shore around Rumson and Sea Bright is a narrow, wind-combed place, and a good one for a photograph. Just east, the shore narrows to a strip of sand and rock called Sea Bright, with the ocean on one side and the river on the other, so that the land seems to be hardly there at all. Further north the Sandy Hook peninsula curls out into the Atlantic, protected as part of Gateway National Recreation Area. It has a historic lighthouse built in 1764, the oldest working lighthouse in the country, and the remains of Fort Hancock, an army base with big gun emplacements facing the harbour approach. Beyond it, on a clear day, the skyline of Manhattan stands out on the horizon. The Navesink Twin Lights, higher on the bluffs at Highlands, were a landmark for ships entering New York for much of the nineteenth century and sit on one of the highest points of the Atlantic coast.
