t.bear mountain and harriman dawn@40.5,-74:
Metuchen is a small borough in central New Jersey with a lively main street and a nickname that locals still use with pride, the Brainy Borough. Its streets are lined with old shop fronts, a good independent bookshop, coffee bars and a handful of restaurants that serve people who come in from Rutgers and the nearby towns. A train station on the line between New York and Trenton sits at the centre, so the town is full of commuters in the morning and quiet by mid-morning, which is the best time to stop.

Menlo Park, a few kilometres north, is where Thomas Edison built his famous laboratory in 1876 and invented a long list of things, among them the first practical phonograph and, a couple of years later, a working electric light. A tall tower topped with a glowing bulb marks the site, and a small museum keeps the story alive. The area is flat, built-up and criss-crossed with highways, but it carries a surprising amount of history, and the Raritan River and the old canal towpath run close by, offering green space for a short walk.

Riding through central Jersey is a matter of linking quiet roads, and the pleasures are small ones. Many local roads are tree-lined and calm, while the highways are fast and busy. The surface is generally good, though there are potholes in spring, and traffic lights are frequent. Sunday morning is the best time, when the roads are clear and cafés are serving brunch. Take care at the busy junctions, which can be confusing, and watch for the jug-handle turns that New Jersey uses in place of left-hand turns.

With fourteen thousand people and neighbouring Edison and Woodbridge nearby, fuel is easy to find. Food is better than you might expect, with Indian, Italian and diner options within a short walk of the station. Park on the side streets, take an hour for a proper breakfast, and enjoy a place that looks unremarkable until you stop.
t.franconia notch@44.2,-71.7:
Franconia Notch is a gap in the White Mountains where a glacier once scoured a deep trough, leaving granite walls rising steeply on either side. The notch is about eight miles long, with Cannon Mountain on the west and the Kinsman and Franconia ranges on the east, and the road threads through the bottom at around 1,900 feet. The ridge above is bare rock and spruce, and the sound of wind in the trees carries down to the highway. For years the main attraction was the Old Man of the Mountain, a natural profile on a cliff face that appeared on the state's licence plates and quarter, until it collapsed in May 2003. A memorial of steel rods and plaques on the lake shore now shows where it once hung.

Today there are other draws. The Flume Gorge, a narrow ravine of moss-covered granite with a boardwalk, is a short walk from the visitor centre. Echo Lake lies at the northern end beneath Cannon's cliff, and the Cannon Mountain Aerial Tramway, the first in North America when it opened in 1938, lifts passengers to the summit for a wide view over New Hampshire and across to the Green Mountains of Vermont on a clear day. The Appalachian Trail passes nearby, and the Pemigewasset River rises close to the road.

Riding here is an unusual experience, since the route is part of Interstate 93 but is built as a parkway, a two-lane road with a low speed limit and no passing in places. It is a scenic, slow ride, with granite on both sides and trees flaming in autumn. The surface is smooth, but frost can linger in shade in spring and autumn, and the notch is often cooler and damper than the valleys. Fog and rain are common, and the best light is in the morning.

Lincoln, to the south, has fuel and food, and Franconia and Littleton lie to the north, with more services. Parking at the main sites is paid, and lots fill up by mid-morning in the peak season, so come early. October brings leaf-watchers by the thousand, so a weekday visit is kinder.
t.hudson to rhinebeck food ride@40.6,-74.1:
The north shore of Staten Island is where this ride begins, and it makes a good first lesson in how New York actually works. Within a few kilometres you have the ferry terminal at St. George, where the free orange ferry crosses to Manhattan in about twenty-five minutes with a view of the Statue of Liberty and the lower skyline, and the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge to the south, which carries traffic over to Brooklyn. The bridge opened in 1964 and was named for the Italian explorer who sailed into the harbour in 1524, and for decades the bridge was spelled with one z before the second was restored in 2018.

Behind the shore, the island rises to wooded hills, and the old Sailors' Snug Harbor, a retirement home for merchant seamen built in the 1830s, is now a cultural centre with gardens and classical buildings. Further inland, Historic Richmond Town recreates a village of the past with houses and shops. The island has a very particular character, more suburban and less hurried than the rest of the city, with Italian delis, Sri Lankan restaurants and a long tradition of pizza.

For a rider, the start of a Hudson Valley food ride begins with a challenge: how to leave. The island is connected to New Jersey by three bridges and to Brooklyn by the Verrazzano, and tolls and traffic vary widely by time of day, so check before you go. Early on a weekend morning, the roads are quiet and the bridges are free-flowing, and you can be across the water within half an hour. Later in the day, delays can be long.

Fuel and coffee are plentiful, with stations along Richmond Terrace and Victory Boulevard, and a long run of bakeries and delis. Wind off the harbour is cold in winter and the ferry docks are crowded at commuter hours. Fill up, eat something light and get ready for a day of good food, since the ride ahead is as much about lunch as it is about the road.
t.hudson to rhinebeck food ride@40.4,-74.1:
Fair Haven is a quiet riverside borough on the Navesink River in Monmouth County, New Jersey, and the food stop here comes with a sense of old money and clean water. The Navesink is a tidal river, wide and calm, with sailboats on moorings and herons standing in the shallows, and the town's quiet streets run down to a park by the water. Across the river sits Red Bank, a livelier place with a train station, a big old theatre named for Count Basie, who was born here, and a main street of record shops, cafés and restaurants.

The area is a pleasant mix of suburban calm and shore-town energy. Ocean beaches are only a few kilometres east, and the Sandy Hook peninsula lies a short ride north, with its lighthouse and old fort. The river's banks are lined with trees and big houses, and the road beside the water, River Road, is one of the prettiest in the county. In autumn, the maples turn red and the light on the river takes on a soft copper tone.

For a food ride, this is the right kind of place. Red Bank has a good concentration of independent restaurants, from Italian and Latin American to old diners, and Fair Haven has a few local bakeries and coffee shops. Bagels, pork roll sandwiches and Italian ice are New Jersey staples, and any of them goes down well after a morning on the road. Weekends are busy, and parking in Red Bank can be tight, but Fair Haven is quieter and bikes are easy to park.

Fuel is available in Red Bank and along Route 35, only a few minutes away. Roads here are generally smooth and flat, with traffic lights and school zones, and speed limits are low and enforced. A thin jacket is wise in the evenings, since the river breeze can be sharp. If you have time, walk along the waterfront and watch the boats come in, a restful way to break up the day.
t.hudson to rhinebeck food ride scenic roa:
Rosedale is the last corner of Queens before the city gives way to Nassau County, a quiet residential neighbourhood of brick houses, small gardens and churches. To the west, the huge expanse of Jamaica Bay, with its salt marshes, islands and wildlife refuge, runs toward the airport. The area is flat, close to sea level, and often windy, with a sky that seems wider than the rest of the city's. Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge, a short distance away, is one of the finest places for birds in the region, with migrating waders and ospreys through spring and autumn.

John F. Kennedy International Airport lies a few kilometres west, opened in 1948 as Idlewild and renamed in 1963 after the assassination of the president. Aircraft pass low over the rooftops and the marsh, and for a plane spotter this is a good place to stand. The roads in the neighbourhood are built around the airport and the parkways, and the Belt Parkway curves around the shore with views across the water.

On a bike, the scenic road label is relative. This is not a landscape of mountain bends or forest roads; it is a calm, level ride on busy suburban streets and parkways, with the thrill coming from the sense of edges, where city meets marsh and runways meet sea. The wind is the main factor, and a strong breeze can push a bike across the lane. Early on a weekend is the best time, when the traffic is light and the marsh is quiet, the air smelling of salt mud.

Rosedale has fuel on Merrick Boulevard and Sunrise Highway, and plenty of Caribbean and soul food places that serve a hot lunch for little money. Jerk chicken, patties and fried fish are local specialities, reflecting the area's large Caribbean community. Parking is easy, and the people are friendly. Just beware of weekday rush hours, when the roads are jammed and the airport traffic is heavy.
t.hudson to rhinebeck food ride high point:
Franklin Square sits on what used to be the Hempstead Plains, a great natural prairie that once covered a large part of central Long Island. For centuries it was open grassland, one of the few true prairies in the east, grazed by herds of cattle and cut by dirt tracks. Much of it was ploughed up for farms and then built over, and a small remnant survives near Nassau Community College, a reminder of what the island looked like before the suburbs.

The flat plain also made an ideal airfield. Roosevelt Field, a few kilometres east of here, was the starting point for Charles Lindbergh's solo flight to Paris in May 1927, and for many other pioneering flights. The old field has long been turned into a shopping centre, with a small air and space museum nearby. Belmont Park, a short way west, is one of the great racecourses of America and hosts the Belmont Stakes each June, the last leg of the Triple Crown.

The label calls this a high point, but there is no height here to speak of, and the joke would be lost on nobody in the neighbourhood. The land is flat from the sea to the moraine hills in the north, and a ride across it is a matter of rhythm and traffic lights, not climbs and corners. Hempstead Turnpike, Jericho Turnpike and the parkways cut across it in straight lines, and the pavements are lined with diners, delis and strip malls.

Food is the real reason to stop. The area has a rich mix of cuisines, with Italian bakeries, Jamaican takeouts, Latin American grills and old-fashioned diners all within a few blocks. Fuel is available on every main road, and parking is easy. Weekday rush hours are slow and tense, and the best time to ride is early on a weekend. Spring and autumn are comfortable, while summer is hot and humid and winter wind is raw across the open land.
t.hudson to rhinebeck food ride photo pull:
North Haledon sits on the western edge of the Watchung Mountains in Passaic County, on a ridge that looks out over Paterson and the Passaic Valley to the skyline of Manhattan, about twenty miles away. On a clear day the towers of the city show as a faint, jagged line on the horizon. The overlooks in nearby Garret Mountain Reservation, with its wooded trails and ponds, offer even better views, and Lambert Castle, a Victorian mansion built by a silk manufacturer, stands on the ridge above Paterson.

Haledon, next door, has one of the more interesting pieces of American labour history. In 1913, thousands of silk mill workers in Paterson went on strike, and since Paterson's mayor banned meetings in the city, they walked up to Haledon, where a socialist mayor welcomed them. Speakers addressed crowds from the balcony of an immigrant weaver's house, and today that house, the Botto House, is a museum, a National Historic Landmark and a proud local landmark.

Riding here is about the ridge. The roads follow the contours of the mountain, with short, steep climbs, tight bends and sudden views, and are often narrow and lined with houses. The surface is mixed, and traffic can be heavy on the main routes, so choose the quieter lanes along the ridgeline. Winter ice can linger in the shade and autumn leaves fall in drifts, so choose your days. Evenings, when the lights of the valley come on, are a good time to stop and look.

The label suggests food, and this part of New Jersey has plenty of it, with Italian bakeries, Middle Eastern restaurants, Peruvian chicken places and old-school diners all within a few kilometres. Paterson, the next city over, has a large and varied immigrant community and some of the best cooking in the state. Fuel is on Hamburg Turnpike and Route 208. Park the bike, walk to a viewpoint and let the city lights come on.
t.palisades parkway north@40.9,-73.9:
Riverdale sits at the northern tip of the Bronx, where New York City presses up against the Hudson and the Palisades rise across the water, and it is probably the greenest and quietest corner of the borough. Big old houses sit on a ridge above the river, and the Henry Hudson Parkway runs along the shore, an elegant, curving road from the 1930s built to give city families a pleasant drive. The coordinates mark the start of the day's escape north, along the river and into the open country beyond.

The area has a long literary and artistic history. Wave Hill, a public garden and cultural centre on an old estate above the river, has hosted guests including Mark Twain, who rented it in the early 1900s, and Theodore Roosevelt, who spent summers there as a boy. The gardens, with their long views across to the Palisades, are among the best in the city. A short way south, Spuyten Duyvil, where the Harlem River meets the Hudson, is a handsome bit of water with a railway bridge and an old Dutch name that translates, so the story goes, as spitting devil.

For the rider, the thing to know is that this is the gateway. The Henry Hudson Parkway north leads onto the Saw Mill and then the roads into Westchester, and the way across the George Washington Bridge to the Palisades Parkway is a short ride south. Traffic in this part of the Bronx can be heavy, and the parkway has low bridges and tight curves that are no place for hurry. Early on a weekend morning, though, the river light is wonderful.

Fuel is easy to find on Riverdale Avenue and in nearby Yonkers, and the neighbourhood has a good supply of delis and bakeries. Parking is simple, and the streets are quiet. Autumn brings gold and red to the park trees, while summer afternoons are humid and hazy. Take a few minutes at the river overlook before you set off.
t.storm king highway@41.4,-74.0:
Highway 218 cuts along the side of Storm King Mountain like a shelf, and few roads in New York State feel so dramatic. The route was blasted out of the cliff in the early twentieth century, a narrow ledge above the Hudson with a low stone parapet and a sheer drop to the river on one side and rock on the other. Opened in the early 1920s, it was among the first scenic roads built expressly for motorists, and for a rider the experience is intimate, twisting and slow, with the river shining far below.

Storm King holds a special place in American conservation history. In the 1960s the power company Con Edison proposed building a giant pumped-storage plant inside the mountain, and local residents and a new group called Scenic Hudson fought it for years, arguing that natural beauty deserved legal weight. The court case that followed helped establish the right of citizens to challenge environmental decisions, and the project was finally dropped in 1980. The movement it started is often seen as the beginning of modern environmental law. Close by, the Storm King Art Center spreads vast sculptures across a hillside meadow.

The land around is steeped in history. West Point, the military academy, stands on the river a few kilometres north, and the old town of New Windsor was the site of the Continental Army's final encampment at the end of the Revolution, in 1782 and 1783, when thousands of soldiers waited here for peace. The Hudson narrows at the Highlands into a fjord-like gorge, with forest-covered mountains rising from the water.

The road demands care. The corners are tight and blind, the shoulders are narrow, there is rockfall in spring, and it is sometimes closed for repairs, so check before you go. Large vehicles are discouraged, but cyclists and walkers are common. The best time is early morning in autumn, when the leaves are turning and the river is misty. Fuel and food are in Cornwall, New Windsor and Newburgh, and there is nothing on the mountain itself.
t.guatavita@4.9,-73.8:
Guatavita is the place where a legend took root, and the legend still pulls people up the mountain. The Muisca people who lived on the high plateau around Bogotá held a lake nearby, Laguna de Guatavita, to be sacred, and the story goes that a new chief would be covered in gold dust, taken out on a raft and would dive into the water while his people threw offerings of gold and emeralds. Spanish chroniclers heard the tale and turned it into the myth of El Dorado, the gilded man, which sent expeditions across the continent for centuries. The lake is a few kilometres away in a nature reserve, a deep round bowl in the páramo.

The town itself has an unusual history. Old Guatavita was drowned in the 1960s when the Tominé reservoir was filled, and the community moved to a new site, Guatavita Nueva, built in a colonial style with white walls, tiled roofs and a handsome plaza. It looks old, though it is barely sixty years old. The reservoir spreads below, a wide blue lake popular with sailors and weekend visitors, and a ring of green hills encloses it.

At 2,650 metres, the air is cool and thin, and mist often gathers on the heights. The riding approaches from Bogotá through dairy farms and cloud-forest edge, on roads that curve and climb with views over the valleys. The surface is generally good, but potholes and landslides can appear in the wet seasons, which run from March to May and from October to November. Cyclists ride these hills in large numbers, so keep an eye out and give them space.

Services in Guatavita are modest but friendly, with cafés, bakeries and restaurants serving local specialities such as roast trout and hot chocolate with cheese. Fuel is available in Tocancipá and Sesquilé, so fill up beforehand. Weekends are busy, and parking around the plaza fills up. Bring a warm layer and a rain jacket, because the weather can change in minutes.
t.yarmouth port@41.7,-70.2:
Yarmouth Port is a village on the north side of Cape Cod, and its main street, Route 6A, is one of the most beautiful old roads in New England. This is the Old King's Highway, laid out in the seventeenth century and lined with the houses of sea captains who made fortunes in the nineteenth. White clapboard mansions with widow's walks, grey shingled cottages and neat gardens sit behind low walls, and the whole village is a historic district. It is slow, quiet and handsome, and the pace seems to adjust you.

The captains' houses tell the story of the Cape's maritime age. The Captain Bangs Hallet House, built around 1840, is open as a museum, and Hallet's Store, with its old soda fountain, has been serving ice cream since 1889. Edward Gorey, the author and illustrator of strange, elegant, darkly comic books, lived in the village for years, and his old house is now a museum full of his drawings and his collections. Down at the bay, Gray's Beach has a boardwalk across the marsh and a long, shallow shore that is warm in summer and ideal for children.

For a rider, the road demands the right mood. The speed limit is low, the lanes are narrow, and the road curves gently between stone walls and old trees. There are cyclists, walkers, and drivers admiring the houses, and local police take speed seriously. This is a ride for looking rather than racing. Traffic builds on summer weekends, with the Cape's bridges backing up at peak times, so go early in the morning or in autumn, when the light is soft and the crowds are gone.

Fuel is available in Hyannis and Yarmouth, a few minutes away, and the village has cafés and a few restaurants. Park and walk, because the details are lovely. Salt marsh smells, the creak of old signs and the occasional church bell make the stop an easy one.
t.dennis@41.7,-70.2:
Dennis is spread across the upper arm of Cape Cod, with Route 6A running through it as a quiet, leafy road past antique shops, white churches and the long, shallow shore of Cape Cod Bay. Founded in the 1600s as part of Yarmouth and incorporated separately in 1793, it was named for the Reverend Josiah Dennis, a local minister, and in the early nineteenth century its sea captains and salt makers did well. Today the town is a mix of old village centres and summer cottages.

The Cape Playhouse, opened in 1927, is one of the oldest professional summer theatres in the country, and over the decades has hosted many famous names, and Bette Davis is said to have started there as an usher. A short walk away, the Cape Museum of Fine Arts shows work by artists associated with the Cape, many of whom were drawn by its clear light. In the village of Dennis, a small stone tower stands on Scargo Hill, the highest point in town, and from the top you can look across the bay to the hook of Provincetown on a clear day. Below it lies Scargo Lake, which legend says was dug by a Native princess for her fish.

The road is a gentle one. The surface is mostly good, the bends are mild, and the speed limit is low, with frequent crosswalks and drivers turning into driveways. Summer traffic is heavy, particularly on weekend afternoons, and bikes share the road with a lot of cyclists on the Cape Cod Rail Trail, which crosses it. Early morning rides, when the marsh is misty and the light is low, are the most rewarding. Evening brings the soft pink glow of sunset across the bay.

Fuel is available in nearby Yarmouth, four kilometres away, and the village has cafés, a bakery and clam shacks serving fried seafood. Dress in layers, since the bay breeze can be cool, and make time to stop at one of the small beaches at sunset.
t.pittsfield@42.5,-73.2:
Pittsfield is the biggest town in the Berkshires, and for a rider it is mostly a useful hinge: an old mill and manufacturing city of forty-odd thousand people sitting in the broad Housatonic valley, with the hills of the Berkshire plateau pressing in on both sides. General Electric once ran its transformer works here and gave the town its working-class backbone, and the downtown still has the long brick blocks and the wide Park Square to prove it. For a motorcyclist, that means fuel stations on every approach, plenty of places to eat, and no fuss.

The good riding starts the moment you leave. North of the city, Route 7 slides up the valley toward Lanesborough and Williamstown with Mount Greylock filling the windscreen. At 3,491 feet, Greylock is the highest point in Massachusetts, and its summit road, which climbs from Lanesborough, is a narrow twisty ribbon with a war memorial tower at the top. The road is only open in the warmer months and the weather up there can change in minutes, so check before you go. West of town, Route 20 and the back roads over the hills toward New York state give you the kind of New England riding that works on any day: modest climbs, wooded corners, stone walls and the odd glimpse of a farm pond.

Herman Melville lived at Arrowhead on the edge of Pittsfield in the 1850s and, the story goes, looked out at Greylock's long back while writing Moby-Dick, seeing a whale in the ridge. Whether or not it is true, the profile of the mountain does look like something large rising from a green sea. The Berkshires also became a summer playground for rich New Yorkers in the Gilded Age, and the music, theatre and dance at Tanglewood and Jacob's Pillow carry on that heritage.

Autumn is the headline season here, and justifiably. Late September into October the maples go red and orange, and the roads fill with leaf-peepers, which means slow cars and cautious corners. Midweek mornings are the answer. Spring is muddy and quiet, summer is warm and humid with afternoon thunderstorms, and winter closes the high roads.

Come to Pittsfield for a proper lunch and a full tank, then spend the rest of the day on the hills around it.
t.lenox@42.4,-73.3:
Lenox is a small town with a famous summer name. Tucked into the hills of the southern Berkshires, it grew in the nineteenth century into the place wealthy New Yorkers and Bostonians went to build enormous summer cottages, which they called cottages with a straight face. Edith Wharton built The Mount here in 1902, and wrote some of her best-known work while living on that hilltop. The big estates are mostly schools, inns and arts venues now, and the village centre is neat, white-steepled and a bit self-conscious, which is part of the charm.

Tanglewood, the summer home of the Boston Symphony Orchestra, is in Lenox, and on concert weekends the town fills with picnickers and the roads fill with cars. If you ride through between early July and the end of August, expect slow traffic around the evening hours and a hunt for parking. Otherwise this is quiet country. The roads out of town toward Lee, Stockbridge and West Stockbridge are the type that reward a loose schedule: gentle ups and downs, stone walls, hardwood forest crowding the shoulder, and little pull-offs by ponds and streams. The state forests nearby, October Mountain being the largest in Massachusetts, give you the sense of how big the woods really are. October Mountain is a forest of hemlock and hardwood that was once an estate belonging to a wealthy family before the state took it over.

Lenox itself has just under two thousand permanent residents, and the services are in keeping: a few cafes and restaurants, a handful of inns, and groceries, but for serious fuel and bigger shops, Pittsfield is ten minutes north and has everything. Lee, a little south, also has fuel and sits right by the Massachusetts Turnpike exit, which makes it a handy stop.

The riding season is long enough that it matters when you go. Summer brings the festival crowds and warm, humid air that smells of cut grass. Early autumn is the best of it, with cool mornings, mist in the valleys and the foliage building toward its peak. Spring has mud, frost heaves and the chance of a cold snap. If you can, take the back roads in the late afternoon, when the low light pushes through the trees and picks out the stone walls one by one.
t.new salem@42.5,-72.3:
New Salem is a hill town in the old sense: a scatter of farms and old houses strung along a ridge in the north-central part of Massachusetts, with no real centre and not much commerce. It sits just above the western shore of the Quabbin Reservoir, which is the thing that explains the landscape. In the 1930s the state flooded the Swift River valley to give Boston its water, and four towns, Dana, Enfield, Greenwich and Prescott, were disincorporated and cleared out. The reservoir that resulted is huge, roughly eighteen miles long, and the forest that surrounds it has been left to grow back with very little interference.

Why does that matter on a bike? Because this is some of the quietest, least developed country in the eastern half of the state. The roads wind through woods and across open fields, and traffic is light even on a summer Saturday. The surface can be patchy, with frost heaves, and the corners are the sort that appear around a stand of birch with no warning, so keep the pace honest. Route 202 and Route 122 give you the main axes, and the smaller roads such as the ones near the Quabbin gates bring you close to the water. Entry to the Quabbin reservation is by foot or bicycle at the gates, not by motor vehicle, so the water mostly stays out of reach from the saddle.

Nature has done well out of the flooding. Bald eagles were reintroduced around the Quabbin in the 1980s and have been nesting since, and the forests shelter deer, moose, bears and coyotes, so dusk is a time to be watchful. The air smells of leaf litter and woodsmoke in autumn, and the light on the water on a clear morning is worth waiting for.

Do not expect services here. Orange, the nearest larger town, has fuel and some food, and Athol up the road is bigger still, with more choice. Pack water if the day is hot, and treat New Salem as a stretch of road for thinking rather than for stopping. The old common with its white meetinghouse is the one place to pause, for the quiet and the view across a field that still looks very much as it did a century ago.
t.ashfield@42.5,-72.8:
Ashfield is the sort of Massachusetts hill town where the main street has a general store, a library, a town hall and a lake, and little else, and nobody sees a problem with that. It sits in the Hilltowns west of the Connecticut River, in the rolling country of Franklin County, with the Pioneer Valley down to the east and the Berkshires beginning to stack up to the west. About eighteen hundred people live here, and most of the road network around them is wooded, twisting and quiet.

Route 116 and Route 112 run through, and the smaller roads between Ashfield, Conway, Buckland and Plainfield are the reason to be here. They climb and fall in short bursts, pass through sugar maple woods and open hay fields, and cross small rivers where the water runs fast over pale rock. The surface varies, so expect patched tar and the occasional frost heave. The classic season here is autumn, when the maples go bright and the farm stands put out pumpkins and cider, but a morning in late spring, when the woods are green but the roads are still empty, may be even better.

The town has an interesting past. It was settled in the 1700s, and farming and small mills shaped its early life. Ashfield Lake, a spring-fed pond on the edge of town, is a popular local swimming place. The town is also known for a few local institutions, including Sanderson Academy, a historic school, and the Ashfield Fair held in late summer. Elsewhere in the region you will find the sugarhouses that make maple syrup in March, when the sap runs on cold nights and warm days. The scent of boiling sap is something you will not forget if you catch it on a spring ride.

For practicalities, remember that this is a small town. The general store is the heart of things, good for a sandwich and coffee, but you should not plan on fuel in the village itself. Greenfield, about seventeen kilometres away, has the nearest larger set of stations and supermarkets, and it is wise to fill up there before heading into the hills. Cell coverage can be patchy in the valleys, so a paper map or an offline one is useful. Watch for deer at dawn and dusk, and for slow tractors at any hour.
t.sagamore@41.8,-70.5:
Sagamore sits at the western end of the Cape Cod Canal, right where the mainland ends and the Cape begins, and it is a place that exists mostly because of a ditch. The canal, dug between 1909 and 1914 and later taken over by the federal government, cuts through the neck of land to give ships a shortcut and spare them the long, dangerous trip around the Cape's outer shore. Today it is a deep tidal channel about seventeen miles long, and the two big arched bridges, the Sagamore and the Bourne, are its landmarks. Sagamore Bridge, which carries Route 6 over to the Cape, is the one most travellers know, mostly from sitting in traffic on it.

For a rider, the interest is in the approach and the water. Service roads run along both banks of the canal, and the bike path alongside is busy with cyclists and walkers. From the road you can watch container ships, tugs and little fishing boats slide through, and on a summer afternoon watch the tidal current race by. The Sagamore Bridge itself is a steep arch with narrow lanes, and the wind can come across it hard, so stay alert on a lightweight bike. Summer weekends can bring grim traffic on the approaches in both directions; a Friday afternoon headed onto the Cape, or a Sunday evening coming off, is the time to be anywhere else.

Sandwich, just across, is the oldest town on the Cape, settled in 1637, and has the sort of harbour, old mill and glassmaking history that make it worth a slow walk. The Sandwich Glass Museum remembers the nineteenth century factory that made the town famous. The pleasure of the Cape Cod Canal area is that it can be tackled in an hour or in an afternoon.

Services are plentiful, because this is a gateway. Fuel is easy to find around the canal on both sides, and Sandwich and Bourne have places to eat. Mashpee, to the south, is larger, with more shops. Pitch-pine and oak woods line the roads here, and the air is cool and salty even when the day is hot. Evening light on the water, with ships coming through lit up, is the quiet reward for anyone who stays.
t.patapampa pass@-15.7,-71.5:
Patapampa is the high point of the road between Arequipa and the Colca valley, at 4,910 metres, and it is one of the highest passes in Peru that you can reach on a paved road. The landscape is a bare, windswept plateau of tawny grass and volcanic rock, with a ring of snow-capped volcanoes standing around it. Ampato and Sabancaya are among them, and Sabancaya is active, sometimes sending a plume of ash into the sky. It is a lonely, startling place, and the thin air makes it feel as if you are standing on the roof of the world.

At the pass, travellers have built apachetas, small piles of stones, each placed as an offering to the mountain spirits, the apus, in the Andean tradition. Add your own stone, and ask for safe passage. A few stalls sell souvenirs and hot coca tea, which helps with the altitude. Vicuñas, the wild, slender relatives of the llama, graze on the plateau, and you may see them in small groups, golden in the sun. They were nearly hunted to extinction for their wool, which is the finest in the world, and they have recovered under protection. The reserve here, known as Salinas and Aguada Blanca, covers a huge area of high steppe.

The road to the pass climbs from Arequipa, at about 2,300 metres, over a long, steady ascent, and the change in the landscape is dramatic, from desert to high steppe. The bends are long and open, the surface is good, and the road is wide, but at this altitude the engine struggles, and the air is thin. The danger is the altitude and the weather. Cold, wind and sudden snow are common, and you should have warm clothing, gloves and a waterproof. Altitude sickness is a risk, so spend a day or two in Arequipa or Chivay first, drink water and do not stay long at the top.

Arequipa has plenty, and Chivay, on the far side, has stations, shops and restaurants. Fill the tank in Arequipa and carry a reserve if you can. Morning is the best time to be here, when the sky is clear and the volcanoes stand sharp against the blue. A cup of coca tea and a few minutes at the cairns are all you need.
t.cruz del condor@-15.6,-71.9:
The Cruz del Cóndor is a viewpoint on the rim of the Colca Canyon, one of the deepest canyons in the world, which reaches more than three thousand metres at its deepest, with the river more than a kilometre below the rail, and it is the best place in Peru to see the Andean condor in flight. The birds, with wingspans of up to three metres, rise on the warm air currents that build as the sun heats the canyon walls, usually between about eight and ten in the morning. They glide past at eye level, often only a few metres from the rail, and the silence of their flight is eerie. Arrive early, since the show is over by late morning, and the crowd of visitors is smaller if you are there at first light.

The canyon is also a landscape shaped by people. Terraces, built before the Incas, step down the slopes, and the villages, with their churches and fields, preserve the traditions of the Collagua and Cabana peoples, who still wear embroidered hats and clothing. The Colca river runs at the bottom, a thin line of white water, and the walls are a patchwork of green terraces and brown rock. The sky is large, the air thin and the sun fierce, and a cold wind blows in the morning.

The ride along the canyon is a fine one, though it has its challenges. The road from Chivay follows the canyon rim through villages, with bends, bumps, and a mix of paved and gravel sections. Altitude is the main issue, since Chivay sits at about 3,600 metres, and the viewpoint is higher still, so give yourself time to adjust, and do not hurry. Keep an eye on the weather, and carry warm clothing. Livestock and children may be on the road in the villages, so slow down.

Chivay, about an hour away, is the nearest town, with fuel, shops, restaurants and hot springs, and it is the best place to base yourself. Women in traditional dress sell handicrafts and snacks near the rail, and a small tip for a photograph is customary. Respect the birds by staying behind the barriers and keeping quiet, and the condors may give you a show you will not forget.
t.kancamagus pass@44.0,-71.5:
Locals call it the Kanc, and every autumn it carries a procession of cars, bikes and cameras through the White Mountains of New Hampshire to see the leaves. The highway, New Hampshire 112, runs thirty-four miles between Conway and Lincoln, and the high point, Kancamagus Pass at 2,855 feet, sits in the middle of the national forest, with spruce and birch forest around it and an overlook looking out over the ridges. It is not a dramatic height, but the effect, rolling green mountains stacked to the horizon, is one of the finest in the eastern United States.

The name remembers Kancamagus, a sachem of the Penacook people in the late seventeenth century, who tried to keep peace between his people and the English settlers before conflict forced him to lead them north. The road itself is modern, finished in the 1960s, and cuts through country that was heavily logged in the nineteenth century, when railroads carried timber out of the valleys. The forest has since recovered, protected as the White Mountain National Forest, and the road is now regarded as one of the best-known scenic drives in New England.

The riding is a real pleasure. The Kanc is smooth, well graded and full of gentle bends, with glimpses of rivers, rock slabs and waterfalls, and the climb to the pass is steady rather than steep. In summer it is cool and green; in autumn, around late September to mid-October, the maples blaze red and orange and traffic crawls, so weekdays and early mornings are far better. Moose wander near the road, especially at dawn and dusk, and a collision with one is serious, so watch the edges. Speed limits are enforced, and frost and ice can occur early in autumn and late in spring.

Facilities at the pass are limited to toilets and an overlook, and parking at trailheads and picnic areas along the route may require a fee or a pass.

At the overlook, take a moment to look at the sea of ridges. In autumn, it is one of the great views in the American east.
t.sabbaday falls@44.0,-71.4:
Sabbaday Falls is the waterfall you can reach in your riding boots. A short, well-made path leads from the roadside car park through hemlock and birch woods for about a third of a mile to a three-step cascade where the Sabbaday Brook squeezes through a narrow granite flume, drops in a series of pools and finishes in a green basin. The stone is smooth and pale, the water is clear and cold, and a bridge and platforms let you look down into the cleft without climbing over wet rock.

The name is old, and the story behind it is vague. One explanation is that early settlers surveying the area came to the falls on a Sunday, the Sabbath, and so gave it the name, though no one is entirely sure. What the geology shows is more certain. The brook has cut a gorge through a basalt dike, a vertical sheet of dark rock that cooled in a crack in the granite hundreds of millions of years ago, and the water has been working through it since the end of the ice age. The result is a compact flume with sharp walls and pools sculpted by swirling water.

The setting is the White Mountain National Forest, along the Kancamagus Highway, which makes it a classic stop on the ride. The road is smooth and gently winding, with the forest pressing close on both sides, and the car park here is easy to find, with toilets, picnic tables and a small fee area where a parking pass is required. In summer the woods are cool and green, and the sound of water is welcome after a warm ride. In autumn the leaves are brilliant and the car park fills early, so weekday mornings are best. After heavy rain the falls roar, and the path can be muddy.

Wildlife in the area includes moose, black bears, deer and many songbirds, and the smell of damp earth and conifers is a pleasure after the road. Take a moment to listen. The only sounds are water and wind in the trees.

The nearest larger town on the map is Moultonborough, but the practical choices are Conway and North Conway, with the towns of Tamworth and Albany nearer the road. Bring water, and wear shoes you can walk in.

Allow half an hour for the walk and the view. It is among the easiest and best short stops on the Kanc.
t.hairpin turn@42.7,-73.1:
The Hairpin Turn on the Mohawk Trail is exactly what it says, and it has been catching bikers' attention since the days of Model Ts. Route 2 climbs the western face of the Hoosac Range out of North Adams in a switchback so tight that the road seems to double back on itself, with a stone wall on the outside edge and a deep view over the town and the Hoosac Valley on the other. At the apex there is a small pull-off, a gift shop and a few restaurants, and a lookout where you can see for miles.

The Mohawk Trail was one of the first scenic highways in the United States, opened in 1914 and promoted to motorists as a way to see New England's hills. The name comes from an old path used by Native peoples, including the Mohawk, to cross the mountains between the Connecticut and Hudson valleys, and the road follows it in places. The route soon became a destination for early motorists, and the hairpin was a showpiece, a place for photographs and thrills. Today it is a popular route for motorcyclists, especially in autumn.

The riding is a pleasure. The climb to the hairpin has good grip, a steady gradient and several tight bends, with a series of tight curves at the top, and the descent into North Adams is equally fun, though the road narrows and the speed limit drops near the town. Traffic is heavy on summer weekends and in leaf-peeping season, when slow-moving cars, tour buses and trucks fill the road, and the shoulder is narrow in places, so patience and care are essential. Early morning gives the best chance of an open road and clear views.

Fall colour is the main attraction, with the maples and birches turning red, orange and gold from late September to mid-October, and the hills around look like patchwork. Mount Greylock, the highest peak in Massachusetts, rises to the south. Weather changes fast, with fog and rain on the summit, and cold early mornings in autumn, so dress warmly.

North Adams, about four kilometres below, has petrol stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and it is also home to a large contemporary art museum in a converted mill. The gift shops at the hairpin sell maple syrup, local crafts and souvenirs, and there is usually somewhere to buy coffee and a doughnut.

Pause at the lookout before you head down. The valley is a picture, and the road is better with the view fresh in your mind.
t.kaaterskill high road@42.2,-74.1:
The Catskills were not always a weekend escape from New York City. In the early nineteenth century, they were the wild backdrop for American landscape painting, and the painters of the Hudson River School, led by Thomas Cole, came here to capture the cliffs, clouds and waterfalls. Kaaterskill Falls, a two-tier cascade of about 260 feet near the top of the clove, was one of their favourite subjects, and it is among the tallest falls in the state. The area also gave Washington Irving his Rip Van Winkle, the man who slept for twenty years on a mountain, and local lore insists that the legend is rooted in these hills.

The road through Kaaterskill Clove, Route 23A, climbs steeply from Palenville, with tight bends and a narrow, shaded corridor between rock walls. It is a classic piece of eastern American mountain riding, with moderate traffic and a few sharp hairpins where trucks are restricted. The surface can be rough, with frost heave and patches, and it can be wet and slick in shade. Water runs down the rocks after rain, and in winter ice can stay on the road long after it has cleared elsewhere.

At the top, the road opens onto the high country, with farms, small inns and views across the valley. Above the clove once stood the Catskill Mountain House, a grand hotel opened in 1824, which hosted travellers who came to see the sunrise from the escarpment. It was demolished in 1963, but the site is now part of a park with views over the Hudson valley and, on clear days, to the Berkshires and the Green Mountains.

Fuel is not on the mountain road. Hudson, a town of about six thousand people on the river, is the nearest large settlement, and smaller villages such as Palenville and Cairo have limited services. Plan to fill up before you start. Food and coffee are available in Tannersville and Hunter, a short ride up the road, where small cafés and delis serve walkers and skiers.

Autumn is the best season, when the maple and beech leaves turn red and gold, but it is also the busiest, so weekends can be crowded. Early morning on a weekday gives you the road to yourself, with mist in the clove and the sound of water over stone.
t.hunter mountain edge@42.2,-74.2:
Hunter Mountain is the second highest peak in the Catskills, at about 1,230 metres, and it dominates the skyline for miles around. In winter it is a ski resort, with trails cut into the slopes, and in summer its fire tower on the summit offers a wide view across the range. The mountain stands at the edge of the Catskill escarpment, where the high plateau drops sharply to the Hudson valley, and the road that skirts it follows this edge for much of its length.

The riding here is a mix of climbing and long, smooth sweeps. Route 23A passes through the village of Hunter, a small mountain town of lodges and shops, and continues along the slope with bends that open to views of the valley and the neighbouring peaks. The surface is generally good, with a wide shoulder in places, and traffic is moderate, though ski season and summer weekends bring crowds. In winter, the road can be icy, and snow can arrive early or linger late, so check the weather before you go.

The geology is the key to the view. The Catskills are not true mountains in the sense of folded ranges but the dissected edge of an ancient plateau, carved by streams into steep valleys called cloves. That is why the summits are at similar heights, and why the escarpment drops so abruptly. The forests are mostly hardwood, with sugar maple, beech and birch, and hemlock in the shaded hollows. Black bears live in these woods, and deer cross the road at dawn and dusk, so ride carefully in the low light.

For practical needs, Hudson is the nearest town of size, though it is some distance away, and Palenville and Cairo have a few shops. The village of Hunter has cafés, a general store and fuel, but hours may be limited outside the ski and summer seasons, so it is wise to start with a full tank. In winter, the village feels like a ski town, with warm lodges and the smell of woodsmoke.

If you stop at the edge, look for pull-offs where the view opens across the valley. On a clear day, you can see the Hudson River as a pale line and the hills of Massachusetts beyond. In autumn, the colour of the maples is intense, and the air is crisp and clean.
t.phoenicia@42.1,-74.3:
Phoenicia is a small hamlet in the Esopus valley, a few streets of wooden buildings along the creek with mountains on every side. It has the relaxed feel of a place that welcomes hikers, tubers and weekend visitors from the city without losing its character. The Esopus Creek, which runs through the village, is a popular spot for tubing in summer, when people float down the shallow rapids in inner tubes, and for fly fishing in cooler months. The surrounding hills are part of the Catskill Park, a vast area of protected forest.

The valley has played a quiet role in the history of New York. Not far downstream, the Ashokan Reservoir was built in the early twentieth century to supply water to the city, flooding several villages and reshaping the landscape. The water that flows from the Catskills still provides a large share of New York's drinking water, and the reservoir has a long walking path with views of the mountains. The nearby town of Woodstock, famous for its arts community, lent its name to the 1969 festival, though the event itself was held in Bethel, some distance away.

For riders, the approach to Phoenicia along Route 28 is a pleasant, flowing road that follows the Esopus through woods and meadows, with moderate bends and a good surface. It is less demanding than the climbs over the high roads, and a good place to relax after the mountain sections. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, with tubers, cyclists and day-trippers, so keep to a steady pace. In autumn, the leaves along the valley are spectacular, and mist often lies on the creek in the morning.

Food is the draw. The main street has a handful of cafés, delis and restaurants that cater to both locals and visitors, and a bakery or diner is a good place to start the day. Prices are moderate, and the portions tend to be large. There is a small railway museum at the old station, and heritage trains sometimes run on the line in season.

Fuel can be limited in the hamlet, so it is better to fill up in Woodstock or Kingston. The nearest town of any size is Marbletown, some distance away, so plan ahead. If you are planning a long day, take a moment to sit by the creek and listen to the water, and let the day settle.
t.guasca@4.9,-73.9:
Guasca sits at twenty-seven hundred metres in the Andes east of Bogotá, in the cold, green country that leads up to the páramo, the high moorland that Colombians treat with a kind of reverence. The town is small, with a square, a church and a scattering of cafes and shops, and the surrounding land is dairy farms, strawberry fields and potato plots, with eucalyptus and pines on the ridges. It feels a long way from the capital, though the capital is only an hour or so away.

The riding here is one of the real pleasures of the Bogotá region. The roads wind through the hills in long, rolling bends, with good views over valleys that drop away in layers of green. The surface varies, and the potholes, landslide repairs and sudden patches of gravel are a reminder that you are in the mountains, but the pace is easy, and traffic is light during the week. On weekends, cyclists and city riders come out in large numbers, so you will share the lanes with plenty of company. The weather can change quickly, with sunshine at breakfast, cloud by midday and rain in the afternoon, so carry waterproofs whatever the morning looks like.

The district is close to places that belong to Colombia's earliest history. Lake Guatavita, a few kilometres away, is a round crater lake that the Muisca people held sacred, and the ritual in which a new chief covered himself in gold dust and floated out on a raft to make offerings to the water is the source of the legend of El Dorado. The Chingaza páramo beyond is a national park whose lakes and wetlands supply a large share of Bogotá's drinking water, with frailejones, the furry-leaved plants of the high Andes, growing in thick stands.

For fuel, Sopó, about eight kilometres away, is a larger town with a regular station, and it is also where the Alpina dairy company has its roots, so the cheese and yoghurt are good. Guasca has the basics, but it is wise to arrive with a decent tank. Local restaurants serve hearty food, from trout to soups with potatoes and corn, and the altitude means that a hot drink is welcome at any time of day. The dry season, December to March and July to August, is the best time to go.
t.quabbin park@42.3,-72.3:
Quabbin Reservoir is a drowned valley, and the quiet around it comes partly from that. When Boston needed more drinking water in the early twentieth century, the state dammed the Swift River in the middle of Massachusetts, and between the 1930s and the mid-1940s the water slowly rose over four towns, Dana, Enfield, Greenwich and Prescott, whose people had been moved out. Roads, houses and farms lie beneath the surface, and at certain gates you can still walk old, abandoned roads that run down to the water and disappear.

The reservoir is one of the largest in the country, and its shoreline, kept free of development to protect the water, has grown into some of the best woodland in southern New England. Forest covers the hills in oak, maple and pine, and the lack of people has allowed wildlife to flourish: bald eagles have been reintroduced and now nest here, loons call on the water, and deer, moose and even black bears are regular residents. The Quabbin is a place for quiet things, such as watching a hawk circle or listening to the wind in the pines.

The park area at the Winsor Dam, the southern end of the reservoir, has a road along the top of the dam and a tower on the hill above, from which you can see the whole expanse of water and the hills beyond, with Mount Monadnock sometimes visible on the distant skyline. The roads around it are short, well-surfaced and leisurely, with low speed limits that are strictly enforced, because this is a protected watershed and the rangers take it seriously. It is not a place for spirited riding, but for taking a break from it, and the roads that approach it through the Pioneer Valley and across the hills to the east are lovely in their own right.

There are rules: gates open at set times, pets and swimming are not allowed, and you must keep to the marked roads and trails. Belchertown, six kilometres away, and Ware, a bit further, have all the fuel and food you need, with small-town diners and cafes along Route 9. October is the finest month, when the foliage turns and the light is soft, and the road can be busy then on weekends. Go early.
t.northbridge@42.2,-71.6:
Northbridge is an old mill town on the Blackstone River, and the Blackstone is a bigger part of American history than its modest size suggests. The river drops about a hundred metres on its way from Worcester to Providence, and in the early nineteenth century that fall of water powered a string of textile mills that helped start the American Industrial Revolution. The canal built along it in 1828 carried goods and cotton between Worcester and the sea, and the valley is now a national historical park, strung with mill villages, locks, towpaths and old brick factories.

Whitinsville, the main village in Northbridge, grew up around the Whitin Machine Works, a firm that made textile machinery and sent it all over the world, and the Whitin family built much of the town, including large houses, a church and a community centre. Even now it has the feel of a company town that took itself seriously, with solid brick and stone and a well-kept main street. It is a population of about fourteen thousand, mostly residential, and it has plenty of places for coffee and lunch.

The riding around the valley is mellow and winding. Route 122 and the smaller roads climb over low, wooded hills, drop into the river valley and cross it on old bridges, with stone walls, farms and mill ponds on either side. The surface is mixed, with frost heave in spring and patched sections, and you should watch for sand in the corners and for the usual New England hazard of a narrow road with a blind brow. Upton State Forest lies a short way to the north-east, with quiet woodland roads that are lovely in the autumn.

The towpath along the river is now a trail for walkers and cyclists, and at several points in the valley you can stop to look at a lock or an old mill race. The industrial landscape, now softened by trees and water, has a quiet beauty that is easy to miss if you are in a hurry. Northbridge has plenty of fuel, with stations on the main roads, and Uxbridge and Upton, a few kilometres off, have more. The best months are May to October, with the leaves turning in the first weeks of October.
t.dover@42.2,-71.3:
Dover has a reputation for money, and a first look at its roads confirms it: long stone walls, tall oak trees and big, discreet houses set well back from the road. It is one of the more rural towns in the Boston area, with no real town centre, no streetlights to speak of and a strong tradition of preserving open land. It is also one of the best places to ride a motorcycle within half an hour of the city, because it has the kind of roads that developers have not yet got around to improving.

The Charles River winds along its southern edge. It is a quiet, slow river here, one of those that seems to be running without much intention, with marshes, meadows and old maples on the banks, and by the time it reaches Boston, some eighty miles after its start in Hopkinton, it will have been dammed, channelled and landscaped. In Dover it is still more or less wild, and canoeists and herons share it. Noanet Woodlands, a large area of conserved forest on the edge of town, has trails through the woods past old mill ponds and the ruins of a nineteenth-century mill complex.

The roads, with names like Farm Street and Dedham Street, wander through the woods and fields in the tight, enjoyable way of roads that follow property lines and old cart paths. They are narrow, with bends and blind crests, and stone walls close on both sides, so there is little room for error. Locals walk and ride horses along them, so go gently and keep your eyes open. The surface is generally good, though it can be rough after the winter. In autumn, the leaves fall thick on the corners, and in spring, frost heave can break the edges.

Dover has little in the way of commercial life, so you will not find fuel in the town itself, and that is the reason to prepare. Wellesley and Needham, six kilometres away, are both substantial suburbs with a full range of services, cafes and restaurants. Fill up there, take a coffee and a pastry, and then go back into the lanes. The best time is a weekday morning in May or October, when the light is soft and the roads are quiet.
t.sherborn@42.2,-71.4:
Sherborn is a very small town with a very old pedigree. It was settled in the 1650s, incorporated in 1674, and it was only a few years old when it was caught up in King Philip's War, the vicious conflict between New England colonists and the Native peoples that devastated frontier towns in 1675 and 1676. The scars of that time are gone from the landscape, but the town still has the compact, thoughtful air of a place that has been looking after itself for a long time, with a green, a library and a few white houses around the meeting place.

Next door lies Natick, and the two together tell a bigger story. In 1651 the minister John Eliot founded a community at Natick for Native Americans who had converted to Christianity, one of the so-called praying towns, and there he translated the Bible into the Massachusett language. It was printed in Cambridge in 1663, and is regarded as the first complete Bible printed in North America. The story is not a simple one, since the praying towns were disrupted and the people were later interned during the war, but it is a vivid reminder that this quiet country has a layered past.

The riding here is relaxed and rural. The roads wind through woods and across meadows, past stone walls, old orchards and farm stands, and the Charles River slides under a few of the bridges. There is little traffic during the week, and the speed limits are low, so the pace is leisurely. The hazards are cyclists, horse riders and dog walkers, and sand and leaves on the corners. Everything is shaded in summer, which keeps the road cool and sometimes damp.

Sherborn has few services and no real commercial strip. Natick and Framingham, both about five or six kilometres away, are the places to fill up and eat, and they have everything from diners to chain restaurants. Natick Center has a pleasant old square, and the Framingham side has a few good places for breakfast. A quiet weekend morning in October, with mist on the river and leaves on the road, is a good time for this ride.
t.wachusett mountain@42.5,-71.9:
Wachusett is the mountain you see from half of central Massachusetts, and it earns the attention by standing alone. Rising to about six hundred metres out of rolling, wooded country, it is a monadnock, a single resistant mass of old rock left standing when the land around it wore down, and its name comes from an Algonquian phrase usually translated as near the mountain. In the summer of 1842 Henry David Thoreau walked here from Concord, and his essay on the trip, A Walk to Wachusett, still reads like the work of a man who loved a day out.

A paved road climbs to the summit, and it is one of the few places in the eastern part of the state where you can ride to the top of something. It switches back through oak and maple, then through spruce and fir near the top, and its tight bends and steep pitches demand slow, careful riding, with a barrier-free edge in places and leaf litter in the corners. It is closed in winter and during bad weather, and sometimes on busy days, so check before you set out. At the top, a clearing with a fire tower gives a view east toward the Boston skyline on a clear day and north to the peaks of southern New Hampshire.

The mountain is also a hawk watch. In September and October, thousands of raptors ride the thermals along the ridge on their way south, and watchers gather with binoculars to count broad-winged hawks, kestrels and the occasional eagle. In winter the slopes belong to skiers, and the ski area is one of the busiest in the state for its size. The whole thing is a protected state reservation, with a network of trails running through mature forest, and a few small ponds and meadows.

Princeton, about five kilometres away, is the village at the foot, a rural town with a pretty common and a handful of shops, but fuel is better done in Westminster, seven kilometres off, where there are stations and diners along Route 2A. Weekends in October are packed, so the best time is a weekday morning, when the air is crisp, the car park is half empty and the leaves are just turning.
t.westminster@42.5,-71.9:
Westminster is a hill town with a long main road and a short memory for fuss. It sits on the high ground of north-central Massachusetts, at the foot of Wachusett Mountain, and its villages, ponds and hills have the particular New England look of a place that was farmed hard in the 1800s and has been quietly returning to woodland since. About seven thousand people live here, and the town has a proper common with a white meeting house and a library, as well as a handful of places to eat along Route 2A.

In the nineteenth century, the town and its neighbour Gardner made furniture, chairs especially, and Gardner still calls itself the Chair City, with a giant wooden chair to prove it. Westminster was less industrial and more agricultural, and the old farms, stone walls and sugar maples still shape the countryside. Nearby, the Wachusett Reservoir stores water for Boston, and the land around it is protected, so there are large areas of woodland and clean water that have escaped development. A local brewery has made a name beyond the district, and a ski area on the slopes of the mountain pulls in a crowd in winter.

For a rider, the town is a handy junction. Route 2, the long highway that becomes the Mohawk Trail farther west, runs fast and straight across the north of the town, and from it, the slower Route 140 and the back roads climb into the hills and wind down toward the lakes and farms. The roads are modest in scale but enjoyable, with moderate gradients and long, easy bends through the woods. Frost heave in spring can make the surface rough, and there is a lot of leaf litter in the autumn. Tractors and school buses are the usual obstacles.

It makes a good place to stop in the middle of a loop, for fuel, a meal and a bit of rest. t.clinton@42.4,-71.7:

t.plum island@42.8,-70.8:

t.ipswich@42.7,-70.8:

t.searsburg@42.9,-73.0:

t.wilmington@42.9,-72.9:

t.west dover@42.9,-72.8:

t.winchester@42.5,-71.1:

t.westborough@42.3,-71.6:

t.northborough@42.3,-71.6:

t.west barnstable@41.7,-70.4:

t.annisquam@42.7,-70.7:

t.pigeon cove@42.7,-70.6:

t.beverly@42.6,-70.9:

t.magnolia@42.6,-70.7:

t.sharon@41.9,-73.5:

t.smugglers notch@44.5,-72.8:

t.williamstown@42.7,-73.2:

t.adirondack@41.0,-74.3:

t.lincoln new hampshire@44.0,-71.7:
Lincoln is a mountain town that plays the role of ski village in winter and gateway in summer. t.tarrytown croton@40.7,-73.6:
Garden City and Hempstead sit on Long Island's flat middle, far from the Croton reservoirs, in what was once a huge natural prairie called the Hempstead Plains. t.berkshires mohawk@40.6,-74.2:
Carteret sits on the shore of the Arthur Kill, the tidal strait that separates New Jersey from Staten Island, and it will not win any beauty contests. t.catskills@40.9,-73.8:

t.vermont green@40.6,-74.3:

t.jersey highlands@40.7,-74.4:
This is the Watchung country, a pair of long, curved ridges that rise suddenly from the flat suburbs of central New Jersey and give the area a surprisingly hilly character. The coordinates sit near Mountainside, Scotch Plains and New Providence, in the folds of the First and Second Watchung Mountains, which lie in sweeping arcs across several counties.

The ridges are made of basalt, the dark rock of ancient lava flows that poured out roughly two hundred million years ago when the supercontinent began to break apart and the Atlantic Ocean began to open. The lava cooled into hard layers that resisted erosion better than the softer red sandstone around them, so the hills stand as long, forested walls. In several places the rock forms small cliffs and waterfalls.

George Washington's army camped behind them for long periods, and from a lookout known as Washington Rock the general could see British troop movements across the plain toward New York. This is the easiest ground of the whole ride, and you can pause here without any difficulty.

t.north@40.9,-74.4:

t.brattleboro@42.9,-72.6:

t.hudson highlands@40.8,-73.6:
Long Island's north shore is a landscape of old money laid over rolling glacial hills, and these coordinates sit in the middle of it, near Albertson and Roslyn Heights in Nassau County. t.salem@42.5,-70.9:
Say Salem to an American and the answer is 1692. That year, in the grip of fear and bitter local feuds, a court in this small Massachusetts seaport condemned nineteen people to hang for witchcraft, and another man, Giles Corey, was pressed to death under stones for refusing to plead. The trials ended within a year, and in the decades afterwards the colony openly regretted them. Today the town leans into the story with witch museums, costumed guides and shops selling crystals, and in October it fills with so many visitors that the streets nearly seize up.

Look beyond the witches and Salem has a quieter and, to my mind, richer story. In the decades after independence it was one of the wealthiest ports in the young United States, with ships sailing to Sumatra, India and China, and merchants built handsome Federal-style houses along Chestnut Street that still make an elegant walk. Derby Wharf, now a national historic site, stretches into the harbour with a little lighthouse at its end, and the Peabody Essex Museum holds a big collection of Asian and maritime art that grew out of those voyages. Nathaniel Hawthorne was born here, worked in the old Custom House and set The House of the Seven Gables in a creaky, dark-timbered mansion that you can visit.

The streets of the old centre are narrow and one-way, parking is a puzzle, and in October you should treat a weekend visit as a test of patience, with the traffic crawling in from Route 128. Weekday mornings and the off-season months are far kinder. The coast roads that lead from here, Route 127 and Route 1A, wander through Marblehead and Beverly toward Cape Ann, with stone walls, salt marsh and a sudden view of masts in a harbour.

Marblehead, a few minutes south, is a tight knot of old lanes around a yacht-crowded harbour and is worth the detour for the sea air alone. Fuel is easy in Salem and Peabody, and there is no shortage of chowder, fried clams, lobster rolls and bakeries; an old Salem candy shop sells the Gibraltar, a hard, ginger-flavoured sweet that dates back to the early nineteenth century and is more of an acquired taste than a treat. t.greenfield@42.6,-72.6:
Greenfield sits where the Green River slides into the Deerfield, a short way above the wide Connecticut, in a part of western Massachusetts where valley farmland gives way to steep, wooded hills. It is a practical, brick-fronted town of about twenty thousand, a county seat that has weathered the decline of its old cutlery and tool factories and found a second wind with farmers' markets, small breweries and a lively main street. Early on a weekday in September is better.

Shelburne Falls has the Bridge of Flowers, an old trolley bridge planted with gardens, and downstream the river has scoured glacial potholes into the rock, great round bowls ground out by stones swirling in meltwater at the end of the ice age. t.great barrington@42.2,-73.4:
Great Barrington is the southern doorway to the Berkshires, a town of low brick buildings on the Housatonic River with a tall church steeple, a cluster of galleries and cafés, and mountains close on all sides. Its permanent population is small, but weekenders from New York and Boston swell it every summer and autumn, so that restaurants fill and the main street hums. The Berkshires themselves are not high, a worn-down range of old rounded hills, but they have a quiet grandeur, especially when mist hangs in the valleys at dawn.

The town has some unexpected distinctions. William Stanley tested an early alternating-current electrical system here in 1886, and Great Barrington is often said to have been among the first places in the United States lit by electricity in this way. W. E. B. Du Bois, the sociologist and civil rights leader, was born here in 1868, and a memorial park on the site of his boyhood home recalls him. Monument Mountain, just north, is a short, steep hike with a great view, and it is where Herman Melville and Nathaniel Hawthorne met on a picnic in 1850, a moment that is said to have helped shape Moby-Dick. Shorter walks lead to waterfalls tucked into the hills.

t.belchertown@42.3,-72.4:
Belchertown is a small town of green commons and white clapboard houses, and its unusual claim is that it sits beside a lake that was made by erasing four towns. The Quabbin Reservoir, to the north and east, was created in the 1930s to supply drinking water to Boston, a hundred kilometres away. To build it, the state cleared the Swift River valley of its people. The towns of Dana, Enfield, Greenwich and Prescott were disincorporated, roughly twenty-five hundred people were relocated, houses were moved or demolished, and cemeteries were dug up and reburied elsewhere. The valley was filled over several years, and the reservoir became one of the biggest man-made water supplies in the United States.

The result is a strange and beautiful wilderness. The land around the reservoir has been protected for nearly ninety years, and without development it has grown back into dense forest. Bald eagles, reintroduced to Massachusetts in the 1980s, now nest here, and moose and coyotes roam the woods. Visitors are limited to certain gates and paths, mostly on foot or bike, and there is a rule against swimming or fishing from the bank. A tower at the park headquarters gives a long view over the water and the forested islands, which are former hilltops.

The reservoir's edge cannot be followed closely, because much of the shoreline is closed to vehicles, so you ride the rim in pieces, on Routes 9, 202, 32 and the local roads. Frost heaves, patched asphalt and deer are your hazards, with the deer especially active at dusk.

Belchertown has fuel, a few small cafés and a pretty central green, and the nearby town of Ware has a larger choice of shops. The best seasons are late spring, when the woods turn bright green, and early autumn, when the maples colour and the reservoir looks dark blue under the clear sky.
t.northampton@42.3,-72.6:
Northampton is the cultural heart of the Pioneer Valley, a college town with an unusually busy centre for a place of twenty-eight thousand. Jonathan Edwards, the preacher who helped set off the Great Awakening, held forth in a church here in the 1730s, and Calvin Coolidge arrived as a young lawyer, served as mayor, and went on to become president. t.plymouth@42.0,-70.7:
Plymouth is a place where history is both obvious and slightly overstated, and it is better for knowing that in advance. Gravel side roads lead to many of the sights and can be loose, so reduce your speed and tyre pressure if you go off the tar. Rain is frequent, and the surface can be greasy, and fog and wind are common on the coast. Livestock sometimes wander onto the road.

Owaka has a few shops and a place to eat, but services are limited. Fuel may be available in the village, though hours are short, so the sure bet is to arrive with a full tank from Balclutha, about thirty kilometres away, and check your range before heading deeper into the Catlins. Cafes and small stores are scattered along the coast, and some close early or in winter, so carry snacks and water.

The climate is cool and changeable, with strong winds, sudden showers and the occasional burst of warm sun. A good waterproof, warm layers and gloves are essential, even in summer. The forests, the sea and the sense of space make the Catlins a place where a slow pace is the only sensible approach.

t.narragansett@41.4,-71.4:
Narragansett is where Rhode Island's south coast stops being a drive and starts being a habit. The town sits on a knuckle of land between Narragansett Bay and the open Atlantic, and the ocean here is the real thing: long gray rollers that arrive from Spain with nothing in between. Ocean Road, Route 1A, hugs the shoreline past the seawall, Scarborough Beach and a string of big shingled summer houses, and on a calm morning it is as pleasant a start to a coast ride as New England offers.

The landmark everybody photographs is the Towers, a pair of stone arches that straddle the road. They are what survived of the Narragansett Pier Casino, a grand resort building designed by McKim, Mead and White in the 1880s that burned in 1900. The arches were left standing, which tells you something about how people here feel about a good ruin. Rhode Island's gilded-age summer crowd once came to this stretch of shore by steamer and train, and the town has been a beach town ever since, with surfers in wetsuits out past the wall even in autumn.

Go early on a summer weekend or choose September, when the water is still warm, the parking lots are half empty and the light has gone golden. South toward Point Judith the land flattens into salt marsh and fishing docks, and the Galilee harbor, where the Block Island ferries leave, is the place for clam cakes and a bowl of chowder. Rhode Island chowder is often clear-brothed, which surprises visitors who expect cream.

Narragansett itself is large enough to have fuel, coffee and everything else you need, and Wakefield-Peacedale a few minutes inland has more supermarkets and stations if you want a choice. The coordinates drop you into Hunterdon County, New Jersey, a long way south and west of the Hudson that the ride's name promises, in the folded farmland around Califon. This is the valley of the South Branch of the Raritan River, a trout stream that runs clear enough over its stones to keep fly fishermen loyal for generations. Califon itself is a tiny place, barely a thousand people, with an old railroad right-of-way now used as a rail trail and a main street you will cross before you notice it. Long Valley sits a few kilometres to the north, and the hills on its far side belong to Schooley's Mountain, the first stretch of real ridge you meet when riding in from the east.

The riding here is gentle and rhythmic rather than dramatic. County roads follow the river and then climb over low wooded saddles, with horse paddocks, stone farmhouses and the occasional covered view across the valley. Corners come in long, readable arcs, the surface is mostly decent but patched after hard winters, and speed limits are low and enforced by small-town police who have nothing better to do on a Sunday. Early morning is the best hour, when mist lies in the river bottoms and the few cyclists out are still warming up. Autumn turns the maples loud with colour, and mid-October weekends bring leaf-peepers who slow everything down.

Schooley's Mountain has a more surprising history than its quiet slopes suggest. In the nineteenth century people from New York and Philadelphia came here to take the mineral waters, and big wooden hotels sat along the ridge for the cool air and the cure. The hotels are gone, but the idea that this is a place to escape the city has not changed. Today the ridge is partly preserved as county and state parkland, and the woods hold white-tailed deer in numbers that make dusk riding a genuine hazard. Slow down when the light goes amber.

For practical matters, Califon and Long Valley are both small enough that you should not count on fuel or a late meal in the village itself. Hackettstown, about fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size and has stations, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat. Beattystown is closer but little more than a crossroads and a few houses. If you are using this point as a start or finish, a swim is possible in the river pools in summer, though the water is cold and the banks are private in places, so ask before you wade in.
