The coordinates land you in Fairfield County, Connecticut, on the quiet side of Newtown, well east of the Hudson. This corner of the state is a landscape of reservoirs, small rivers and stone walls, with the Housatonic River held in two long lakes behind dams at Lake Zoar and Lake Lillinonah. The ride that uses this point is billed as a Delaware Water Gap long day, and that lies a long way west, so treat this as a starting or finishing area for a much bigger loop through New York and New Jersey.

Newtown has the feel of a New England village that has been politely absorbed by commuters. A tall flagpole stands in the middle of Main Street, raised in the 1870s as a Civil War memorial, and white clapboard houses line the road on both sides. Easton, a little further south, is dominated by water, with the Aspetuck Reservoir and its surrounding woodland keeping the region leafy and the traffic light. Trumbull, much bigger, has fuel, food and the usual retail strip.

The roads here are not dramatic, but they are good fun for an easy morning. Route 25 and Route 58 undulate over low hills and through farm country, with tight little corners, blind crests and the odd dip where a brook crosses the road. The surface is patched and sometimes rough after winter. Deer are frequent, and so are cyclists. Near the coast the Merritt Parkway, a 1930s road famous for its Art Deco bridges and its landscaped verges, is a pleasure at a gentle pace, but trucks are banned and the limit is strictly kept, so do not expect to hurry.

You are about 11 kilometres from Easton, the nearest town with more than five thousand people, and you will find fuel there and in Trumbull. Smaller villages have a general store or a deli, but the night belongs to the commuter belt, and many places close early. A swim is possible at the lakes and reservoirs, though access is controlled and some of the beaches belong to residents. In late October, when the maples turn, the whole region is gloriously, almost theatrically, red and gold.

Central Valley is a small community in Orange County, New York, wedged between the Hudson Highlands and the New York State Thruway, and its claim to fame is that it sits beside Woodbury Common, one of the largest outlet shopping centres in the United States. On a weekend the shops draw tour buses from all over the region, and traffic backs up on the approach roads. Woodbury, the larger town about six kilometres away, has about eleven thousand people and plenty of fuel, supermarkets and diners.

Away from the mall, the land rises into the wooded hills of Harriman State Park, a huge protected area that covers more than forty thousand acres of rocky ridges, lakes and old forests. The park was created in the early twentieth century with land donated by the Harriman family, and it is a haven for hikers, with miles of trails crossing the Appalachian Trail. Its main road, the Seven Lakes Drive, winds through the hills with gentle, well-surfaced curves and lakes visible through the trees. It is a delightful ride, though cyclists and families fill it on warm weekends.

The nearby Hudson River, about ten miles east, runs through the Highlands in a deep, narrow valley, and Bear Mountain, with its summit tower, lies close at hand. Route 32 runs north from the area through the hamlet of Highland Mills toward Cornwall and Newburgh, a pleasant road with farms and ponds. Storm King Mountain rises above the river further north, and Route 218, a twisting road on its flank, has some of the most dramatic views on the Hudson.

For riders, the gateway is simple: the exit off the Thruway puts you minutes from the park. Early mornings are quiet, with mist in the valleys, while Saturdays and Sundays bring crowds. Fuel and food are straightforward, and the outlet complex offers coffee and plenty of fast food for those in a hurry. Autumn is the star season, when Harriman glows with colour, and winter closes some park roads. In spring, the redbuds bloom along the hillsides, and the streams run high and loud.

Like several of its neighbours, this point is not in the mountains. The coordinates land in Long Island Sound, off the Connecticut coast, in a scattering of small islands near Norwalk. The mainland behind it, East Norwalk and the harbour district, has a few thousand people and everything a rider needs. The Catskills, the name on the ride, lie roughly a hundred miles up the Hudson, so treat this as a start or a pause on the shore rather than a summit.

The Norwalk Islands are a group of some twenty-odd small islands, mostly low and wooded, strung across the mouth of the harbour. They are a haven for birds, with herons, egrets and ospreys nesting in season, and a refuge for seals in the winter. On Sheffield Island stands a lighthouse built in 1868, a stout stone building with a mansard roof that looks more like a country house than a beacon, and in summer a ferry takes visitors across for picnics. Norwalk was once a centre of the oyster industry, shipping millions of shellfish a year, and the tradition survives in a festival held every September.

Riding here is gentle and urban, a matter of picking your way through the busy, built-up shore of Fairfield County. The Merritt Parkway, built in the 1930s and lined with Art Deco bridges, each one different, is one of the loveliest roads in the Northeast, and a short hop from here; trucks are banned and the tree-lined curves reward a relaxed pace. Local roads along the shore are slow, with traffic lights and weekend crowds, and the surface is patchy in places after the winter frosts. Early mornings are best.

Fuel and food are no problem. East Norwalk and South Norwalk, known as SoNo, have a lively collection of restaurants and cafes, and the harbour area has fish places where you can eat with the boats in view. Norwalk has some eighty thousand people, and the mix of old industrial buildings and new apartments gives it a livelier feel than the quiet suburbs of the coast. Wind off the Sound can be cool even in summer, especially in the late afternoon. If you have time, walk the waterfront and look out at the islands, and notice how the tide changes the shore.
